docs.s: What SATOM is, which Fortinet appliances it manages, and the working principles behind every page of the console.

docs.x: SATOM ( System Automation & Task Orchestration Manager ) is a multi-user web console for operating a fleet of Fortinet application-delivery and analytics appliances from one place. Instead of signing in to every appliance and clicking through its own GUI, you register the appliances once and then browse, change, back up, upgrade and monitor them from SATOM. It covers five product families, each in its own workspace (called an ADOM , see ADOMs and products ): Product What SATOM does with it FortiWeb (web application firewall) Server policies, server objects, web protection profiles, exceptions

Audience Typical use Viewer Look at policies, health, metrics and backups without changing anything. Operator Day-to-day changes: policies, objects, exceptions, backups, upgrades inside an approved window. Administrator Users and profiles, settings, appliance registration, automations, the database and SATOM's own updates. Advanced user Engineers using the API, the Python console, Plugin Studio or Lua Studio. What each person can do is decided by their profile (a set of granular permissions). The three profiles shipped with SATOM are readonly , operator and admin ; administrators can compose o

docs.h: How SATOM works — the principles you will notice everywhere
It reads from its own copy first
docs.x: SATOM keeps a local, queryable copy of every appliance's configuration (filled by Rediscovery and Deep capture ). Most pages render from that copy, so they stay fast and usable even when an appliance is slow, unreachable or licence-locked. Pages that do this show how fresh the data is; when you need the current state of the box, use the page's refresh-from-device control.

docs.h: Changes are previewed before they are applied
docs.x: Writes to an appliance are prepared first and shown as a preview of what will be sent. Nothing reaches the appliance until you confirm. Applied changes are recorded in the Audit Log with before/after history.

docs.h: Long work runs as a job
docs.x: Backups, discoveries, bulk changes and firmware work run as background jobs . You can keep navigating while they run; a dock tracks their progress and the notifications bell tells you when they finish.

docs.h: Risky work goes through change control
docs.x: A firmware upgrade is bound to an approved change request and runs inside its maintenance window. Recurring housekeeping runs as scheduled actions .

Each ADOM only shows its own product's appliances, jobs, notifications and bookmarks. The Global ADOM shows everything. The ADOM is remembered per browser tab , so you can keep FortiWeb open in one tab and FortiADC in another.

docs.s: The moving parts of a SATOM installation — web console, background services, database, metrics store and the appliances it manages — and how they fit together.

docs.t: System overview — the components at a glance
docs.x: A SATOM installation is one Linux server (or a primary + standby pair) running a Flask web application, a handful of small background services, a PostgreSQL database and a metrics store. Operators reach it with a browser; SATOM reaches the appliances over their management APIs and SSH. Browser ──HTTPS──▶ nginx (TLS) ──▶ gunicorn: SATOM web console │ ├──▶ PostgreSQL (inventory, settings, audit, jobs index, SoT index …) ├──▶ data/ directory (SoT blobs, config-backup vault, runtime files) ├──▶ metrics store (VictoriaMetrics, local only) └──▶ appliances: REST / JSON-RPC and SSH FortiWeb · FortiADC

docs.t: System overview — the components at a glance
docs.x: SATOM does not install anything on the appliances. Each registered appliance is reached with the address, port and credentials stored on its Appliances entry (the password is stored encrypted): FortiWeb, FortiADC — REST API, plus SSH where the API cannot reach (for example CLI configuration dumps and configuration backups). FortiAuthenticator — REST API. FortiAnalyzer — JSON-RPC API. Which REST path to call for which firmware is not hard-coded: it is resolved through the endpoint registry (see API registry ).

docs.t: System overview — the components at a glance
docs.x: Topology What you get Standalone One node with a local PostgreSQL. Primary + standby PostgreSQL streaming replication to the standby, plus a data sync of the data/ directory from the primary. The standby is read-only; the scheduler only fires on the primary. The top bar shows PRIMARY or STANDBY on each node. See High availability for promotion and failover.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.x: Every person who uses SATOM signs in with their own account. The account is either local (the password is stored in SATOM) or external (the password is checked by a directory: Active Directory, LDAP or RADIUS). After signing in you land on the Global home and can adjust a few personal preferences on your Profile page.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.x: Signs you in with a username and password, optionally keeping you signed in ( Remember me ). Asks local accounts that enabled two-factor authentication for a 6-digit code (or a one-time backup code). Lets a local account with a recovery email reset a forgotten password by email. Protects accounts: 10 consecutive failed sign-ins lock the account for 15 minutes, and sign-in attempts are limited to 5 per minute. Stores your personal preferences in the database (not in a browser cookie): language, bookmark grouping order, top-bar banner per product, and — for administrators — whether the Calendar

First login, your profile and signing out
docs.x: Possible causes - Wrong username or password (passwords are case-sensitive). - A directory account while the directory is unreachable or rejects the bind. Solution 1. Retype the password using the eye icon to check it. 2. Directory users: confirm you can sign in to another directory-backed system. 3. Use Forgot password? (local accounts with a recovery email) or ask an administrator. Verification — the next attempt lands on the Global home.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.h: "Too many failed attempts — account temporarily locked. Try again later."
docs.x: Possible causes - 10 consecutive failed attempts on this account; it is locked for 15 minutes, whatever address the attempts come from. Solution 1. Wait 15 minutes, then sign in with the correct password. 2. If you suspect someone else is guessing, tell an administrator — lockouts are logged in the audit log ( login.lockout ). Verification — a successful sign-in clears the failure counter.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.h: HTTP 429 "Too Many Requests" when pressing Sign In
docs.x: Possible causes - More than 5 sign-in attempts per minute from your address. Solution — wait one minute and try again. Opening the sign-in page itself is not counted.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.h: "Your account was imported from the directory but is still awaiting administrator approval."
docs.x: Possible causes — the directory accepted your password, but new directory accounts need approval. Solution — ask an administrator to enable your account in Users and profiles .

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.x: Solution — an administrator must re-enable the account.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.x: Possible causes - The code expired while you typed, or the phone's clock is wrong. - A backup code that was already used. Solution 1. Wait for a new code and enter it promptly; check the phone's time is set automatically. 2. Use an unused backup code. After a backup code works, the page tells you how many are left: "Backup code accepted. N backup code(s) left." 3. Lost the device and all codes: an administrator must reset your 2FA.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.h: "Please log in to access this page."
docs.x: Possible causes — you opened a page without being signed in, or your session ended. Solution — sign in again; you are sent back to the page you asked for.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.h: "Your session was locked after N minutes of inactivity."
docs.x: Possible causes — nothing was done in this browser for longer than the Session Lock time (Settings → General). Background refreshes do not count as activity. Solution — sign in again; you return to the page you asked for. An administrator can change the time in Settings → General → Session Lock (minutes) (5–1440).

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.h: "Access denied — You don't have permission to view this page."
docs.x: Possible causes - Your profile lacks the permission the page requires. - Your address is not on the administrator's IP allow-list. Solution — ask an administrator to check your profile or the allow-list. See Permissions .

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.h: "That language is not offered on this installation."
docs.x: Possible causes — the administrator withdrew that language after your page was loaded. Solution — reload the Profile page and pick a language from the list. If your saved choice was withdrawn, it is shown as no longer offered here and kept for when it is switched back on.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.h: "Current password is incorrect." / "New passwords do not match."
docs.x: Solution — retype the current password exactly, and make sure New Password and Confirm New Password are identical.

docs.t: First login, your profile and signing out
docs.x: Advanced Account protection and sessions Every failed sign-in to a local account writes a login.fail audit entry (directory failures are logged as login.external_fail ). Lockout: 10 consecutive failures → locked for 15 minutes ( login.lockout audit entry; further attempts while locked are logged as login.locked_attempt ). A successful sign-in resets the counter. Rate limits: sign-in POST 5/minute, 2FA page 10/minute, forgot-password 5 per 15 minutes, reset link 10 per 15 minutes (per client address). Password reset links are signed tokens valid for one hour; directory accounts cannot use them.

docs.x: Brand — the SATOM mark and product title. Clicking it opens the home page of the current ADOM. ADOM: — the active administrative domain, colour-coded (Global blue, FortiWeb red, FortiADC green, FortiAuthenticator purple, FortiAnalyzer amber, FortiGate teal). docs.s: SATOM's six workspaces (Global, FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAuthenticator, FortiAnalyzer, FortiGate) — what each is for, how to switch between them, and how data is kept separate.

docs.x: An ADOM (administrative domain) is a workspace inside SATOM scoped to one product family, in the style of FortiManager ADOMs. Every ADOM shares the same look, but has its own sidebar menu, its own appliances, and its own jobs, notifications, bookmarks, templates and scheduled actions. ℹ️ Note In SATOM, ADOM means a SATOM workspace. A FortiWeb appliance can also have its own administrative domains; SATOM registers such an appliance once per appliance-side ADOM. The sidebar then shows ADOM: under the selected device. Do not confuse the two.

ADOM Home Purpose Global / One console over the whole fleet: dashboard, monitoring, search, Architecture and Service Diagram, fleet objects, jobs, certificates, and SATOM administration. See Global home . FortiWeb /web/ Web application firewall management: FortiWeb's own menu for the selected device (server policies, server objects, web protection, system settings …), the device-scoped WAF tools under Operations → WAF, backups, firmware. FortiADC /adc/ Application delivery: the appliance's own menu (load balancing, WAF, network security …), signatures and an API console. See FortiADC . FortiAu

docs.h: What a device ADOM's sidebar holds
docs.x: Each device ADOM draws the device's own menu , built from the GUI layouts measured on the selected device's firmware build, inside the same SATOM groups in every ADOM: ‹ Global , Device , Operations (the fleet pages first, then the backup entries), the device menu, Automation (with the API console as a sub-menu), Administrator and Plugins . An entry whose page does not work for that product is greyed out and says why on hover. The Global ADOM has no device menu; it draws the Global block, ADOMs , Automation and Administrator . See Navigation for every group and entry.

docs.h: The ADOM is per browser tab
docs.x: Each browser tab remembers its own ADOM. You can work in FortiWeb in one tab and FortiADC in another; switching in one tab does not change the other. A new tab, or a page opened by typing its address, starts in the ADOM you switched to most recently.

If you can see exactly one appliance in an ADOM, it is used without asking.

Possible causes — you tried to register an appliance of another product while inside a product ADOM. Solution — switch to that product's ADOM (or Global) and add it there.

Only explicit switches (the chooser, the ADOM links, / and /web/ ) change the session default; ordinary navigation never does. Infrastructure health — the state of the SATOM installation itself: the HA nodes (role, CPU, memory, disk), the Git repository and the backup server. ADOM cards — one card per active product ADOM, with the number of appliances you can see. Clicking a card enters that ADOM. Jobs card — the number of active jobs ; opens the job list. Certificates card — the number of device certificates SATOM knows and how many expire within 30 days; for administrators it opens the Certificate Manager . You are signed in. Visiting / always switches the current tab to the Global ADOM. Appliances appear once they are registered (see Quick start ).

Without it the table says Appliance inventory not available — Your profile does not include viewing appliances. and the cards count 0. It loads a moment after the page (it probes the nodes and services in the background) and shows updated … when done. Read the cards: appliances per ADOM, active job(s) , and certificates — N expiring ≤30d is highlighted in amber when anything expires soon. Scroll to Fleet for the full appliance table.

🧪 Example — Morning check You open SATOM and land on Global. Infrastructure health shows both nodes primary and standby reachable. The FortiWeb card shows 12 appliances, the Jobs card 2 active job(s) (last night's backups still finishing), and the Certificates card 3 expiring ≤30d in amber. You click the Certificates card to plan renewals, then use the FortiWeb card to start your policy work.

Solution — register an appliance under Appliances (the link in the message, or Administrator → Appliances in the sidebar; without the administrator capability, Global → Appliances ). docs.x: Possible causes — it is in maintenance mode and you lack appliances.view_maintenance . Solution — ask an administrator, or check the Appliances page with an account that has the permission.

Possible causes - The peer node, the Git repository or the backup server is down or unreachable from this node. - They are not configured. The Backup server card then says not configured and Settings → Source of Truth & Backup → Backup Server (a link to that tab for administrators). docs.x: Possible causes — the job store could not be read; the card falls back to 0 instead of breaking the page. Solution — open Jobs directly to see the list.

Advanced How the cards are built The ADOM cards are generated from the ADOM registry, so a product declared in Settings → ADOMs gets its card and its fleet rows without any change to the page. An appliance whose product key matches no active ADOM is visible on Global only, and is listed after the others. The certificate card counts every device certificate row whose expiry is within 30 days of now (UTC), including already-expired ones. The infrastructure data endpoint answers only in the Global ADOM.

docs.s: The ideas every other page builds on — ADOM, appliance, the device cache and source of truth, jobs, scheduled actions, change requests, profiles and permissions, processes and templates.

docs.x: 1 Register an appliance It belongs to one product ADOM 2 Discover it Rediscovery / Deep capture fill SATOM's own copy of its configuration 3 Work from the copy Pages are fast and work even when the box is not 4 Change it Preview → confirm → applied, snapshotted and audited 5 Run long work as jobs Track them in the job dock and the Jobs page 6 Automate and control Scheduled actions repeat work; change requests gate risky work

A workspace scoped to one product family: Global , FortiWeb , FortiADC , FortiAuthenticator or FortiAnalyzer . Each ADOM has its own menu and only sees its own appliances and records; Global sees everything. The ADOM is remembered per browser tab. → ADOMs and products

A Fortinet device registered in SATOM: name, product ( Kind ), management address and port, credentials (stored encrypted), and classification (Zone, Line, Department, Tags). An appliance can be a single box or an HA cluster (node 0 plus member nodes). An appliance in maintenance mode is hidden from users without the permission to see maintenance devices. → Appliances

docs.h: Device cache, snapshots and the source of truth
docs.x: SATOM keeps its own copy of each appliance's configuration so pages can be rendered without contacting the box: Rediscovery — one read-only sweep that re-reads every configuration object of the appliance. The first run is called Discovery . Deep capture — follows server policies and web protection profiles into their dependencies (members, rule lists, disabled signatures, exceptions) for the analysis pages. Optional and slower. Source of truth (SoT) — a versioned history of each appliance's configuration. Each version is a snapshot identified by the hash of its content, so an unchanged configu

Changes to an appliance are prepared, shown as a preview of exactly what will be sent, and only written when you confirm. The write is snapshotted and recorded with before/after detail in the Audit Log .

Anything long — a backup, a discovery, a bulk change, a firmware transfer — runs as a background job . A dock in the corner of the screen tracks it while you keep navigating, and the Jobs page lists running and finished jobs with Pause , Resume and Stop . You control your own jobs; administrators control everyone's. Stopping is cooperative: the job stops at its next safe point, never in the middle of a device write. → Jobs

A unit of work that runs on a schedule without anyone clicking. The scheduler fires them on the primary node. There are two lists: Page What it holds Who Automations (Automation menu) Fleet work somebody planned for a chosen time — a cutover, draining a backend, a certificate swap or renewal, an upgrade, a reboot, an HA failover. Upgrade, reboot, HA failover, the Cert Manager lifecycle sweep and Custom REST calls run only bound to an approved change request, inside its window. Users with write access System Automations (Administrator → System) SATOM maintaining itself — backups, source-of-trut

The control record for a risky change done inside a maintenance window — above all a firmware upgrade: which appliances and policies are affected, when, an approval step, and the one-shot scheduled action that executes it inside the window. A live FortiWeb firmware upgrade is refused unless an approved change request names the appliance and its maintenance window is open (a dry run is allowed without one). The Upgrade Flow page chains pre-upgrade checks, one change request, the customer-impact export and execution for many appliances at once. → Change requests , Upgrade flow

A permission is one granular right, such as backups.create or protection.apply . A profile is a named set of permissions assigned to a user. Three profiles ship with SATOM: Profile In short readonly Read access to every section; cannot change anything. operator Read everything plus manage appliances, protection, network, backups and operations. No user or registry administration. admin Full access, including users and profiles. Administrators can create other profiles from the permission catalog. Menu entries you cannot use are hidden, and every page checks again on the server. → Users and pro

An operator-drawn procedure — a recovery plan, a post-upgrade validation, an onboarding check — that SATOM walks for you: each step asks the system a question and the arrows say where to go next depending on the answer. A run is a rehearsal (write steps are dry-runs) unless you arm it, and each run keeps a copy of the diagram as it was when it started. → Process

Versioned desired state kept in the Template Library . A template is saved as a pending draft, approved by an administrator to become fleet-deployable, and can be applied to an appliance as a separate, audited action. → Template library

Sign-ins, configuration changes, sharing a bookmark, approving a template and other actions are written to the Audit Log with who, when and what. → Audit log See also the Glossary for every other term used in the console.

docs.t: Quick start — from a fresh install to your first backup
docs.x: You need: SATOM installed and reachable over HTTPS (see Installation ). The installer asks for the admin password; the guided setup can generate one into a root-only file on the server. One appliance — FortiWeb is used in this guide — with its management address, HTTPS port and an API-capable administrator account on the appliance. Network access from the SATOM server to the appliance's management port (and SSH, if you want SSH-based backups or CLI capture). 1 Sign in as admin Change the installation password 2 Create your own accounts One person, one account 3 Register the appliance Appliance

docs.t: Quick start — from a fresh install to your first backup
docs.h: Step 1 — Sign in and secure the admin account
docs.x: Browse to your SATOM address, for example https://satom.example.com . Sign in as admin with the installation password. You land on the Global home , which says No appliances registered yet . Open Settings (bottom of the sidebar) → My Account → Change Password , set a new password (12 to 1024 characters) and click Update Password . Optional but recommended: on the Security tab click Set up 2FA . See First login for details.

Stop ends the sweep after the current read; nothing is written and the previous snapshot is kept. Discovery is read-only: it fills SATOM's own copy of the configuration so the policy and object pages can render. It needs appliances.apply . See Rediscovery .

docs.t: Notifications — the bell and the notifications page
docs.x: The bell in the top bar is SATOM's personal inbox. Background work you started — a backup, a firmware transfer, a hardware scan — and events addressed to you, such as an alert or a resolved bug report, arrive here as notifications . docs.k: glossary terms definitions vocabulary terminology dictionary definitions what does it mean dictionary terminology
docs.s: Short definitions of the terms used in the SATOM console and documentation, in alphabetical order, each linked to the article that covers it.

docs.x: Administrative domain. A SATOM workspace scoped to one product family — Global, FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAuthenticator, FortiAnalyzer or FortiGate — with its own menu and its own appliances, jobs, notifications and bookmarks. Global sees everything. Not to be confused with the ADOMs configured on a FortiWeb appliance. → ADOMs and products

A signed file ( satom-apipack-<version>.tar.gz ) that carries vendor API knowledge — which endpoints and fields each firmware build serves, release notes, field catalogs — to a node that cannot measure it itself. Since 3.0 packs come in two lanes : the API pack pinned to each release and the rolling knowledge pack . Never carries configuration or device identity. → API library

A credential for machine-to-machine access to SATOM's /api/v1 , sent as a Bearer token. Each token has a scope (read, write or admin), is bound to one ADOM, belongs to a user and can never exceed that user's permissions. The token is shown once, at creation; only a hash is stored. → API tokens
A Fortinet device registered in SATOM (name, product, management address, encrypted credentials, classification). Also called device in the console. → Appliances
The record of who did what and when — sign-ins, configuration changes, approvals — with before/after detail for changes. → Audit log
The page where users with write access schedule fleet work for a chosen time (a cutover, draining a backend, a certificate swap). One of the two lists of scheduled actions . → Scheduled actions
The per-appliance store of configuration backups: created from the appliance (REST or SSH) or uploaded as a .conf file, downloadable and usable by the restore and upgrade flows. → Backups
An entry in your right-hand bookmarks panel: a device, a link, or a folder. Personal by default; can be shared with the team. → Bookmarks

The control record for a risky change done inside a maintenance window — above all a firmware upgrade: affected devices and policies, timing, an approval step and the one-shot action that executes it. → Change requests
An administrator-editable option of the change request form's type of change picker, including the text it contributes to the change document. → Change requests
The Zone, Line and Department values assigned to appliances. Maintained by administrators (Administrator → Classification) and used for grouping in Architecture, bookmarks and baselines. → Appliances

The control panel for fleet metrics collection: every scrape target with its own interval, and the health of the local metrics store; since 3.4.0 also the SNMP targets and the syslog receiver. → Metrics

In the Network Automation Forum's framework, the block that reads the live network. In SATOM: device sync, deep capture, the scrape targets, SNMP polling, the syslog receiver and the FortiAnalyzer log view. The Knowledge Harvester is not the Collector — it harvests vendor knowledge, not network state. → Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
The footer page listing every page of the console grouped by what it is for. → Concept Map
A page authored in Plugin Studio and published to the Plugins → Custom Views menu of the FortiWeb or FortiADC ADOM. → Plugins

An optional, slower read that follows server policies and web protection profiles into their dependencies (members, rule lists, disabled signatures, exceptions) and stores them in SATOM's device cache for the analysis pages. Enabled with Capture full WPP + policy depth on the rediscovery page. → Rediscovery
A check that reaches into the appliance — synthetic HTTPS against a policy's front-end, interface drift, CPU, memory and the proxy daemon — to answer is the service actually serving? → Deep monitors
The selected device that per-device pages work on, chosen with Switch device in the top bar. Kept separately for each ADOM. → Navigation
The first rediscovery of an appliance, before any snapshot exists.
The Config drift finding: an appliance's harvested configuration changed since its previous snapshot. Says that the device changed , not that it is wrong — compare intent deviation . → Alerting
A preview of a change that shows exactly what would be sent, without changing the appliance. Also the mode of an unarmed process run.
SATOM's database catalog of appliance API paths per product and API version, which lets SATOM follow firmware changes as data rather than code. → API registry
A WAF or signature carve-out authored in SATOM and bound to a server policy, recording which policy it was written for even when the web protection profile is shared. → Exceptions

The FortiWeb predefined (factory) Web Protection Profiles, stored once per firmware version, build number and REST API version. A deep rediscovery rebuilds a predefined profile from it when the appliance's own rows match, instead of reading it again. → Factory catalog

A read-only troubleshooting tool (Operations → Troubleshooting → Path Diagnostics) that walks a ladder of checks against a named server policy or virtual server and names the first layer that fails. Called Scout until 2026-10-14. → Path Diagnostics
A read-only, fleet-wide browser of FortiWeb objects, read from SATOM's device cache. → Fleet objects

In the NAF Framework, the block that writes to the network. In SATOM: the CLI writer, the REST clients' writes, Policy ops and Clone, Provisioning, the write actions of the catalogue, firmware upgrades and Observatory fixes. Not to be confused with the "executor" that runs one step of a process . → Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework

The NAF Framework's name for the desired state of the network. In SATOM: templates , template bindings and baselines — not the Source of Truth, which is the actual state. → Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework

The finding (and the Compliance column of a template's bindings) raised when an appliance bound to an approved template no longer matches it, field by field: met , deviates or unmeasured . Names the differing fields, never a value. Unlike drift , it does not care when the device stopped matching. → Alerting
A background task — backup, discovery, bulk change, firmware transfer — tracked in the job dock and on the Jobs page, with Pause , Resume and Stop . → Jobs

The rolling lane of signed packs ( satom-apipack-kb-YYYYMMDD[.N] ), published by the SATOM team whenever the vendor knowledge changes, fetched daily from the knowledge feed or uploaded on air-gapped networks. Verified with the knowledge key only. → Knowledge packs
Which publication series a 3.0 pack belongs to — api_pack or knowledge — and therefore which key may sign it. One key, one use. → Pack trust
A short lease taken while you edit an object, so two users do not overwrite each other's changes. → Locks
An appliance flag that hides the device from users who lack appliances.view_maintenance . → Appliances

One SATOM server. In a high-availability installation there are two: the primary and the standby . The top bar shows which one you are on. Also used for the node's own TLS certificate (Node TLS). → High availability
A message in your top-bar bell — a job that finished, an alert, a resolved bug report. → Notifications

The Network Automation Forum's vendor-neutral reference model of six functional building blocks — Intent, Executor, Collector, Observability, Orchestrator, Presentation — around the network infrastructure. SATOM is mapped to it; the conformance matrix is published with the product documentation. → Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework

In the NAF Framework, the block that coordinates the others into end-to-end workflows without touching the network itself. In SATOM: processes , scheduled actions , change requests and integration hooks. The reconciler is not the Orchestrator — it keeps a standby node's code in step. → Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
One granular right, such as backups.create . Permissions are grouped into profiles. → Permissions
The read-write node of a high-availability pair. Only the primary fires scheduled actions. → High availability
A monitoring check SATOM runs on a schedule against an appliance and stores as samples. Deep monitors and Service Monitor are two views of the same probes. → Probes
An operator-drawn procedure (recovery plan, post-upgrade validation, onboarding check) that SATOM walks step by step. Runs are rehearsals unless armed. → Process
A named set of permissions assigned to a user. Shipped profiles: readonly , operator , admin . → Users and profiles
A background service running on both nodes that compares each node's code with the expected version; in automatic mode it drives the staged self-update. → Software update
A read-only sweep that re-reads every configuration object of an appliance and refreshes SATOM's copy of it. → Rediscovery

A unit of work that the scheduler fires on a schedule. Shown on two pages: Automations (fleet work, Automation menu) and System Automations (SATOM's own housekeeping, Administrator → System). → Scheduled actions

The AI chat assistant (Operations → Troubleshooting → Scout): WAF false-positive triage, Lua drafting and configuration-history search. Called AI Advisor until 2026-10-14; before that date, Scout was the name of the tool now called Path Diagnostics . → Scout
A named back-end network (CIDR, interface, gateway) scoped to a classification value, used when a new policy builds its server pool. → Segments
SATOM's incident console: open incidents, evidence, and the response engine. Global ADOM. → Sentinel

Runtime telemetry read over the appliance's monitor API — sessions, per-policy sessions and latency, throughput, HTTP transactions — answering how much is this service carrying? It keeps working on a licence-locked appliance. → Service monitor
FortiWeb attack signatures. SATOM reads the signature catalogue from a base appliance and caches it so signatures can be shown by name. → Signatures
One stored version of an appliance's configuration in the source-of-truth store, identified by the hash of its content. Also the _config.json file a rediscovery writes.

SATOM's versioned history of every appliance's configuration. An unchanged configuration creates no new version. In NAF terms this is Observability (the actual state and its history), not Intent — the desired state is the template . → Data and storage , Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
The second node of a high-availability pair. It receives the database by replication and the data files by sync, and is read-only. → High availability
What an ADOM holds on the SATOM server — configuration backups, source-of-truth payloads and bundles — listed on Administrator → Stored Assets . → Stored assets

The administrator page (Administrator → System → System Automations) for scheduled actions that maintain SATOM itself (backups, source-of-truth syncs, probe sweeps, signature and CVE refreshes). → Scheduled actions
Versioned desired state in the Template Library : saved as a pending draft, approved by an administrator, and applied to an appliance as a separate, audited action. → Template library
The certificate authorities SATOM trusts when it connects to an appliance, so Verify SSL certificate works for appliances signed by a private CA. → Trust store

The offline reviewer that reads harvested vendor release notes for a firmware move and returns a verdict ( blocker , caution , clear , unknown or unavailable ). It is on when Path Diagnostics is switched on (Settings → Path Diagnostics). Shown as Scout until 2026-10-14. → Release notes
A staged workflow for a maintenance window across many appliances: bulk pre-upgrade checks, one change request citing them, the customer-impact export, and execution. → Upgrade flow

docs.s: SATOM's own REST API for your systems (not the Fortinet device API) — the token-authenticated integration API at /api/v1: how tokens, scopes, capabilities and ADOM binding work, every endpoint, the error format and the rate limits.

docs.x: This is SATOM's own API — the one your systems use to talk to SATOM. It is not the Fortinet device API SATOM uses internally to manage the appliances: that one is described in API registry and API library . SATOM exposes a small, versioned HTTP API for integrations and automation: Base URL: https://<your-satom-host>/api/v1 — the address of your own SATOM server Authentication: Authorization: Bearer <token> on every request Format: JSON in, JSON out — errors included (never an HTML login page) CSRF: not used on this surface; the token replaces it The API is deliberately narrow. It can read the

An administrator creates tokens on the API tokens page (requires users.manage ). The token is shown once : fmk_<public_id>_<secret> Only a scrypt hash of the secret is stored. A token can be given an expiry in days, edited, or revoked. Every call is checked against these limits, in order; the first that fails decides the answer: Limit Meaning Valid The token exists, is not revoked and not expired Owner active The user who owns the token is still enabled Scope read < write < admin ; a higher scope satisfies a lower requirement Owner permission The owner must still hold the permission the scope

Capability Grants Granted by default? backend_edit , backend_config , policy_status , cert_swap Scheduled actions that change one server policy (AppID-scopable) Yes, while the list is empty maintenance , reports Fleet maintenance and report actions Yes, while the list is empty inventory POST /appliances/<id>/firmware-check No — must be listed waf_exception_draft , waf_exception_apply WAF carve-outs (FortiWeb tokens or global ) No — must be listed adc_rule_draft , adc_rule_apply FortiADC rules (FortiADC tokens or global ) No — must be listed template_draft (3.4.0) Create templates and versions,

Method Path Scope Purpose GET /ping read Token identity: name, owner, scopes, capabilities, AppIDs, ADOM GET /appliances read Appliances visible to the token: id, name, kind, host, port, status, last check, maintenance, firmware, model, hardware type GET /appliances/<id> read One appliance POST /appliances/<id>/firmware-check write + inventory Ask the appliance for its firmware now and record it (10/min) GET /actions read Scheduled actions in the token's ADOM, with danger and api_runnable POST /actions/<id>/run write Run a non-destructive action now (30/min) GET /actions/runs/<run_id> read Sta

GET /openapi.json needs a read token and returns the document for the routes as registered on this node and release — paths, methods, the scope each route enforces, the capability it declares and a one-line summary from the view itself. A route without a summary is a test failure in the product's suite, not an undocumented endpoint. Nothing is kept in a second list, so the document cannot lag behind the code.

Reads are scoped to the token's ADOM like a console session and need the owner to hold the Template Library's view permission. Writes need the explicit capabilities above and follow the console's rules exactly: a new version lands pending ; approval is four-eyes (never the author); an apply is a preview unless confirm is true, and then the same canary-gated background job behind the firmware compatibility gate; a fleet rollout needs an approved template and an owner with Run operations . The API never writes to a device on its own path. Audit entries carry the token id.

config-history and config-diff read the Source of Truth (the actual configuration, version by version); /findings evaluates the alert engine 's checks on call and returns the current findings of the token's product; /metrics/query is the only way into the metrics store from outside the node — the store itself stays on loopback with no account of its own. The query must reference satom_* series only (anything else is a 400 ), answers within 10 s or returns store_timeout , and a product-bound token is handed only the series of its own devices (node series included for a global token only).

/processes lists what the token's ADOM may see; POST /processes/<id>/run queues a walk against appliance and returns the run — a rehearsal unless "armed": true , which needs process_arm and scope write ; /process-runs/<id> returns the run with its steps. Diagrams that cannot run answer invalid_diagram ; a diagram with device steps and no appliance answers appliance_required . See Process .

POST /actions/<id>/run runs the action exactly as the operator saved it — you cannot change its parameters. It is refused when the action is destructive ( destructive_blocked ), disabled ( disabled ), outside the token's ADOM ( wrong_product ), outside its capabilities or AppIDs, or already running. curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://<your-satom-host>/api/v1/actions curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ https://<your-satom-host>/api/v1/actions/42/run # {"ok": true, "run_id": 99, "action_id": 42, "status": "ok", "summary": "…"} curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK

GET /system/nodes and GET /system/nodes/history return the readings behind SATOM health → Resource history : CPU, memory and disk of the SATOM nodes themselves, not of the appliances. The token must be bound to the global ADOM ( 403 wrong_product otherwise), because SATOM health is a Global-only page. A token restricted to named capabilities also needs monitoring . Node addresses are never in the answer. history takes range ( 1h , 6h , 24h , 7d , 30d , 90d ; default 24h ), node (one node name) and metrics ( cpu , mem , disk in percent by default; also mem_used_mb , mem_total_mb , disk_used_gb

Opens one status call to the appliance and updates SATOM's record. On success it returns the firmware string verbatim ( "source": "live" , changed , previous ). If the appliance does not answer it returns 502 with the last known value and firmware_checked_at and records nothing.

POST /waf/exceptions body: Field Required Meaning appliance_id yes A FortiWeb visible to the token exc_type yes A type from GET /waf/exception-types wpp_mkey yes The web protection profile the carve-out belongs to payload per type The carve-out fields policies for AppID tokens Server policies the carve-out is for name , reason no Free text apply no true to push to the appliance (needs waf_exception_apply ) target when applying The device object the entry goes into create_container no Create the container object if missing Without apply the carve-out is saved as desired state (an operator appli

Allowed types: security_waf_exception and security_dos_exception . Body: appliance_id , logical , mkey (object name), fields (object), apply . Without apply: true the response is a preview of the exact request that would be sent, and nothing is sent. An existing name is refused ( 409 already_exists ). There is no DELETE, and AppID-scoped tokens cannot use this surface ( not_appid_scopable ).

All errors are JSON: {"error": "<code>", "message": "<text>"} (some add errors , allowed or detail ). A 401 also carries WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="satom" . HTTP error When 400 bad_request Body is not a JSON object, or a required field is missing 400 type_not_allowed Carve-out type or ADC rule type not on the allow-list 400 invalid_payload Fields missing or invalid for the type 400 target_required apply: true without target (the record is still saved) 400 unknown_action The scheduled action's type is not in the catalog 401 unauthenticated No Authorization: Bearer header 401 invalid_token

Endpoint Limit per client IP POST /appliances/<id>/firmware-check 10 per minute POST /actions/<id>/run , POST / DELETE /waf/exceptions , POST /adc/rules 30 per minute each Read endpoints have no specific limit. Calls that change something, and every refused object write, are written to the audit log with the token, its name and its owner. The token's last-used time and address are updated (at most once a minute). Advanced The internal /api endpoints /api/… (without v1 ) is the internal JSON used by the web interface. It uses the browser session and CSRF, not tokens, and is not a supported inte

docs.s: The FortiWeb Server Policy workspace — list, filter, inspect, edit, create, enable, disable and delete the server policies of the selected FortiWeb, served from SATOM's local copy of the configuration.

docs.x: The Server Policy workspace is the main FortiWeb page in SATOM. It lists every server policy of the selected FortiWeb, opens each one in a FortiWeb-style form, and lets an operator change, create, enable, disable, delete, clone or migrate policies. The list and the detail view are read from SATOM's local copy of the configuration, so browsing does not load the appliance; the device is contacted when you press Refresh from device , save a change, or ask for live health.

Lists the policies in FortiWeb's own layout for the device's firmware build: FortiWeb's toolbar and columns in FortiWeb's order, plus a checkbox per row. With no GUI layout imported (no knowledge pack yet), the list draws FortiWeb 7.6's default columns with the same toolbar. Filters the list in the browser by name ( Name or /regex/… ) and, under Filters , by VIP, back-end pool, back-end server IP, certificate type and status. Text filters accept a plain substring or a /regex/ . Shows a badge with the age of the local data and pulls fresh configuration on demand with Refresh from device (⟳). Ed

At least one FortiWeb registered in SATOM (see Appliances ). A selected device. When the FortiWeb ADOM is active and no device has been chosen yet, the workspace redirects you to the Service Diagram to pick one. Data in SATOM's local store. A device that was never synchronised shows the badge no local data — refresh ; press Refresh from device once. The VIP / IP… and Backend server IP… filters need a deep capture (run from Analysis ).

protection.view opens the list, the detail page, the Check live health probe and the reference dropdowns, for every device you can see. Devices in maintenance mode are hidden unless you hold appliances.view_maintenance . Every action that writes or reads the whole device — Refresh from device , saving a form, creating an object with ＋ , Create New , From a line profile , and every toolbar action on the selected rows (Clone, Clone to, Migrate to, Enable, Disable, Delete) — requires the legacy config_write permission. Any granular key that implies it unlocks these actions; the natural ones for s

In the sidebar, open FortiWeb → Policy → Server Policy . The list for the currently selected FortiWeb opens. The header shows the device name, its address and firmware; the toolbar shows the local-data badge. Click a row to select it; double-click it, press Enter or click Edit to open the policy. To work on another FortiWeb, press Change Appliance . It opens the Service Diagram , where you pick the device.

Type into Name or /regex/… in the toolbar, or open Filters below it and type into VIP / IP… , Backend pool… or Backend server IP… . Plain text is a case-insensitive substring; /pol-.*-prod/ is a regular expression (case-insensitive unless you add flags). Narrow with Any certificate (Local, Multi (SNI), Let's Encrypt, None) and All Status (Enabled, Disabled). The × button clears every filter. A filter box turns red when the pattern is invalid, longer than 200 characters, or too slow to evaluate; that box is then ignored until you edit it. Filtering never contacts SATOM or the device.
Press Refresh from device (needs config_write ). SATOM reads the whole configuration from the appliance, stores it and returns to the list with Refreshed from <device>: <detail> .

With a GUI layout for the device's build, Edit opens FortiWeb's Edit Server Policy dialog: fields show and hide as you edit, Save shows Review the change , and Apply to <device> writes it, through the same gates listed below. The steps that follow describe SATOM's policy view, which Edit opens when no layout has been imported. Open a policy. The header shows its status, deployment mode and protocol; the name is marked name locked because it is the object key. An entry marked conditional may be hidden on this device by a setting SATOM cannot see. A policy with no HTTP, HTTPS or HTTP/3 service is refused before anything is written. With no layout imported, Create New opens SATOM's New Server Policy form: On the list, press Create New . Fill Policy name (required). Optionally fill Virtual Server name and add rows with ＋ Add VIP , and Server Pool name with ＋ Add member rows. Se

Select a row, or tick several rows (the toolbar counts N selected ). Press Enable , Disable or Delete in the toolbar. Press Preview (dry-run) . For Delete , the preview lists what WILL BE DELETED and what WILL BE KEPT , with the policies a kept object is shared with or the reason it is never deleted (for example Web Protection Profile (never auto-deleted) ). The dialog says it up front: objects used only by this policy (virtual server, VIP, server pool…) are deleted with it; Web Protection Profiles, certificates, services and objects shared with other policies are kept. Press Apply for real .

Field saves and object creations are written through SATOM's audited write path: each change is recorded with a before/after snapshot in the change history and the audit log . Row and bulk actions run as a background job titled <Action> — N server policies on <device> . Each policy gets an audit entry ( policy.enable , policy.delete , …) and the run gets a summary entry; the user who started it receives a notification . docs.h: "VIP / backend filters need a deep capture"
docs.x: Possible causes - No deep capture exists for this device, so VIP and back-end data are not in the local store. Solution 1. Run a deep capture for the device from Analysis . 2. Reload the Server Policy page. Verification — the badge disappears and the VIP / IP… filter narrows the list.

docs.h: "No server policies cached for this device. Use Refresh from device."
docs.x: Possible causes - The device has no server policies. - The local store is empty for this device. Solution 1. Press Refresh from device (⟳). 2. If the flash message reports an error, check the device's reachability and credentials on its appliance page . Verification — the toolbar counts the expected number of policies.

Possible causes - The device could not be read (unreachable, authentication failure, license lock). The last good local copy is kept. Solution 1. Open the device's appliance page and test the connection. 2. Quote the error ID to your administrator; it identifies the log entry. Verification — a new refresh reports Refreshed from <device>: … .

docs.h: The save buttons and the policy actions are missing
docs.x: Possible causes - Your profile lacks every key that implies config_write : the list shows no Create New , Clone , Enable , Disable or Delete button, and SATOM's policy view says Read-only: changing this policy needs the config_write permission. Solution 1. Ask an administrator for network.edit or another key listed under Permissions . Verification — the save buttons appear and the Confirm change to the live device dialog opens.

Possible causes - A reference field names an object the device does not have. SATOM checks references before writing instead of letting the device answer with a bare -651 . Solution 1. Pick an existing object from the dropdown, or create it with ＋ . 2. If the dropdown is stale, press Refresh from device . Verification — the dialog opens and Apply to device returns Saved to device .

Possible causes - The device is offline or license-locked, or refused the status query. Solution 1. The page itself keeps working from the local copy; retry later. 2. Check the device on its appliance page. Verification — the message changes to N of M back-end(s) matched live status.

Solution 1. Read the result under the error: applied lists every step with its outcome, rolled_back the objects this run deleted again (the FortiWeb-style dialog names them after undone: ). docs.x: Possible causes - Another user holds the edit lease on the policy, or on the object the row you are saving belongs to. Solution 1. Wait until the other user finishes, or take over the edit lock (see Locks ). Verification — the preview opens and Apply to device saves.

docs.s: A guided build that turns a line profile and one or more web addresses into complete server policies — address, DNS record, certificate and device objects — and reports exactly what was undone and what was left behind if a step fails.

docs.t: New Server Policy from a line
docs.x: The wizard builds new server policies from a line . The line's profile supplies the network segment, the certificate class and the Web Protection Profile; you supply the web addresses and the real servers. One run can reserve the VIP in IPAM, publish the hostname in DNS, issue the certificate and create the objects on the FortiWeb — and if a step fails, it lists separately what it undid and what it deliberately left behind.

docs.t: New Server Policy from a line
docs.x: Builds one server policy, virtual server, VIP, DNS record and certificate per domain , and one server pool shared by all domains of the run. Derives every object name from the web address through the FortiWeb patterns saved on the Naming page (built-in defaults where no pattern is saved). Checks the whole plan before anything is written, including a live check of the device for a policy or pool with the same name and for the line's Web Protection Profile, and reports every blocker at once. Serves HTTPS with the certificate it issues: the new server policy is bound to it. ℹ️ Note Changed in 2.1

docs.s: Copy a server policy and its whole object tree on the same FortiWeb, onto another FortiWeb, or migrate it there — with a pre-flight checklist, a mandatory dry run, dummy VIP addresses and a reconciliation report.

docs.x: Three buttons on the toolbar of the Server Policy list copy a policy together with everything it references: Clone , Clone to and Migrate to . Their dialogs are titled Clone (same box) , Clone to another FortiWeb and Migrate to another FortiWeb . A guided dialog runs a pre-flight checklist, asks only what it needs (name, VIP address, interface mapping, profile handling), requires a dry-run preview, and then runs the copy as a background job with a per-object reconciliation report.

Walks the policy's whole tree on the source — virtual server and VIPs, server pool and members, health checks, content routing and, optionally, the Web Protection Profile with its sub-profiles — and creates on the destination what is missing there. Leaves the copied policy disabled , so it cannot take traffic before a manual cutover. Rewrites the VIP address of the copy to a dummy address following the administrator's rules (always in a bulk run; as a prefilled suggestion for a single policy). Migrate clones first and, only if the copy landed cleanly, disables the source policy. The source is

For Clone to and Migrate to : at least one other FortiWeb visible to you. Otherwise these buttons are disabled ( No other FortiWeb is registered ). The source must answer live . A clone is never built from cached data; an unreachable source blocks the checklist. The administrator's defaults in Settings → Clone / Migrate (dummy-IP rules and the copy-profile default). Fact

docs.x: Possible causes — the destination refused one or more objects. For a migrate, the source stays enabled. Solution 1. Open the clone report and read Failed objects . 2. Fix the cause and run the clone again; existing objects are skipped. Verification — the report shows success .

docs.x: Possible causes - File-backed objects were skipped, or Only add what is missing held rows back ( rows not added ). The copy is then not equivalent, so the source is left enabled on purpose. Solution — complete the destination (upload the files, or add the rows), then disable the source by hand.

docs.s: Browse and maintain a FortiWeb's Server Objects (virtual servers, pools, health checks, certificates, ciphers, allow lists, IP groups and more) on the pages of the device's own Server Objects menu, drawn in FortiWeb's layout.

docs.x: Server Objects is a group of the FortiWeb device menu: the Server Objects menu of the appliance's own GUI, measured on the selected device's firmware build. It holds the objects a FortiWeb uses to publish and balance applications — virtual servers, server pools, health checks, certificates, cipher lists, allow lists, IP groups and so on. Each entry opens a page drawn in FortiWeb's layout (its tabs, toolbar and columns) inside the SATOM frame, with SATOM's tools added, and each object opens in FortiWeb's own dialog.

Draws FortiWeb's Server Objects menu under the FortiWeb group of the sidebar, in FortiWeb's order, with the pages the device's build has. All pages shows the same menu as a grid. Shows the entries that FortiWeb draws as tabs of one page (for example Local | Multi-certificate ) as tabs above the list. Lists the objects of the selected tab with FortiWeb's columns, a Search box and an object count. Advanced How sub-tables are found and read Sub-tables are derived from the endpoint registry: a collection owns every registry path shaped <collection>/<segment> . Rows are always read scoped to the parent ( ?mkey=<parent> ); path-style reads can return every parent's rows. The NTP server list is the one exception — it hangs off a singleton and has no per-row delete, so editing or removing a row rebuilds the whole list and puts the original rows back if a re-add fails. docs.s: When a firmware build serves a setting only through the CLI, the object editor writes that field by CLI in one transaction, aborts on any error and reads every field back.

docs.t: CLI writer (fields only the CLI serves)
docs.x: SATOM writes configuration through REST. On some builds of some products a setting exists only in the CLI . For those fields — and only those — the object editor uses the CLI writer : it types the change into the appliance's CLI as one transaction, discards it on any error, and reads every field back.

docs.t: CLI writer (fields only the CLI serves)
docs.x: Routes each field of a save by what the appliance's exact build serves, per the API library : fields served by REST go by REST as always; fields classified CLI only or hidden go by CLI; fields SATOM cannot classify keep the REST path and are named. Runs one transaction : config / edit / set / unset / next / end , sub-table rows included, values quoted and escaped. Stops at the first error the box prints and discards the pending change with abort , so nothing is half-applied. Reads back the object in a new SSH session (and over REST where REST serves it) and fails the save if any written field

docs.x: A Web Protection Profile is usually shared by several Server Policies, and FortiWeb keeps no record of which policy an exception was written for. The Exceptions & Signature page records that intent in SATOM: each carve-out (a WAF exception or a signature customisation) is stored as desired state, bound to one or more Server Policies, and pushed to the appliance only when you explicitly ask.

Authoring — a typed form for ten WAF exception types and eight signature types, bound to a Web Protection Profile and to Server Policies, with a reason. Team rules enforced by SATOM 1. Templates stay clean — a carve-out cannot target a profile governed by an approved template; the save is refused and a guided clone is offered. 2. Lifecycle — re-binding a Server Policy to another profile in SATOM marks its carve-outs STALE (never deletes them); purging a policy previews what is deleted and what is only unbound. A change made on the device itself, outside SATOM, is flagged DRIFT (see Carve-outs

docs.x: Click Deploy on the row. Every visible FortiWeb scope is listed with a verdict: Ready to place , Already has this carve-out , Profile is template-managed , Profile not recorded on this scope or Source scope . Select destinations, click Preview , then Place on selected scopes . Placing is not pushing. Each placement is recorded as desired state on its scope and must be injected from that scope.

Click Delete . The panel What deleting this would take away shows a verdict: - Safe to delete — offers Delete ; - Needs review before deleting — offers I have read the above — delete anyway ; - Cannot delete — clone per policy first — offers Clone one per policy (N) , which splits the carve-out into one copy per Server Policy. Confirm Delete this carve-out? . If the carve-out predates version history the panel warns that deleting it cannot be undone.

A carve-out is flagged DRIFT when none of the Server Policies it names still binds its profile on the device: the policy is gone, or now uses another profile. That change was made on the device itself, outside SATOM, where the STALE hook never ran. A banner says <n> carve-out(s) no longer match the device — a Server Policy they name is gone or now uses another Web Protection Profile. It changed on the device, outside SATOM. 🧪 Example — Per-policy signature exception on a shared profile wpp-shop on fweb-01 is bound by shop-www and shop-api . An operator authors a Signature Exception (per-id) for signature 010000001 , bound to shop-www only, and saves it. docs.x: When FortiWeb blocks a request, the block page shows the caller an Attack ID such as id-fweb-01-000000004117 . Search Attack ID turns that reference into the attack-log entry it points to and puts the whole triage on one page: what was blocked and why, whether it looks like a false positive, and — if it is — the exception that would let it through, written onto the appliance in two deliberate steps.

Lookup — parses the reference, finds the appliance from it, and searches that appliance's attack log for the MSG ID. On a miss it shows the newest ten entries, so you can tell a stale ID from a broken feed. Each field has Explain this field (local analysis, no external lookups) and, when Scout (the AI assistant) is on, Ask the AI about this field . Analyze with AI — Scout judges the entry ( false-positive , true-attack

The FortiWeb that blocked the request is registered in SATOM and visible to you. The device part of the reference is matched to the appliance name (case-insensitive), then to its management address. SATOM can log in to the appliance's GUI to read its attack log. For the AI functions: Scout, the AI assistant (called AI Advisor until 2026-10-14), is enabled with a working provider (see Scout ). No current device is needed; the page works from the reference.

docs.s: Read the full FortiWeb signature catalog (classes, sub-classes, signatures and descriptions) from one base FortiWeb into SATOM, so signature pages can show names and be searched.

docs.x: The Signatures page builds SATOM's local reference copy of the FortiWeb signature database. Because the same FortiGuard signature package is on every FortiWeb, one reachable unit — the base device — is enough: SATOM reads every category, sub-class and individual signature with its description, read-only, and keeps the result for the whole instance. Since 3.0 the same page also shows Signature DB freshness per device — how old each FortiWeb's own signature database is, checked daily. See Signature freshness .

Shows the state of the cached database: number of signatures, number of sub-classes, firmware, signature set and when it was synced. Starts a background job that reads the catalog from the chosen base FortiWeb and replaces the cached copy. Notifies you through the job dock and the notification bell when the job finishes. The cached catalog is what the Web Protection signature policy editor uses for signature names, descriptions, the class filters and the Signature Details search.
At least one registered FortiWeb that SATOM can reach. Nothing is written to the device; the read is read-only.

The page and the sync require users.manage — in practice the Administrator profile. The Administrator menu group, which holds the Signatures entry, is not drawn for users without it, and opening /signatures/ directly returns 403 Forbidden . ℹ️ Note The FortiADC ADOM has its own Signatures entry in its Administrator menu. That page lists the FortiADC Web Attack Signature policies live from the selected FortiADC and is not related to this catalog; see FortiADC .

Open Administrator → Signatures in the FortiWeb ADOM. Check Cached database : a Cached badge with counts, or No signature database yet . Under Sync from a base device , choose the Base FortiWeb . Click Sync now . The page returns at once with Signature sync from started — follow it in the job dock (bottom-right). You'll get a notification when it finishes. Follow the job ( Connecting to… , Selecting signature set… , Reading signature database (set …)… , Saving catalog… ). When the notification arrives, reload the page to see the new counts. Re-run the sync after a firmware upgrade or a signatu

🧪 Example — First sync on a new instance After registering fweb-01 , an administrator opens Administrator → Signatures , picks fweb-01 (192.0.2.10:443) and clicks Sync now . A few moments later the bell shows Signature database synced — N signatures , and the signature editor ( FortiWeb → Web Protection → Known Attacks → Signatures , then Signature editor ) now lists every signature with its description.

A job named Syncing signatures from in Jobs , finishing with N signatures across M sub-classes . A notification: Signature database synced — N signatures on success, Signature sync read 0 signatures from when nothing was read, or Signature sync from failed on error (see Notifications ). docs.s: A daily read of each FortiWeb's signature database version that raises a device alert when a box stops updating from FortiGuard — or when its version cannot be read.

docs.x: Every FortiWeb downloads its own signature database from FortiGuard; SATOM never carries signatures, not even in a pack. What SATOM does since 3.0 is notice when a box stops updating : the daily scheduled action signature_check reads each FortiWeb's signature database version and records when it last changed, and the alert engine raises a device alert when the database is too old or cannot be read.

Reads, per FortiWeb, only the signature database version — one read-only CLI command over SSH ( diagnose system update info ) — and the device's own Last Update Date . Re-reads the full signature catalog only when a version changed, instead of hundreds of REST reads every day. Classifies each device as current , stale or unreadable : stale — older than the limit (default 7 days ), measured from the device's own last-update time or, when it gives none, from when SATOM saw the version change; or the device reports it never downloaded an update; unreadable — the version could not be read (SSH off

FortiWeb appliances with working SSH credentials (FortiADC and the other products are not checked). The scheduled action signature_check exists. Scheduled actions are data, not code: on a node updated from 2.x, create it once on the primary with sudo satom execute seed actions --yes (daily at 06:15), or on the Scheduled actions page. Alert delivery configured under Email & alerts if you want the finding to reach someone.
The Signatures page needs users.manage . Alerts reach whoever the alert routing sends them to.

In the FortiWeb ADOM open Administrator → Signatures . Read the card Signature DB freshness per device : Device , Version , Last update , Checked and Status ( current , stale , unreadable ). Hover a badge for the reason. For a stale device, check its FortiGuard connectivity and licence on the appliance; for an unreadable one, its SSH access from SATOM. Before the action has run, the card says No reading yet — the scheduled action signature_check has not run and shows how to seed it.

Field Description Required Example alerts.signature_max_days Age in days after which a signature database is stale. An application setting; 3.0.0 has no field for it on the Settings pages No 7 (default) Scheduled action signature_check When the daily read runs Yes daily 06:15

🧪 Example — A box that lost FortiGuard fweb-02 lost its route to FortiGuard after a firewall change. Eight days later the morning signature_check reads the same version with a last update eight days ago: the card shows stale and the alert engine sends Signature DB on fweb-02 is stale to the operations channel.
The state per device is stored as an application setting, so it replicates to the standby with everything else. The finding clears on its own once a later check sees a fresh database.
Possible causes - SSH is disabled on the appliances or SATOM's credentials do not allow SSH. Solution 1. Test the SSH console of one appliance from its detail page.

docs.h: A new lab box reads "stale" right away
docs.x: Possible causes - A FortiWeb that never reached FortiGuard reports its last update as the epoch (1969/1970): SATOM treats that as "never updated", which is stale. Solution 1. Let the box reach FortiGuard, or put it in maintenance.

docs.h: No alert arrives although the card shows "stale"
docs.x: Possible causes - The device alert family is off, or no sink accepts warnings. Solution 1. Check the alert routing under Email & alerts .

Advanced FortiGuard metadata When a knowledge pack carries signature metadata (public FortiGuard encyclopedia data: name, severity, category, CVEs, a link), the signature search shows a severity badge and the CVEs next to each id, and signature details add a FortiGuard row. No pack carries it today: FortiGuard's terms do not permit collecting and redistributing that data, so the harvester's enrichment is disabled and the signature-meta section ships empty until it is permitted.

docs.s: What an ADOM holds, per device - configuration backups on the backup server, the configuration SoT history and firmware images, plus SATOM's own backup bundles in the Global ADOM.

docs.x: Stored Assets answers one question per ADOM: what does SATOM hold for these devices? It brings four kinds of stored artifacts onto one page: Device config backups that the appliances wrote and pushed to the backup server. The Configuration SoT : the configuration history SATOM records itself at every harvest. Firmware images held to be installed onto a device. SATOM's own backup bundles. These are console-wide, so they appear in the Global ADOM only. These four are separate things, with separate retention, and none of them is a copy of another. The page is not FortiWeb-specific: it exists in e

Tiles for the whole ADOM: Devices (with the number retired), Backups on server , Never pushed , Stale (older than 8 days), SoT versions (with the number off-box), Firmware images (with total MB), and in Global SATOM backups . The tiles never change with the filter. One row per device (chassis). A FortiWeb in ADOM mode is one appliance row per ADOM but has one flash and one backup file. Its ADOM rows are folded into the device, and their counts are added. Appliances configured to push their backups to that server (an appliance-side backup job). SATOM does not create these files.

users.manage is required for every action on this page ( Administrator ). The entry is in the Administrator group, which is hidden without it. A direct request returns 403 Forbidden . The download links use System Backup 's download endpoint, which has the same requirement. The page is reachable from every ADOM, including FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator.

An empty serial means "never observed" and never overwrites a known one. A device is shown retired only when every one of its rows is retired. Card 2 is not narrowed by Backup state . docs.x: Seven FortiWeb API Protection object types keep only a name in the configuration. Their content is a separate file. A clone that copies configuration alone therefore creates these objects empty , and a rule bound to an empty object fails only after the cutover. WAF Artifacts is SATOM's own store of those files. It lets a clone or migration upload the real content to the destination. Three of the seven types can't be read back from any FortiWeb one object at a time, so for those SATOM's copy is the only one that can be moved on its own. The device's Entire configuration backup does carry the co

The section has three pages, all scoped to the device and ADOM you selected on the Architecture map : Object types ( /artifacts/ ): the catalog of the seven types, how an artifact reaches a server policy, and statistics for this device and ADOM. Inventory ( /artifacts/inventory ): what SATOM holds for this pair, which server policies need each object, which needed objects are not held, and which held copies are EMPTY . This is where you add content and refresh the index. Device audit ( /artifacts/audit ): every server policy walked on this device, the artifacts it needs, the Web Protection Pro

Four ways, all on Inventory . None of them writes to an appliance: Upload a file : the only way a gRPC IDL can enter the store. Fetch from the application : SATOM downloads a WSDL or XML Schema from the service that publishes it, with the schemas it imports from the same host. This is how you bring in the files of a FortiWeb that is already in production. Author content : type or paste the body. Capture from device : SATOM reads the object off this device. This is read-only on the appliance and available for the four readable types only. Content reaches a device only when the clone/migrate eng

In Refresh the index , leave Only this policy (optional) empty, keep Walk budget at 25 , and click Refresh . SATOM walks the server policies (read-only) and records which objects each one needs. 🧪 Example — Migrating an API policy with an XSD Policy pol-orders on fweb-01 validates XML against the schema xsd-order . Inventory lists xsd-order under Needed by a policy and NOT held , and Device audit shows it as blocked , because XSD can't be read back. Uploads, saves and captures store a content-addressed version. Identical content creates no new version, and the flash says so ( … — identical to the copy already held or … (unchanged, no new version) ). Audit entries: artifact.upload , artifact.fetch (also when nothing was stored, with the reason), artifact.capture , artifact.save , artifact.delete and artifact.refs . A refresh writes only SATOM's own index. It never deletes an edge when a walk fails.

docs.h: " cannot be read back from any FortiWeb … Upload the file instead."
docs.x: Possible causes - You tried to capture XML Schema, WSDL or gRPC IDL. Solution 1. Use Fetch from the application for a WSDL or XSD the service publishes, or get the original file from whoever authored it and use Upload a file . Verification - The object appears in Held artifacts , and its verdict is ok .

docs.h: "Nothing was stored — could not be fetched: refused: is …"
docs.x: Possible causes - The host resolves to loopback, a link-local address or one of SATOM's own addresses. SATOM never fetches from those. Solution 1. Use the address the service is reachable at on the network, not localhost or the SATOM node. Verification - The result starts with Fetched from .

docs.h: "… could not be fetched: redirected to — fetch that URL instead"
docs.x: Possible causes - The service answered with a redirect (often to a login page). SATOM doesn't follow redirects. Solution 1. If the target is the document, fetch that URL. If it's a login page, the WSDL needs authentication: get the file from the service team and upload it. Verification - The result starts with Fetched from .

docs.h: "Still pointing at what SATOM did not fetch …"
docs.x: Possible causes - A document references a schema on another host, or one that failed to download. It was stored with that reference unchanged. Solution 1. Fetch or upload the missing schema, and upload or fetch the referencing document again so its reference names the stored object. Verification - Pushing the document to a FortiWeb no longer fails with device refused the file: … Connecting to '<url>' … .

docs.h: "device refused the file: Cannot open '/data/etc/xml_schema/root/ ' to retrieve schema"
docs.x: Possible causes - The file references a schema that doesn't exist on the destination FortiWeb under that name, or that hasn't been created yet. Solution 1. Make sure the referenced schema is stored in SATOM under exactly that name and created on the device first. Verification - The object is listed on the device under API Protection → XML Protection .

docs.h: "errcode -3000: Internal error processing requested file. — FortiWeb 8.0.6 build0116 refuses every gRPC IDL upload …"
docs.x: Possible causes - The destination runs FortiWeb 8.0.6 build0116. It refused every gRPC IDL upload tried (ten contents and archive formats), through SATOM's API path and through the GUI's own session path, while 7.6.8 accepts the same file. The cause is the firmware, not the file. Solution 1. Open a case with Fortinet for gRPC IDL uploads on 8.0.6 build0116. 2. Until it's fixed, keep gRPC-protected policies on 7.6.8 appliances, or recreate the gRPC rule without the IDL on the 8.0.6 destination. Verification - The object is listed on the destination under API Protection → gRPC .

docs.h: " " " came back EMPTY from — nothing was stored."
docs.x: Possible causes - The object exists on the device by name, but has no content. Solution 1. Upload the real file instead. Verification - The object is listed as held, not as EMPTY .

docs.h: "The file is empty — there is no content once whitespace is discarded. …"
docs.x: Possible causes - The uploaded file has no content apart from whitespace. Solution 1. Pick the right file and upload again. Verification - The flash reads Stored <type> "<name>" (<n> bytes).

docs.h: "Not saved — this copy is read by device/ADOM pairs (…)."
docs.x: Possible causes - You edited a shared library copy without saying where the change goes. Solution 1. Choose All of them or Only one pair under Where does this change go? and save again. Verification - The flash reads Saved … or Forked … into a copy scoped to … .

docs.h: "Not saved — no walked policy on this device/ADOM reads this copy, …"
docs.x: Possible causes - You chose Only one pair , but no walked policy of the current device reads this copy. Solution 1. Refresh the index for this device first, or save for all pairs. Verification - The object page lists this device under Used by .

docs.h: An object shows "no known user" although a policy uses it
docs.x: Possible causes - No walk has recorded the edge yet, or the edge is older than 7 days and shown as stale. Solution 1. Click Refresh in Refresh the index . Verification - The object's row lists the policies that use it.

Advanced Storage and scope rules Blobs are stored gzip-compressed and addressed by SHA-256. A version row points at a blob, and deleting a version keeps the blob if another version shares it. Scope is always the session's device. Old links with ?appl= or ?scope= move the session to that device, then reload without the parameter. Stored versions are addressed by id. Blob, raw and delete requests for another device's version answer 404 or are refused. An edge older than 7 days is shown as stale. The scheduled action artifact_refs refreshes the index across the fleet in bounded, oldest-first batc

docs.s: A versioned library of desired-state templates (web protection profiles, system profiles, server policies, structures and captured configuration objects) with an approval workflow and a dry-run-first, canary-first apply.

docs.x: The Template Library stores reusable desired-state configuration as named, versioned JSON templates. A template is authored or captured once, reviewed by an administrator, and then pushed to one or many devices on demand. Editing never overwrites: saving produces a new version and the previous one stays.

Lists templates of four built-in kinds — Web Protection Profile , Server Policy , System Profile , Structure — plus configuration templates captured from Configuration sections (kind config:<section> ).
