Advanced Behaviour details Each appliance's API is read once per run, however many lines name it. Probing is chunked (20 targets) so the budget is checked often. Retired devices registered on a *.invalid host are refused before any connection is attempted. Reading pool members and deciding reachability reuse the same logic as the post-clone backend probe, so both report the same verdict for the same backend.

docs.s: Draw the network path of a service, bind each device element to its SATOM appliance, and read it live by layer (L2, L3, L4, L7). FortiGate interfaces and policies with hit counters are drawn segment to segment, back-ends answer an HTTP probe, and a flow trace asks every FortiGate on the way for its own verdict.

docs.x: Architecture is a page where you draw the network path of a service, the Internet, LANs, segments and VLANs, firewalls, WAFs, load balancers and back-end servers, and SATOM lays what the devices report on top of your drawing. You state what the network is. SATOM then reads the bound FortiGates and back-ends to check the drawing against the live devices. ℹ️ Note New in 3.1.0. The cache-based fleet map that used to be called Architecture is now Operations → Service Diagram ( /architecture/ ); see Service Diagram . The Service Diagram is derived : SATOM draws it from the FortiWeb cache. Architect

Drawings : named diagrams stored in SATOM. Every drawing is listed in every ADOM. Pick one from the Drawing list. Elements : Internet, LAN, Segment / VLAN, FortiGate, FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAuthenticator, FortiAnalyzer, Back-end server, Management host and Other host. Device elements can be bound to a SATOM appliance of the same kind. Read devices : reads the bound devices now, read-only and in parallel, and draws the result as a live overlay. You can repeat the read every 30 s . Layers L2 , L3 , L4 and L7 each show a different part of that overlay (see Layers ). Trace a flow : enter source,

At least one drawing. A user with configuration write permission creates it (see Create a drawing ). For the live overlay, appliances registered in SATOM (see Appliances ): FortiGate elements are read over the FortiGate REST API, with the credentials SATOM already holds for the appliance. FortiWeb elements show their server policies from SATOM's device cache , so the FortiWeb must have been synchronised at least once. Back-end server , Management host and Other host elements are probed only when you give them a Probe URL . FortiADC, FortiAuthenticator and FortiAnalyzer elements can be bound an

Without it: New drawing , Undo , Redo , Elements , Link , the delete button and Delete drawing are hidden. The inspector shows the element's values read-only, and elements cannot be dragged. docs.h: Put firewall policies on the drawing
docs.x: A policy can only be drawn between networks that SATOM can tie to the FortiGate's interfaces. Add a FortiGate element and bind it to its appliance ( SATOM appliance ). For each LAN, Segment / VLAN or Internet element behind that firewall, set Behind FortiGate to the FortiGate element. Either enter the FortiGate interface (for example port2 ), or enter the network's Network (CIDR) . Without an interface name, SATOM matches the network to the FortiGate port whose address falls inside that CIDR. Click Read devices . Each policy is then drawn as an arrow from its source network to its destination

Click Read devices . The status line reports how many devices, probes and policy flows were read, and at what time. Tick every 30 s to repeat the read while the tab is visible. Select an element to see its live detail in the inspector. Status dots on the elements: green means read, amber means some reads failed but policies were read, red means the read or probe failed, and grey means the element is bound to a device this ADOM cannot see.

Click Trace a flow . You can also select an element that has an IP address and click Trace from here or Trace to here . Enter Source IP and Destination IP , choose TCP , UDP or ICMP , and for TCP or UDP enter the destination Port (default 443). Click Trace . The path is drawn from the source to the destination: cyan if allowed, red if denied and amber if the verdict is unknown. The inspector shows the verdict with its reason and lists every firewall asked, with its ingress → egress interface, gateway, route, matched policy and action. A firewall that could not be read is listed with its error

Open pages check for a colleague's save every 15 seconds and redraw. The badge then reads Updated by with the colleague's name and the time. If you change the drawing while someone else saves it, their version is shown, the badge reads Updated by … — your change is in Undo , and Undo brings your version back. Undo and redo: the buttons, Ctrl+Z , and Ctrl+Shift+Z (or Ctrl+Y ).
Click Delete drawing below the canvas and confirm. The drawing is removed for everyone.

The layer buttons change what the overlay shows. L3 is the default. 🧪 Example — Is HTTPS from the LAN to the web server allowed? A drawing has an Internet element, a FortiGate element bound to fgt-01 , a LAN 198.51.100.0/24 and a Segment / VLAN 192.0.2.0/24 (both Behind FortiGate = fgt-01 ), and a Back-end server 192.0.2.20 linked to the segment, with Probe URL https://192.0.2.20/ . Click Read devices . In L3, the arrow #12 LAN-to-DMZ runs from the LAN to the segment. In L4 the same arrow reads #12 HTTPS · 3 sess · 4812 hits . Select the back-end and click Trace to here . Enter 198.51.100.50 as Source IP , keep TCP / 443 , and click Trace . The path turns cyan

Every save stores the whole drawing and writes an audit entry netarch.save (with the number of elements and links). Creating and deleting a drawing write netarch.create and netarch.delete . See Audit log . Every trace writes netarch.trace with source, destination, protocol, port and verdict. Read devices and the trace change nothing on any device and store nothing. Every value is read when you ask for it and is not cached.

docs.x: Enter a port, or choose ICMP .
The probe gets no HTTP answer within about 4 seconds. The error is shown in the inspector. The probe runs from the SATOM server, so check that SATOM can reach that address.

Advanced How the trace decides For each FortiGate, SATOM asks the device for its route to the source (the ingress interface) and to the destination (the egress interface). It then asks the device's own policy lookup for that ingress interface, addresses, protocol and port. SATOM never evaluates a rule base itself. The walk continues to the network drawn behind the egress interface and stops on the first deny, at the destination network, or when no firewall is drawn beyond. docs.s: Grade every site a FortiWeb server policy or FortiADC virtual server publishes with the MDN HTTP Observatory tests and scoring, see whether the FortiWeb, the application or the certificate caused each finding, and apply the FortiWeb fix with a preview of the grade it gives.

docs.x: The HTTP Observatory grades the sites your appliances publish the way the MDN HTTP Observatory (developer.mozilla.org/observatory) grades a public site: twelve tests, a score that starts at 100, and a letter from A+ to F. Unlike a public scanner it knows the configuration of the FortiWeb in front of the site, so for every result it says who produced it — the FortiWeb, the application or the certificate — and offers the FortiWeb change that fixes it.

Lists the published sites of the appliance you pick: one row per FortiWeb server policy or FortiADC virtual server, with its VIP, the HTTP and HTTPS ports it serves and a site name (the Host and SNI of the requests). Lets you choose which of them to work on: Select sites is a searchable checkbox list (policy, site name, Protected Hostnames, VIP), and only the ticked sites appear in the table. Searching never unticks; the selection is remembered per appliance in your browser. Grades one site ( Grade ) or every ticked one ( Grade selected ), with the tests and scoring of the MDN HTTP Observatory

A FortiWeb or FortiADC appliance SATOM can read. The SATOM server must reach the VIP of the policy on its HTTP/HTTPS ports. For fixes: a FortiWeb whose server policy has a Web Protection Profile (for the header and cookie fixes) and, for the redirect, both an HTTP and an HTTPS service.

Grading needs no free-target permission: SATOM dials only the VIP of a policy on an appliance visible to you, never an address you ty

docs.h: Grade the sites of an appliance
docs.x: Open Troubleshooting → HTTP Observatory and pick the appliance. Open Select sites , search, and tick the sites to grade. Select all matches ticks what the search shows; the ✕ on a row removes a site. Check the Site name of each row. It defaults to the first plain name of the policy's Protected Hostnames, otherwise the VIP. Type the name your users browse to — it is sent as Host and SNI, so a name-based site answers as it does for them. Click Grade on a row, or Grade selected . The Result card shows the grade, the score, how many tests passed, the previous grade, the redirect routes, the certif

Each test row shows the test, its modifier ( +5 , -20 …), the result and a Who badge: Badge Meaning FortiWeb The appliance sets it: an HTTP Header Security row, HSTS or the redirect on the server policy, or its own cookiesession1 cookie. A header the profile adds replaces the application's. Application The backend sent it; the FortiWeb passes it through. Certificate The points are lost to an untrusted certificate (HSTS and the redirect test fail whatever the headers say). Not sent Nobody sends it. Trace this request opens the Transaction Tracer on the site.

In the result, tick the fixes you want and adjust their options (header value, Content Security Policy text, HSTS max-age, cookie flags). Click Preview changes . You get the writes in order, the server policies they affect and Grade now … → after these fixes … . If other server policies share the profile, they are named and the confirmation tick appears: tick it to apply to all of them. Click Apply . Each write is re-read from the device ( verified ), and the site is graded again.

docs.h: Deploy a Content Security Policy without breaking the site
docs.x: On a site without a CSP, the Content Security Policy row offers Step 1 — send it as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only . Tick it, edit the policy to list the sources your site uses, Preview changes and Apply . The preview shows the grade does not change: the Observatory scores Report-Only like no CSP. Browse the site and watch the developer console (or the report-uri the policy names) for what the policy would block. Adjust the policy until nothing legitimate is reported. Grade again. The finding now names the Report-Only row, and Step 2 — enforce it starts from that exact policy. Apply it.

Right after Apply , click Revert these changes — or later, open History : Fixes applied to this site lists every applied set with its writes, and Revert on the one to undo. The Revert a fix card reads the appliance again and lists, newest write first, what it would do: will undo , left as is (with the reason) or nothing to do . If other server policies share the profile, tick the confirmation. Click Revert . The site is graded again.

Export CSV (next to Reload ): every published site of the appliance, its site name, ports, latest grade and score, and one column per test with its result code. PDF report (on a result): that result as a document, with who produced each finding and the fixes.
Click History in the result: every grade of the site, with who or what started it ( manual , scheduled , fix ). Open shows that grade with its findings recomputed against the current configuration.

A node arms HTTP Observatory — grade published sites by itself (daily 05:30, every FortiWeb and FortiADC) and HTTP Observatory — refresh the HSTS preload list (Monday 05:00). On a node installed before these existed, run sudo satom execute seed actions --yes ; satom diagnose install reports them missing until then. Edit or retarget them in Scheduled actions . The grading summary starts with Grade dropped: … when a site scored lower than in the previous run.

🧪 Example — A bare site behind a FortiWeb shop on fweb-01 grades F (0): no CSP, no HSTS, no X-Frame-Options, a session cookie without Secure or HttpOnly , no redirect to HTTPS, and a self-signed certificate. Ticking every offered fix previews 14 writes and Grade now F 0 → after these fixes C 55 . After Apply the site grades C 55 ; the remaining 40 points are the certificate (the summary says the site would score A+ 145 with a trusted one) and 5 are an external script without SRI, which only the application can fix.

Every grade is stored (60 per site); results keep headers, statuses, redirect routes and cookie flags — never cookie values or page bodies. Every applied set of fixes is stored with its writes and their previous values, so it can be reverted. Audit entries: observatory.scan per grade, observatory.fix per applied set of fixes (with the writes), observatory.fix.refused when a fix was refused, observatory.fix.revert per revert, observatory.export per CSV or PDF, observatory.hsts_preload.refresh / .import . Applied writes also appear in the appliance's change history, like edits made in the object

docs.h: "not graded" with "the site did not answer"
docs.x: Possible causes - The SATOM server cannot reach the VIP on that port (routing, firewall). - The policy is enabled but its back end does not answer. Solution 1. Open the site in the Transaction Tracer with Trace this request . 2. Fix the reachability, then Grade again. Verification — the row shows a grade.
Possible causes - The site answered with an error status; the Observatory does not grade error pages. Solution — fix the application or try another site name, then grade again.

docs.h: The redirect route ends with "not followed: outside this policy"
docs.x: Possible causes - The site redirects to another host or port. SATOM never dials a destination the policy does not publish. Solution — grade the destination site from its own policy. The redirect test still scores the route it saw.

docs.h: A fix shows "cannot add this header from HTTP Header Security"
docs.x: Possible causes - The appliance's firmware does not offer that header in profile rows (Cross-Origin-* headers on FortiWeb 7.x). Solution — set the header in the application, or upgrade the appliance.
Possible causes - An approved template governs the profile. Solution — change it in Template Library ; saving an approved template deploys to all devices.

docs.h: "… is being edited by …; nothing was sent to the device."
docs.x: Possible causes - Another user holds the edit lease on an object of the plan. Solution — wait, or take over the lock (see Locks ).

docs.h: Revert shows "left as is: changed since the fix"
docs.x: Possible causes - Someone changed that field (or edited the row) after the fix. SATOM never overwrites a change it did not make. Solution — the other steps are reverted; change that field by hand if it should go back too. A partly reverted fix can be reverted again later. Verification — the fix shows reverted in History once nothing is left to undo.

docs.h: "HSTS preload list: not on this node"
docs.x: Possible causes - The node has never downloaded it, or has no internet access. Solution — Refresh now , or Import file with a copy of Chromium's transport_security_state_static.json . Until then a preloaded site scores 5 below mozilla.org.

docs.h: HSTS still fails after enabling it
docs.x: Possible causes - The certificate is not trusted ( Certificate badge). Browsers ignore HSTS over an untrusted session; the test shows the header arrived but cannot pass. Solution — replace the certificate in Certificate Manager .

Advanced Differences from mozilla.org The HSTS preload list is the node's copy (refreshed weekly); a node without one grades every site as not preloaded. A non-numeric HSTS max-age is scored invalid (mozilla.org passes it). The SRI test's "same site" uses a short built-in list of multi-label public suffixes instead of the full Public Suffix List. Redirects are followed only while they stay on the scanned policy. Advanced What is fetched https://<site>/ and http://<site>/ with their redirects (up to 10), /robots.txt , and an OPTIONS preflight with Origin: https://observatory.satom.invalid for t

docs.t: Path Diagnostics — localise a broken service
docs.x: When someone says "this service is broken" , Path Diagnostics answers which layer is broken? You pick an appliance and name one published object — a FortiWeb server policy or a FortiADC virtual server — and Path Diagnostics walks a ladder of checks in dependency order. The first rung that fails is the verdict; every rung below it is marked not walked . Path Diagnostics is read-only : it issues only GET -type requests and never writes configuration. Path Diagnostics can be switched off for the whole site; the menu entry then stays visible but disabled, with the reason. A user without the permis

docs.t: Path Diagnostics — localise a broken service
docs.x: Advanced Rules of the ladder The first fail stops the walk; warn does not. A rung that cannot run is unknown and counted as a blind spot. Appliance health stops the walk only for capacity and deep-monitor signals; a stale harvest does not, because it describes SATOM's reach, not the data path. Each rung records its vantage (this node, the appliance, the collector); the three are never merged. Internally the page keeps its old identifier ( scout ): the URL, the blueprint, the settings keys and the audit action all still say scout .

docs.s: Every background task SATOM runs — and every action that talks to an appliance — is a job you can watch, pause, stop and inspect, from the Jobs page, the toast dock or a dedicated wait page.

docs.x: A job is a unit of background work with a status, a progress bar, an owner and a log. Firmware image verification, bulk applies, monitoring sweeps — and, above all, every POST that acts on an appliance — run as jobs, so a slow device never freezes a button or times out a page half-way through a change. You follow jobs in three places: the Jobs page (the Job Manager), the toast dock in the bottom-right corner of every page, and — for a classic form whose device action takes a while — a dedicated wait page .

Lists every running and finished job with its status, progress, owner, where it runs (server host and process id, appliance) and duration. Lets you Pause , Resume and Stop a job. Control is cooperative : SATOM sets a flag and the worker obeys it at its next safe checkpoint, so a write already in flight to a device is never cut in half. Shows, for device actions, one step per call to the device ( GET /api/v2.0/cmdb/server-policy/policy · 200 · 0.4 s ), so you can see where a slow action is. Queues writes to the same appliance behind each other, so two people pushing to one box at once cannot in

You must be signed in. No other permission is needed to see your own jobs. Device actions run as jobs only on the primary node. On a standby, and for API-token (Bearer) callers, the action runs inline as before (see What is excluded ).

The Jobs page and its endpoints require only a signed-in session. Who Sees Can control Any signed-in user Their own jobs (jobs whose owner is their user name) Pause / Resume / Stop their own jobs A user with users.manage ( Administrator ) Every user's jobs — the page header says "You are seeing all users' jobs." Pause / Resume / Stop anyone's job Jobs are additionally filtered by ADOM: a job stamped with a product is listed only in a console that can see that product. A job owned by someone else answers 404 not found rather than 403 . The response of a device action ( /jobs/<id>/response ) is

In the sidebar open Operations → Jobs (in the Global console: Global → Jobs ). The page is also linked from the Global home page and from All jobs → on an appliance's Jobs on this device card. The table refreshes itself every 3 seconds; the badge next to the title shows how many jobs match. Narrow the list with the All states dropdown, the Filter by title, type, user, device… box, or the Active only switch. Click a row (or the expand button) to see its detail: the list of Steps (for device actions, the last 200 calls) and the full job record as JSON, with a Copy button. Click the job ID to cop

docs.x: In the Actions column press Pause , Resume or Stop . Stop asks "Stop this job? It will halt at its next safe checkpoint." The status turns to Stopping… , then Stopped . A job that can no longer be interrupted shows a locked chip instead of the buttons. Status label Meaning Pending Created, worker not started yet Running Working Pausing… Pause requested; the worker has not reached a checkpoint yet Paused Parked at a safe checkpoint — "Paused — waiting at a safe checkpoint" Stopping… Stop requested; finishing the current step Stopped Ended by a Stop. Not a failure Success Finished normally Error

When an action on an appliance takes longer than the inline window (2 seconds by default): On a scripted page (buttons that call the server in the background) a toast appears in the dock and follows you across pages. When the job ends, the page that started it receives the real answer as if it had come back immediately. On a classic form you land on the wait page ( /jobs/<id>/wait ): a progress bar, the current message, every device call as it happens, and the buttons Stop (while it is still safe), Keep working — it continues in the background , Open in Jobs and Show result . When the action f

Each foreground job you own gets a toast in the bottom-right corner: Stop — shown only while the server says the job is cancelable. − ( Minimize ) — shrinks the toast to one line with the title, the percentage and a thin bar. Press □ ( Restore ) or click the title to bring it back. The minimised state survives page changes and a full reload of the tab. × ( Dismiss ) — removes the toast; the job keeps running and stays on the Jobs page. When the job ends the toast turns green, red or amber and offers View job → , plus Show result → for an action that produced a page or a file, or View before/af

Setting Description Required Example SATOM_JOB_INLINE_S Seconds a device action may run inline before it becomes a visible job. Default 2.0 No 2.0 SATOM_DEVICE_LOCK_MAX_WAIT_S How long a queued write waits for another job's lock on the same device before giving up. Default 1800 No 1800 SATOM_DEVICE_JOBS 0 / false / off / no disables device jobs entirely; every action runs inline No 1 These are environment variables of the web service (see Configuration files ).

🧪 Example — Two operators push to the same FortiWeb Alice saves a server policy on fweb-01 ; the save makes several REST calls. Thirty seconds later Bob applies a protection profile to the same box. Bob's job shows Queued — waiting for "Save object (objedit) · fweb-01" on this device and its toast title ends in — queued . Bob can still Stop it — nothing has been sent. When Alice's job finishes, Bob's job takes the device lock, its Stop button disappears (a multi-call write cannot be stopped half-way), and its steps start appearing.

A job record is written under data/jobs/<id>.json . A device action that answered inside the inline window and never reached a device leaves no record — a validation error or a pure database edit does not clutter the list. A device action's final response is stored under data/jobs/responses/ so it can be replayed (maximum 50 MB; larger bodies are not kept). The job's progress reflects real calls: an action with known phases shows a phased bar; otherwise the bar creeps towards 95 % per call and never claims completion early.

docs.x: Possible causes — the web service restarted (update, crash, reboot) while the job's worker thread was alive. Solution — check on the device whether the change was applied (for device actions: the steps list shows which calls completed) and repeat the action if needed.

Advanced How the scheduler fires satom-scheduler.service ticks every 45 seconds. Each tick first reclaims stale leases, then fires every enabled action whose next run has arrived. A fire claims the action with an atomic database update ( running_at ), so an action runs exactly once even if Run now is pressed at the same moment. The lease is always released when the run ends; a lease held longer than scheduler.lease_ttl_minutes (default 60) is reaped, the dead run is recorded as failed with "Lease reaped: …" , and the action fires again on its normal schedule. docs.x: A change request (CR) records a planned change to one or more appliances: the type of change, the affected devices and the published services they take offline, the maintenance window, the risk, the rollback plan and the approval. It carries a permanent reference of the form CR-2026-0042 . A CR is also a gate . Destructive automations — firmware upgrade, reboot, HA failover, the Cert Manager lifecycle sweep, Custom REST call — run only when bound to an approved CR that covers them (same action, only the devices it names), and only while the clock is inside its window. A value pasted with an explicit offset (for example 2026-08-10T22:00+00:00 ) is taken exactly as written. For scheduled actions , daily , weekly and monthly times are also local wall-clock times, so "every night at 02:00" stays at 02:00 across daylight-saving changes; interval schedules are durations. The Once → Run at field of the scheduled-action form is read in the same console timezone (its label names the zone) and stored as UTC.

Advanced How events are computed Future automation fires are projected from the schedule (never drawn on past days); the past comes only from recorded runs. All ranges are computed in the console timezone and converted to UTC for the queries. Each event links to the page that owns it: Automations or System Automations for an automation (by its scope), the change request for a change, the run history for a run. The day panels of up to 400 events are pre-rendered; beyond that a day still opens through its own link.

docs.k: lock edit lock lease concurrent editing take over heartbeat being edited conflict object lock checkout mutex editing conflict locked by another user protection.edit network.edit
docs.s: A short, self-renewing lease that marks a configuration object as "being edited" in the object editor, so two people do not overwrite each other's changes — with a Take over button when the other editor walked away.

docs.x: When you open an existing object in the object editor — full page or the inline editor embedded in configuration pages — SATOM takes a short lease on it — for example server-policy/policy:pol-shop on appliance fweb-01 . While you keep the page open the lease is renewed every 30 seconds. A second user opening the same object sees that it is being edited and is blocked from saving until the lease expires or they take it over. Edit locks are separate from the per-device write queue of jobs : the lease protects one object while somebody is editing it in the browser; the job queue serialises writes

Acquires a lease when an existing object is opened in the editor (not when creating a new object). Renews it every 30 seconds; a lease not renewed for 120 seconds expires. Shows other users a banner: "Being edited by . Saving is blocked to avoid a conflict." with a Take over button. Refuses, on the server, a save or delete of the object while another user holds its lease. Releases the lease when you leave the page or close the inline editor panel, and after a successful apply. If your own lease is lost, shows "Your edit lock was lost (expired or taken). Reload before saving." with a Reload but

A signed-in session with an edit permission (see below). The appliance is one of the devices visible to you in the current console. The object is opened in the object editor, full page or inline (for example the section configuration panel).

Acquiring, renewing and taking over a lease require any key that grants the legacy config_write — for example protection.edit , network.edit or operations.apply . A read-only user cannot take or take over a lease (they cannot save the object either). Releasing a lease and reading its status need only a signed-in session. Acquiring, taking over and reading the status of a lease work only on appliances visible to you (your visible devices in the current ADOM); a lease on any other appliance is refused. Saving the object still requires the editor's own permission (for example protection.edit or n

Open the object in the object editor. If nobody else holds it, no banner appears and you can edit normally. Save as usual. After a successful apply the lease is released. Closing or leaving the tab releases the lease (best effort); if the release is lost, the lease simply expires after 120 seconds.

The banner "Being edited by . Saving is blocked to avoid a conflict." appears and the Save actions answer "This object is locked by another user. Take over the lock first." A save or delete that reaches the server anyway is refused with " is being edited by . Take over the edit lock first; nothing was sent to the device." Check with the named user. If they are gone, press Take over . The lease becomes yours, the banner disappears and saving is enabled. The other user's page will show "Your edit lock was lost (expired or taken). Reload before saving." at its next renewal.

There is nothing to configure in the console. Value Description Default Lease duration Seconds a lease stays valid without a renewal 120 Renewal interval How often the editor page renews its lease 30 s Resource key <cmdb collection>:<object name> , scoped per appliance server-policy/policy:pol-shop

🧪 Example — Two operators open the same policy Alice opens pol-shop on fweb-01 at 10:00. Bob opens it at 10:05 and sees Being edited by alice . Alice went to lunch without closing the tab, so her page keeps renewing the lease. Bob calls her, she does not answer, and he presses Take over . When Alice returns, her page says the lock was lost and asks her to reload before saving.
One lease row per (appliance, object) in the database, holding the owner, acquisition time, last heartbeat and expiry. No audit entries are written for acquiring, releasing or taking over a lease.

docs.h: "Being edited by " but that user closed the page long ago
docs.x: Possible causes — the release was lost and the lease has not expired yet, or the user still has the tab open somewhere (an open tab keeps renewing). Solution — wait up to 120 seconds and reload, or press Take over .

docs.h: "Your edit lock was lost (expired or taken). Reload before saving."
docs.x: Possible causes — someone pressed Take over, or your browser could not renew the lease for more than 120 seconds (sleep, network loss). Solution — press Reload , re-apply your edits on the fresh object and save.

Advanced Scope and limits The lock is enforced in the browser and on the server : the editor blocks its own Save while another user holds the lease, and the object editor's save-object, save-row, delete-row and delete-object endpoints answer 409 while another user holds the lease on the object (or on the object a sub-table row belongs to). Creating or cloning an object is not gated by a lease. Other pages that write to the appliance do not check leases. Several editors on one page (inline panels) each hold their own lease. Leases are re-entrant: the same user opening the object in a second tab

docs.t: Integrations — NetBox, issue trackers and your own Python
docs.x: Settings → Integrations is where SATOM connects to systems it does not own: NetBox — records the maintenance window of a change request on the NetBox object of each appliance, and keeps a map of which NetBox object each appliance is. Issue tracker — opens a real ticket in Jira Cloud , OpenProject or Vikunja when you raise the ticket for a change request. Integration hooks — your own small Python scripts, run on SATOM events (a change requested or approved, a window opening or closing, an upgrade finished or failed, an alert fired) by a separate, unprivileged runner. Everything here is optional

Queues hooks to a runner that executes them out of the web process, with a hard timeout and only the secrets they declare. Lists every hook run with its status, duration and redacted output.

docs.h: A hook's ticket reference never appears on the change
docs.x: Possible causes — the reference is recorded only when the hook is bound to change.requested , its run ends ok , and its ctx.result data carries a non-empty crq_ref . A crq_url that does not start with http:// or https:// is dropped (the reference is still recorded), and a change that is already closed is left untouched. The hook's run status says whether the reference was recorded and, if not, why. Solution — check the hook's Recent runs ; fix the result keys or the failure, or copy the reference and press Record on the change's External change record card.

docs.k: certificate tls ssl chain fullchain intermediate expiry san wildcard private key openssl probe cert checker ssl checker chain checker unable to get local issuer certificate monitoring.probe_free
docs.s: Paste a certificate chain or probe a live TLS endpoint and find out whether the chain is complete, every link verifies, the hostname is covered and the private key matches.

docs.x: The certificate inspector answers "will a client accept this certificate?" . You either paste PEM text, or let SATOM open a TLS connection to a server and read what it presents. It puts the chain in leaf-first order, cryptographically checks each link, looks for the missing intermediate, and reports expiry, weak keys, hostname coverage and — if you supply it — whether a private key belongs to the certificate.

Accepts a single certificate, a fullchain file, or a whole openssl s_client -showcerts transcript (annotation lines and CRLF endings are tolerated). Up to 12 certificates are read from one paste. Orders the chain leaf → intermediate(s) → root, and lists certificates that belong to no position in the chain. Verifies every link by checking the child's signature with the parent's public key — not by comparing names. Decides whether the chain is complete : the top certificate is either a self-signed root in the bundle, or its issuer is found by name in the SATOM server's own CA trust store. Checks

For Paste PEM : nothing. For Probe a host : the SATOM server must be able to reach the target on the network. To read the full chain from a live server, the openssl binary must be installed on the SATOM node; without it only the leaf certificate can be read and chain completeness is reported as UNKNOWN . The probe tab tells you which case applies before you click.

Inventory destinations never need this."> monitoring.probe_free — users with users.manage also qualify Without mo

Open Tools → Certificate inspector . The Paste PEM tab is selected. Paste the certificate or fullchain into Certificate / fullchain (PEM) . Optional: type the name clients use into Hostname to check (for example shop.example.com ). Optional: paste the matching key into Private key . It is checked in memory against the leaf and is never stored or logged. If the key is encrypted, type its passphrase into Key passphrase (a password field; like the key, it is used in memory only). Click Inspect .

docs.h: Check a live server (Probe a host)
docs.x: Open the Probe a host tab. Either pick an appliance from Inventory destination , or type a target in …or a free target — host , host:port , [IPv6]:port or a full https:// URL. Optional: type a name into SNI / hostname to check . SATOM sends it as SNI and checks the certificate against it; left empty, the target's own host is used. Click Probe . SATOM resolves the target once and connects to that address. ℹ️ Note When you pick an inventory appliance, SATOM connects to the appliance's management address and port. Appliances are usually reached by IP address, so the hostname check will normally r

🧪 Example — A wildcard that "works in testing" You paste the fullchain for *.example.com and type example.com in Hostname to check . The verdict is critical: No presented name covers example.com — a wildcard covers one label ( www.example.com ) but not the apex. Reissue with example.com added to the SAN list.

Paste: nothing leaves the SATOM process and nothing is stored. Probe: one outbound TLS connection from the SATOM server. Every probe is written to the audit log as cert_inspect.probe (target, mode, dialled address, SNI, error if any); every refused free-target attempt as cert_inspect.probe_denied . See Audit log .

docs.h: "No PEM certificate block found. Paste the text between -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- and -----END CERTIFICATE----- (a fullchain may hold several)."
docs.x: Possible causes - You pasted a DER/binary file, a private key only, or a CSR. Solution 1. Convert or export the certificate as PEM and paste it again. Verification - The result shows at least one certificate card.

docs.h: "Free-target probing requires the 'monitoring.probe_free' permission. Inventory destinations remain available."
docs.x: Possible causes - Your profile does not include monitoring.probe_free . Solution 1. Pick the appliance from Inventory destination instead, or 2. Ask an administrator to add the permission to your profile. Verification - The …or a free target box is enabled and has no permission required badge.
Possible causes - The selected appliance is no longer visible to you (deleted, moved to maintenance, or belongs to another ADOM). Solution 1. Close and reopen the inspector to refresh the list.

docs.h: "… is not in the inventory for this request. Switch the tool to free-target mode to dial a host SATOM does not manage."
docs.x: Possible causes - The host you selected does not match an appliance address in the current ADOM. Solution 1. Use the free-target box (requires monitoring.probe_free ).

docs.h: "cloud instance-metadata address — it serves credentials to anything that can reach it, so SATOM never dials it"
docs.x: Possible causes - The target (or one of the addresses its name resolves to) is a cloud metadata address such as 169.254.169.254 . This is refused in every mode and cannot be configured. Solution 1. Probe the real service address instead.

docs.h: "port N is not an HTTP/TLS port — dialling it from the server cannot produce a meaningful result"
docs.x: Possible causes - The port is one SATOM never dials: 0, 22, 25, 465, 587, 6379 or 11211. Solution 1. Use the TLS port of the service.

docs.h: "Could not read a certificate from host:port (address) — …"
docs.x: Possible causes - The server is unreachable from the SATOM node, the port is not TLS, or the connection timed out ( timed out after 6s ). Solution 1. Confirm the service listens on that port and the SATOM node can reach it. 2. Try the Transaction tracer for TCP/TLS timing details.

Possible causes - openssl is not installed on the SATOM node, so only the leaf certificate could be read. This is not the same as incomplete . Solution 1. Install openssl on the node, or 2. Paste the server's fullchain file into the Paste PEM tab. Verification - The probe tab note reads The full chain is read with openssl s_client, so chain completeness is measured.

docs.h: "The private key was not checked — this private key is encrypted — supply its passphrase"
docs.x: Possible causes - The pasted key is passphrase-protected and Key passphrase was left empty. Solution 1. Type the key's passphrase into Key passphrase and click Inspect again. Verification - The Private key card shows whether the key matches the leaf. A wrong passphrase reports the private key could not be parsed instead.

Advanced How completeness is decided The chain is assembled by name (subject → issuer). Each adjacent pair is then verified by signature. Above the last presented certificate, SATOM looks for the issuer's distinguished name in the server's CA bundle (Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL, openSUSE or Alpine paths, falling back to certifi ). That last step is a name match, not a signature check , and the banner says so. Advanced Destination policy for probes Names are resolved once; every returned address must pass the policy, and the connection is made to the resolved address (not re-resolved), with the hostnam

docs.k: false positive carve-out exception attack log waf signature syslog decode base64 triage fp triage waf block blocked request why was this blocked
docs.s: Paste a FortiWeb attack-log entry or a raw HTTP request and see which module blocked it, which exception (carve-out) fits, and the exact payload SATOM would build — without saving anything.

docs.x: When the WAF blocks something legitimate, the question is "what exactly do I create so it stops — and nothing else stops with it?" . The false-positive explainer answers that from text you paste: an attack-log line from a ticket or syslog, a JSON entry from an API, or the raw HTTP request a developer used to reproduce the problem. It explains and drafts; it never saves.

Reads three input formats and says which one it detected: key=value (FortiWeb syslog / CEF-style), json (an object, or the first entry of a results / data / entries / rows envelope), and http-request (a request line such as POST /api/v2/tickets HTTP/1.1 plus headers). Maps field names from the different FortiWeb spellings onto SATOM's attack-log fields (for example srcip → src , url → http_url , sigid → signature_id ) and lists the renames. Lists what it could not use (keys that are not attack-log fields) and what is missing — main_type , signature_id , http_url , http_host , policy — together
None. The explainer does not contact any appliance and does not read the database for the entry; everything comes from the text you paste.

Any signed-in user can use it. Because it never saves, it needs no write permission. Saving the carve-out happens in Attack Search and needs the permissions documented there — see Attack search and Exceptions .

Open Tools → False-positive explainer . Paste the entry into Attack-log entry, or a raw HTTP request . Click Load a sample to see the expected shape. Optional: type the Web Protection Profile of that server policy. It is used only to name the profile in each card's Where on the device: path. Click Explain . Read the cards from top to bottom: - Entry read — the detected format, the fields used, the renames, and a Not used: warning for keys SATOM does not recognise. - Absent from this entry, and what each one decides — missing fields. - Payload, decoded — each decoding step, if any applied. - On

docs.h: Decode a payload without a log entry
docs.x: Paste the encoded value (for example %3Cscript%3E… or a base64 string) into Decode a payload on its own . Click Decode . The Payload, decoded card shows each step, or the panel says No encoding layer found when the value is already readable or does not decode to readable text. ℹ️ Note Changed in 2.11.0: the explainer has an optional Web Protection Profile field, shows Where on the device: under each carve-out, and has a Decode a payload on its own control.

Field Description Required Example Attack-log entry, or a raw HTTP request Up to 64 KB of text in one of the three formats Yes main_type="Signature Detection" http_url="/api/v2/tickets" signature_id="090200001" policy="pol-shop" Web Protection Profile Profile name shown in the Where on the device: path; does not change the recommendation No wpp-shop Decode a payload on its own A single encoded value, up to 64 KB For Decode %3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C%2Fscript%3E

🧪 Example — A cross-site-scripting block on a ticket form Pasted entry (shortened): main_type="Signature Detection" sub_type="Cross Site Scripting" policy="pol-shop-cms" http_url="/api/v2/tickets?draft=1" http_host="support.example.com" signature_id="090200001" The explainer recognises the key=value format, finds every deciding field, and recommends a per-signature exception for signature 090200001 scoped to the request URL and host — the narrowest change that clears the block. Alert only and Disable signature appear as wider alternatives at the bottom. 💡 Tip A raw HTTP request carries no main
Nothing is stored, nothing is sent to an appliance, and no audit entry is written. The panel always ends with No Save here. and the location Attack Search → the entry → Carve-out .
Possible causes - The input box is empty. Solution 1. Paste an entry, or click Load a sample .
Possible causes - Decode was clicked with an empty Decode a payload on its own field.

Possible causes - The text is not in one of the three supported formats, or none of its keys map to an attack-log field. Solution 1. Paste the original key=value line or the JSON object, not a screenshot transcription with labels such as "Source IP:". 2. For a request, make sure the first lines are METHOD /path HTTP/1.1 followed by headers. Verification - The Entry read card shows key=value , json or http-request .

docs.h: The recommended exception is narrower (or wider) than expected
docs.x: Possible causes - A field you consider important appears under Not used: — SATOM did not recognise its name, so the recommendation never saw it. - A deciding field is listed under Absent from this entry . Solution 1. Rename the key to the FortiWeb attack-log name (for example http_url , http_host , signature_id ) and click Explain again.

docs.h: I need to save the carve-out
docs.x: Possible causes - This tool deliberately has no Save button: an exception built from pasted text would let whoever supplied the text author the exception. Solution 1. Open the entry in Attack search on the appliance and use the carve-out panel there.

Advanced Same engine as Attack Search The explainer converts your text into the same row structure the Attack Search carve-out panel uses and then calls the same recommendation and assembly code, so the previewed payload is the payload that panel would build. Only the source of the evidence differs. Advanced Endpoints POST /fp-triage/triage (parse + recommend, used by Explain ; optional wpp ), POST /fp-triage/parse (parse only) and POST /fp-triage/decode (decode one value, used by Decode ). All require a signed-in session and accept up to 64 KB.

docs.s: Send the same HTTP request through the appliance and directly to the backend, compare the two answers and their cookies, read the result as a HAR in the page, and see what the appliance is configured to change in between — the fastest way to tell "is it the WAF or the application?".

docs.x: The transaction tracer answers the question every WAF incident starts with: is the appliance causing this, or the application? It sends one request through the appliance (leg A) and the same request straight to the backend (leg C), with the same Host header, and compares status, body and headers. A third view (leg B) lists what the appliance is configured to change on the way through — read from its server policy, never measured. It is a page under Operations → Troubleshooting , in every ADOM. Until 2026-10-16 it was a window in the top-bar Tools menu.

Leg A — through the appliance. A real request from the SATOM server to the address you give, measured phase by phase (TCP, TLS, time to first byte, total), with TLS version, cipher and certificate details. Leg C — direct to the backend. The same method, path, headers and body, sent to the backend address but carrying leg A's Host header (and SNI), so both legs ask the same virtual host. Diff and verdict. When both legs complete, one sentence tells you what the comparison means (see Result ). Leg B — derived. For a FortiWeb appliance and server policy you name, SATOM reads the policy, its pool,

The SATOM server must be able to reach the appliance address and the backend over the network. For Derive (leg B): a FortiWeb appliance that SATOM can read, and the exact server policy name. For Correlate attack log : a completed trace and an appliance whose attack log SATOM can read.

docs.h: "A free target requires the 'monitoring.probe_free' permission. Inventory destinations remain available."
docs.x: Possible causes - A request reached the server with a backend or a typed leg A address from a user without monitoring.probe_free (the panel disables both boxes for such users). Solution 1. Trace leg A from the inventory list only, or 2. Ask an administrator for monitoring.probe_free .

docs.h: "POST writes to the target application. It requires the 'monitoring.probe_free' permission."
docs.x: Possible causes - You chose a mutating method without the permission. Solution 1. Use GET , HEAD or OPTIONS , or request the permission.

docs.h: "POST is a real write to that application, issued from this server. Tick the confirmation to send it."
docs.x: Possible causes - The confirmation box was not ticked. Solution 1. Tick I understand this sends a real write… and click Trace again.

docs.h: "Give at least a VIP or a backend."
docs.x: Possible causes - Both leg A and leg C are empty. Solution 1. Fill in at least one of the two.

docs.h: "Only one leg was traced, so there is nothing to compare…"
docs.x: Possible causes - Only one of the two legs was given. Solution 1. Give both a VIP and a backend to get the diff.

docs.h: "Both legs must have completed. Leg A (via the appliance): TCP connect failed: …"
docs.x: Possible causes - A leg could not connect ( TCP connect failed ), failed the TLS handshake ( TLS handshake failed ) or the HTTP exchange ( HTTP exchange failed ). Solution 1. Check that the SATOM node can reach that address and port. 2. A backend without a scheme is traced as plain HTTP except on 443/8443; give https://host:port for a TLS backend on another port, or http://host:443 for a plain one on 443.

docs.h: What data is sent, and where
docs.x: Situation What leaves SATOM Local provider: kind ollama whose base URL host is localhost or a loopback, link-local or private address Your message, attachments, recent conversation history and (if enabled) tool results are sent unredacted to the Ollama base URL. External provider: any other kind, or an ollama provider whose base URL host is public or cannot be resolved The same content, sent to the provider's base URL. Your new message, its attachments, any tool results and every earlier message sent along as history (up to 19, yours and the model's) are first passed through SATOM's identifier

🧪 Example — Drafting a carve-out from a pasted block An operator pastes a FortiWeb attack-log line and asks "Is this a false positive? What exception would you add?" . The reply explains the signature and ends with a proposal card waf_exception — Allow ticket drafts . A user holding protection.edit clicks Apply as draft ; the exception appears on the Exceptions page for that appliance, not yet pushed.

Every message is stored in the conversation, with duration, token counts and the tools used. Every provider call — local or external, successful, failed or stopped — is recorded in the request ledger; calls to external providers are also recorded in an export log (provider, destination, bytes sent, redaction count). Audit log entries: advisor.send per exchange, advisor.proposal_apply and advisor.proposal_dismiss . See Audit log . A stopped reply keeps the text generated so far, marked stopped by you .

docs.s: Run your own Python over curated, read-only fleet datasets inside a locked-down sandbox — for one-off reports and checks that no built-in page answers.

docs.x: ℹ️ Note Now part of Python Studio. The console and the Script Library share one page, Administrator → Studio → Python Studio : the Console pane is this tool, and every script's editor has a Console tab with it too. The old address /database/py-console opens the Console pane. The Python Console runs a Python script you write against a snapshot of selected SATOM datasets — appliances, cached server policies, pools, WAF profiles, certificates, recent audit activity and so on. The script runs in an isolated sandbox: it can read only the data you ticked, cannot reach the network, the database or SA

Lets you tick one or more datasets ; each becomes data['<key>'] , a dictionary with columns and rows (a list of dictionaries). Runs the script and shows Output (stdout) and Errors (stderr) , a status badge ( ok , timed out or exit N / exit killed ), the duration and the datasets used. Offers Browse examples — a catalogue of ready-made scripts grouped by topic (fleet, certificates, audit activity, cross-references, data-quality checks…). Inserting an example also ticks the datasets it needs.

Key Contents fleet_appliances The managed devices visible to you: name, kind, firmware, host, port server_policies Cached FortiWeb server policies with their key columns server_policies_full Cached server policies with traffic log, web protection profile, monitor mode, comment and the App ID parsed from the comment server_pools Cached back-end pools with type and protocol web_protection_profiles Cached WAF profiles with their signature and bot-mitigation references certificates Certificates tracked by the Certificate Manager (no key material) audit_recent The 200 most recent audit-log rows; em

The console runs inside the web service, so it is bounded tightly: nothing in the jail is writable (no /tmp , read-only root and /dev — a file in a memory filesystem is memory no per-process limit counts), 512 MiB per process, a few processes or threads beyond those that exist, the output read as it arrives and kept up to 200 KB per stream, and one run at a time per node (a second one is told the console is busy).

The bwrap (bubblewrap) program must be installed on the SATOM node. Without it every run returns sandbox unavailable: bubblewrap (bwrap) is not installed . A python3 interpreter under /usr on the node (the sandbox runs /usr/bin/python3 ).

Action Needs Open the console and run scripts studio.python_console studio.python_console is an admin-only permission; only the seeded admin profile includes it. Users without it do not get the Console pane of Python Studio nor the editor's Console tab, and the console's run endpoint ( /studio/console/run ) answers 403 — even for a holder of studio.script_library , who opens Python Studio on the Scripts pane only. In the Global ADOM Python Studio is under Administrator → Studio . A profile that holds studio.python_console (or another Studio permission) but not users.manage cannot see Administr

Open Administrator → Studio → Python Studio (or Studio → Python Studio if your profile has no Administrator group) and click Console in the Explorer on the left. In Data bundle , tick the datasets your script needs. Write the script in Script , or click Browse examples and insert one. Click Run . The status shows Running in sandbox… and then the result. Read Output (stdout) ; if the script failed, Errors (stderr) shows the traceback (the sandbox's own frames are hidden).

Item Value Script size Up to 100,000 characters Wall-clock limit 8 seconds per run Memory 1 GiB address space Processes 256 Largest file the script may write (in its scratch /tmp ) 16 MiB Open files 128 Captured output 200,000 characters each for stdout and stderr Rows per dataset Up to 1,000

🧪 Example — Policies without a WAF profile Tick server_policies_full and run: rows = data['server_policies_full']['rows'] missing = [r for r in rows if not r.get('wpp')] print(f"{len(missing)} of {len(rows)} policies have NO WAF profile") for r in missing: print(' -', r['device'], '/', r['policy'])

Nothing is written anywhere: the script receives a read-only JSON copy of the data, and its scratch space is discarded after the run. Every run is written to the audit log as py_console.run , including the datasets, whether it succeeded, the exit code, whether it timed out, the duration and the first 1,000 characters of the source . See Audit log .

Possible causes - The bwrap package is missing on this SATOM node. Solution 1. Install bubblewrap on the node (an operating-system package), then run again. Verification - A trivial script such as print('ok') returns the ok badge.
Possible causes - The script ran longer than 8 seconds (or exhausted its CPU allowance). Solution 1. Tick fewer datasets, or avoid nested loops over large row lists.
Possible causes - The dataset was not ticked, so it is not in the bundle. Solution 1. Tick it in Data bundle and run again.

Advanced The sandbox Each run starts a fresh bubblewrap jail: all namespaces unshared (so no network), the environment cleared (SATOM's keys and database address are not visible), only /usr , /proc , /dev and an empty /tmp mounted, and the script plus its data bundle bound read-only at /sandbox . The application directory, its configuration file and the database are not mounted. Resource limits are applied with prlimit and the run is killed with timeout . Inside the jail the root and /dev are read-only, a file is at most 256 MB and the output is read as it arrives. At most 50 runs wait in the queue; run records are kept 30 days. Open Administrator → Studio → Python Studio , click New script and create a script: a name and an id (lowercase letters, digits, - , _ ; the id cannot change later). Write main.py . Read the form values from satom_script : ```python from satom_script import inputs, result, log, tcp log("checking %s:%s" % (inputs["host"], inputs["port"])) result({"ok": True}) ``` On Form , add one row per value the operator must give: variable name, label, type, required, default and help text. The preview is the exact form. For a value that should come from the SATOM database, choose the type lookup , lookup_m

inputs — a dictionary of the form values, keyed by field name. Numbers arrive as numbers, checkboxes as True / False . Only fields you defined reach the script: anything else a form submits is dropped. The values come on standard input, never as environment variables. Database fields arrive as rows SATOM read when the run was queued, for the ADOMs of the person it runs for (the operator for Run now , the owner for a saved run). It claims the request (at most once), copies the frozen files into a fresh directory and runs main.py inside bubblewrap: private process, user, IPC and network namespaces; only the system libraries, the Python environment (read-only) and the run's own directory a

docs.x: A data store is a table you define in the UI: a list of typed columns and the rows that fill it. Apps read and write its rows, form lists can take their choices from one of its columns, and you can edit it by hand.

Columns with a name, a label, a type — text , number , boolean , date (YYYY-MM-DD) or json — and required . Every row also has _id , _created_at , _updated_at and _by (who last wrote it). Rows : add, edit and delete them from the store's page; search the grid. Every value is checked against its column's type, and a column the store does not declare is refused , not dropped. docs.x: Python Studio runs code and diagrams that administrators write, for operators to use. This page is the model that keeps that code away from SATOM itself. It was checked by a security review and an adversarial test on a running node (2026-10-20); every rule is pinned by a test.

docs.t: What Python Studio code cannot do to SATOM
docs.x: Property What protects it Confidentiality Scripts and the console run in a bubblewrap jail with none of SATOM mounted — no .env , database socket, keys or other processes. The scripts runner has no database and no encryption key. A connection's secret reaches a run only as a single-use vault token unwrapped outside the jail. A connection never dials this node, the other HA node, loopback, link-local (cloud metadata) or reserved addresses. Changing where a connection points clears its secret. An answer that echoes the credential is masked. Operators see an app's outputs, not its step details. I

docs.s: Write, lint, statically analyse and (dry-run) deploy FortiWeb Web Scripting and FortiADC Scripting scripts, with a draft → tested → deployed lifecycle.

docs.x: Lua Studio is an editor for the scripts that run on the appliances: FortiWeb Web Scripting (Lua) and FortiADC Scripting (an event-block language). It checks the script without running it, explains what it touches, keeps a simple lifecycle, and builds the request a deployment would send. Deployment is a dry run unless you explicitly confirm a real push.

Lint : FortiWeb scripts are parse-checked with luac -p (compiled, never executed) and errors come back with line numbers. FortiADC scripts get a structural check instead — balanced parentheses and braces and at least one when <EVENT> { block — because they are not standalone Lua. Static analysis : What it does (functions from a curated FortiWeb or FortiADC API list, such as reads a request header or redirects the client ), Warnings (unterminated blocks, = inside a condition, os.execute / io.popen ), calls not in the target API, line count and a binding hint. Lifecycle : Draft → Tested → Deploy

A luac binary on the SATOM node ( luac5.4 , luac5.3 , luac5.1 or luac ). Without it, lint fails with luac not available on server — for FortiADC scripts too, even though they get only the structural check. For a real deploy: a device selected on the script, reachable by SATOM.

docs.s: Sentinel turns FortiWeb attack-log events, HTTP outcomes, appliance and infrastructure metrics and vulnerability data into scored incidents that explain themselves, and proposes — never silently performs — responses.

docs.x: Sentinel answers "what is actually happening right now, across every layer at once?" . It reads the FortiWeb attack log and traffic outcomes, lines them up with appliance, VM, hypervisor and backend metrics and with a local copy of vulnerability intelligence, and groups related events into incidents with a score from 0 to 100. Every number on an incident can be traced back to its evidence. When a response is warranted, Sentinel proposes it; whether anything is ever executed is decided by the response policy, a set of gates, and — in most configurations — a person.

Collects FortiWeb attack-log events in sweeps (run on demand or by the sentinel_sweep scheduled action). FortiADC appliances are not swept — they have no attack log. Correlates events into incidents (reference INC-<year>-<number> ), with a timeline, an evidence table and time-aligned charts of every layer. Scores each incident with a fixed, published weight table, including factors that lower the score (for example, a WAF that is already answering 403). A behavioural baseline (per hour of the week) is used once it has learned enough; immature buckets never fire. Proposes responses from a close

Open Monitoring → Sentinel in the Global ADOM. Click Run sweep now . The Run a sweep window lists FortiWeb appliances; ones in maintenance or with a retired host are shown but cannot be selected. Pick devices ( Select all / Select none ; nothing selected means every eligible device) and click Start sweep . The sweep runs as a job: Sweep started as job N over M device(s). Progress is in the Jobs dock; this page does not wait for it. See Jobs .

In Incidents , click Open on an incident. Read How this score was reached and Evidence . Use Re-correlate to rebuild them from current data. Optional: Ask the model for an AI assessment (only if AI reasoning is enabled in settings). In Response , expand an action to see each gate, add a note and click Record decision . An allowed action is queued for the response runner, which re-checks every gate before writing anything; a refused one is recorded as rejected with the reason. Close it under Close : choose closed — handled , mitigated — an action worked or false positive . A false positive need

Open Response policy . Under Operating mode , review the four presets — Alert only , Alert and block , High , Ultra high — and their Risk notes. Click Apply <mode> . A mode only writes values into the existing settings and policy rows; edit any of them afterwards and the posture reads Custom . ❗ Important No mode changes AI consent, vulnerability-feed consent, the never-block list or hardened profiles. Blocking a country never goes beyond recommend , even in Ultra high . An action whose mechanism has not been verified against a live appliance executes nothing in any mode.

/sentinel/docs (also Settings → Sentinel → Architecture ) explains the design in twelve numbered sections — the two paths (deterministic pipeline vs. optional AI), diagrams, correlation layers, the baseline, the live weight table and bands, HTTP outcomes and vulnerability intelligence, the response catalogue and gate order , the AI wall and its allowed answers, false-positive reasons, attack families, every setting and what it changes , and the scheduled actions that run it. Tables on that page are generated from the running code, so they always match the installed version.

Incidents, evidence, actions and decisions are kept in SATOM's database; the timeline of each incident records every decision and who made it. Arming a policy for enforcement is written to the audit log as sentinel.arm . Scheduled actions: sentinel_sweep , sentinel_baseline , sentinel_vuln_sync , sentinel_feed_publish . Queued actions are executed by the separate response runner service. See Scheduled actions .

docs.h: "Sentinel is disabled in Settings — nothing was collected."
docs.x: Possible causes - Sentinel is switched off. Solution 1. Switch it on in Settings → Sentinel → Settings (configuration-write).

docs.h: "Every device you picked is in maintenance or retired — a sweep would skip all of them, so none was started."
docs.x: Possible causes - Only ineligible appliances were selected. Solution 1. Take the appliance out of maintenance, or pick other devices.
Possible causes - No sweep heartbeat has reached the metrics store yet. Solution 1. Run a sweep, or schedule the sentinel_sweep action. Verification - The tile shows Ns ago .

docs.h: "AI reasoning is disabled in Settings — the incident keeps its deterministic score and evidence."
docs.x: Possible causes - AI reasoning is off in Sentinel settings.
Possible causes - A gate refused the action (kill switch, band, rate limit, never-block list, unarmed policy…). The reason is shown and recorded on the timeline.

docs.h: "… approved and recorded, but NOT queued: its mechanism has never been run against a live appliance of this product, so there is nothing to execute."
docs.x: Possible causes - The action's transport is not verified. This is by design.

docs.h: "a false positive must record why it was one"
docs.x: Possible causes - false positive was chosen without a reason.
Possible causes - A line in the never-block list is not a valid address or range. Those lines protect nothing. Solution 1. Fix them in Settings → Sentinel .

Advanced Where to read more The full design — scoring factors, gate order, operating-mode presets, border corroboration and the blocklist feed — is described on the architecture page of your installation. For the background services involved, see Services and timers . Advanced What never happens A page view never contacts an appliance. Approving an action only queues it; the runner re-evaluates every gate at execution time and confirms the result by re-reading the device. Response arming (binding Sentinel's list to a policy's protection profile) is a separate, explicit, audited operator action
