docs.s: Fleet-wide defaults for the Server Policy Clone and Migrate dialogs — the dummy-IP rules that keep a copied VIP from taking real traffic, the fallback dummy IP, and whether the Web Protection Profile is copied by default.

docs.x: Clone / Migrate holds the defaults the Server Policy Clone and Migrate dialogs start from. A bulk clone or migrate always rewrites each copy's VIP to a dummy IP using these rules, so the copy cannot take real traffic; a single-policy dialog prefills the same suggestion but lets the operator decide. How cloning works is described in Policy cloning .

Dummy-IP transformation rules — ordered rules that replace the leading octets of the source VIP and keep the rest (first match wins). 10 → 240 turns {ip} into 240.1.10.1 . Fallback dummy IP — used when no rule matches (or the source is not parseable). Copy the Web Protection Profile by default on clone / migrate — the default for the dialog's WPP choice. Operators see these values in the dialog and can override them per run only after ticking Override admin defaults .
users.manage to edit.
🔑 Permission POST /settings/clone-rules requires users.manage ; others get 403 and do not see the tab. Operators running a clone see the values read-only unless they tick Override admin defaults .

Open Settings → Fleet & Devices → Clone / Migrate . Edit the rules under Dummy-IP transformation rules (first match wins) ; two empty rows are offered for new rules. Clear both cells of a row to remove it. Set Fallback dummy IP (no rule matches) . Tick or untick Copy the Web Protection Profile by default on clone / migrate . Click Save clone/migrate rules — "Clone/Migrate rules saved (N IP rules)."

Field Description Required Example IP starts with (octets) 1–3 leading octets, each 0–255. Per rule 10 Replace with Same number of octets as the match, each 0–255. Per rule 240 Fallback dummy IP (no rule matches) A valid IPv4 address. Blank saves the default 203.0.113.9 . No 203.0.113.9 Copy the Web Protection Profile by default on clone / migrate Default on . No on Shipped default rules: 10 → 240 and 162 → 241 .

🧪 Example — Rewrite two private ranges Rules: 10 → 240 , 172.16 → 240.16 . A bulk migration of a policy on VIP {ip} creates the copy on 240.16.4.20 ; a VIP 192.0.2.80 matches no rule and the copy gets the fallback 203.0.113.9 .
The policy is stored in app_settings ( clone.rules ); audit entry settings.clone_rules with rule count, fallback and WPP default. The next Clone or Migrate dialog shows the new defaults.

docs.h: "Clone/Migrate rules NOT saved: match '…' and replace '…' must have the same octet count"
docs.x: Solution — use the same number of octets on both sides (for example 172.16 → 240.16 ).

docs.h: "Clone/Migrate rules NOT saved: a rule matches 1 to 3 leading octets, got '…'"
docs.x: Solution — a rule cannot match a full four-octet address; use at most three octets.

docs.h: "Clone/Migrate rules NOT saved: octet '…' is not in 0-255"
docs.x: Solution — correct the octet.

docs.h: "Clone/Migrate rules NOT saved: fallback IP '…' is not a valid IPv4 address"
docs.x: Solution — enter a dotted IPv4 address. Nothing is saved while any error remains; all errors are listed together.
Advanced Notes Rules are evaluated in the order shown; the first rule whose octets prefix the source VIP wins. Leading and trailing dots in a rule are ignored ( 10. equals 10 ).

docs.s: Choose which of SATOM's five interface languages users of this installation may pick; English, the source language, is always offered.

docs.x: SATOM speaks five languages: English ( en , the source language), Español ( es ), Deutsch ( de ), Français ( fr ) and Italiano ( it ). The Languages tab answers a different question from that list: which of them may a user pick on this installation . A withdrawn language disappears from the profile language picker, from the change-document language question and from browser language negotiation.

Lists every language the product speaks, including withdrawn ones, so a withdrawal can always be undone from the same page. Shows two read-only columns: Change documents — produced if a complete change document can be generated in that language, not translated yet otherwise. It describes the catalogue, not the switch. Chosen by — how many users have that language as their stored preference (or nobody ). Enforces three rules on the server: English is always offered (rendered ticked and disabled, and added back on save). Withdrawing never rewrites a user's stored preference; it is simply not hon
users.manage .

🔑 Permission POST /settings/languages requires users.manage ; others get 403 and do not see the User Interface group. Every user picks their own language on their profile page (see Users and profiles ).

Open Settings → User Interface → Languages . Check Chosen by before withdrawing a language that people use. Tick the languages to offer in the Offered column; untick to withdraw. Click Save language availability . The flash reads, for example, "Language availability saved — 3 offered, 2 withdrawn."

Field Description Required Example Offered One switch per language. Default (never saved): all offered. The English switch is always on and disabled. No en , de Status hints next to the button: Never configured — every language is offered until you save here. The stored setting is unreadable and is being ignored — every language is offered. Saving here replaces it.

🧪 Example — A German-speaking operations team Tick English (fixed) and Deutsch , untick the others, save. Users now choose between English and German. A user who had picked Français keeps that preference, sees English or German pages, and their profile page notes that French is currently not offered. Re-enabling French later restores it for them without any action.

The offered set is stored in app_settings ( i18n.offered ); the audit entry settings.languages records both the offered and the withdrawn codes. Translation catalogues are untouched; a re-enabled language is complete immediately. Since 3.1.0 every interface string has a translation in all four languages, and a release guard keeps it that way (a string without a translation, or with a lost placeholder, fails the build).
Possible causes — a database error (for example on a read-only standby). Solution — save on the primary node.

docs.h: A user sees English although they chose another language
docs.x: Possible causes — their language is withdrawn here, or their browser asks for a language that is not offered. Solution — offer the language, or ask the user to pick an offered one on their profile page. If only some labels stay in English, the node runs code newer than its compiled catalogues: run satom execute restart-all after an update (the updater compiles them), or compile by hand as the service user with venv/bin/pybabel compile -d app/translations .

docs.h: "That language is not offered on this installation."
docs.x: Possible causes — shown on the profile page when a user tries to save a withdrawn language. Solution — offer the language here first.

Advanced Notes The Change documents column is computed before the availability switch on purpose, so it never claims a language is unusable merely because it is switched off. A language marked not translated yet can still be offered for the interface; the change-request form then keeps asking which language a document is drafted in instead of picking that one.

docs.h: A page with that banner is still in the menu
docs.x: Possible causes — the switch is off, or the page has another tab that is configuration. Solution — check the switch; open the page and look at its tabs: only a page whose every tab is of a hidden kind leaves the menu.

docs.s: The two self-service Settings tabs every signed-in user has — two-factor authentication, backup codes, recovery email and session sign-out on Security, and the Change Password form.

docs.x: My Account is the only Settings group a non-administrator sees, and the page they land on is Security . It holds two tabs: Security (two-factor authentication, recovery email and sign-out) and Change Password . Accounts that sign in through a directory (Active Directory, LDAP or FortiAuthenticator) manage their password and multi-factor authentication at the directory instead.

Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP) — set up an authenticator app, receive ten one-time backup codes, regenerate them, or disable 2FA. Account Recovery — a Recovery email used by Forgot password on the sign-in page. Active Sessions — your current session and a Sign Out button. Change Password — current, new and confirm.
A signed-in account. 2FA, backup codes and the recovery email are for local accounts. For password reset by email: server email configured on Email & Alerts and a recovery email on file.

🔑 Permission No permission is needed: every route on these two tabs requires only a signed-in user, and acts only on that user's own account. Directory accounts see "Your account authenticates against a directory — manage multi-factor authentication there." and "Directory accounts recover their password at the directory." instead of the 2FA and recovery controls.

Open Settings → My Account → Security and click Set up 2FA . Scan the QR code with an authenticator app (or type the secret shown). Enter the 6-digit code under 2. Enter the 6-digit code to confirm: and click Enable . The flash reads "Two-factor authentication enabled. Save your backup codes now — they are shown only once." Copy the ten codes from the yellow box; they are not shown again. From then on, sign-in asks for a code after the password; a backup code works once in its place.
Click Regenerate backup codes — "New backup codes generated. Save them now — the old ones no longer work." The card always shows Backup codes remaining: N .
Type your password in Confirm password to disable , click Disable 2FA and confirm the dialog Disable two-factor authentication? — "Two-factor authentication disabled."
Enter the address under Recovery email and click Save — "Recovery email updated." Leave it empty and save to remove it ( "Recovery email cleared." ).

Open Settings → My Account → Change Password . Fill Current Password , New Password (a strength bar shows Password strength: … ) and Confirm New Password . Click Update Password — "Password changed successfully." ℹ️ Note Changed in 2.11.0: a new password must have 12 to 1024 characters, the same policy as every other password path (before, this form accepted any non-empty password), and the static Security Status card was removed from the Security tab.

Field Description Required Example 6-digit code Current TOTP code from the app (one step of clock drift is tolerated). To enable 492817 Confirm password to disable Your current password. To disable — Recovery email Must contain @ and a dot in the domain; empty clears it. No alice@example.com Current Password Your current password. Yes — New Password 12 to 1024 characters, length only (no character-class rule) — the same policy as the profile page, the reset link, the administrator's Add User / Reset password and the root CLI. A shorter password is refused. Yes — Confirm New Password Must equal

🧪 Example — Secure a new local account After first sign-in , open Security, enable 2FA with your phone, store the ten backup codes in your password manager, set a recovery email, then change the initial password on Change Password.

Audit entries: settings.2fa_enable , settings.2fa_disable , settings.2fa_backup_regen , settings.recovery_email , settings.change_password . The TOTP secret is stored encrypted; backup codes are stored so that each works once.

docs.h: "Invalid code — 2FA was not enabled. Re-scan the QR and try again."
docs.x: Possible causes — wrong code, phone clock out of sync, or the setup was started in another browser tab (the pending secret lives in your session). Solution — sync the phone's clock, click Set up 2FA again and use the new QR code.
Solution — type your current account password.
Solution — backup codes exist only while 2FA is enabled on a local account.

docs.h: "Directory accounts manage MFA at the directory."
docs.x: Solution — use your directory's MFA (for example FortiToken on FortiAuthenticator).

docs.h: "Current password is incorrect." on Change Password
docs.x: Possible causes - A typo in the current password. - Your account is a directory account: it has no usable local password, so this form always fails. Change the password at the directory.

docs.h: "New passwords do not match." / "A password is required."
docs.x: Solution — retype both fields identically.

docs.h: "The password must be at least 12 characters."
docs.x: Possible causes — the new password has fewer than 12 characters. Solution — choose a password of 12 to 1024 characters. A long passphrase is fine; no particular mix of character types is required.
Solution — correct the recovery email.

docs.h: "Too many failed attempts — account temporarily locked. Try again later." at sign-in
docs.x: Possible causes — ten consecutive failed sign-ins lock the account for 15 minutes. Solution — wait, or ask an administrator to click Unlock on your row in Users (see Users and profiles ).

Advanced Notes Forgot password sends a reset link valid for one hour, only for active local accounts with a recovery email, and only when server email is configured; the sign-in page never reveals whether the account exists. The link in that email uses the host the request came in on only when it is one of the node's own names or is listed in LINK_HOSTS ; any other host is replaced by the node's FQDN. See Configuration files . Active Sessions shows the current session only; signing out elsewhere is not offered.

docs.s: Configure how SATOM sends email (local relay or external SMTP) and the alert engine's delivery policy — which checks run, their limits, the cooldown, and which of the five sinks (bell, email, webhook, integration hooks, syslog/CEF) receive which findings.

docs.x: The Email & Alerts tab holds two forms. Email (SMTP) Configuration is the mail transport every feature uses. Alerts & notifications is the delivery policy of the proactive health engine ( satom-alerts.timer , every 15 minutes): which checks may raise findings, the limits they use, how often a finding may repeat, and where each finding is delivered. What counts as bad for probes and devices is measurement policy and lives on Thresholds .

Sends mail through the node's local relay or an external SMTP server, with a Send test button. Turns alert dispatch on or off and sets the alert recipients. Enables or disables each of the eight checks: Cert expiry , Git divergence , Device health , Backup freshness , Config drift , Scheduled automation , Host resources , API catalog integrity . Routes findings to five delivery sinks , each with its own on/off switch, minimum severity and family mask: In-app bell , Email , Webhook (HTTP POST) , Integration hooks , Syslog / CEF feed . Preview now (no send) evaluates every enabled check and show

users.manage . For external SMTP: host, port and (optionally) credentials of a mail server reachable from the node. For the webhook: an HTTP(S) endpoint. For syslog: a collector such as FortiAnalyzer or a SIEM.

🔑 Permission All routes ( POST /settings/email , /settings/email/test , /settings/alerts , GET /settings/alerts/preview ) require users.manage . Without it the Monitoring & Alerts group is hidden and calls return 403 .

Open Settings → Monitoring & Alerts → Email & Alerts . Switch on Enable email sending , choose Server type , fill the fields and click Save email settings — "Email settings saved." In Send a test email , enter a Recipient and click Send test . The test uses the saved settings. Success shows e.g. "Sent to ops@example.com via smtp.example.com:587 (starttls)."

In Alerts & notifications , switch on Enable alert dispatch , fill Alert recipient(s) and tick the Checks enabled . Adjust the limits on the right (see Configuration ). In Delivery sinks , set each sink's On , Minimum severity and Families delivered . Fill Webhook endpoint and/or Syslog collector if you use those sinks. Click Save alert settings — "Alert settings saved." Click Preview now (no send) . It lists the findings that would fire and the resolved recipients, e.g. "3 finding(s) would notify ops@example.com (nothing sent — preview only):" or "No findings — all checks green. Recipients: …

Settings are stored in app_settings ( email.* , alerts.* , alerts.sink.* , alerts.webhook.* , alerts.syslog.* ); audit entries settings.email , settings.email_test and settings.alerts . On the next engine run (every 15 minutes) findings are routed per sink. The six limits shared with the SATOM (the application) scope on Thresholds are the same stored values.

docs.h: "Enter a recipient (or set a default recipient)."
docs.x: Solution — type a Recipient in the test card or set Default recipient(s) and save.
Solution — fill From address (or a username) and save before testing.
Possible causes — wrong username or password, or the server needs an app password. Solution — re-enter the password (blank keeps the old one), save, test again.

Possible causes — the transport security does not match the port, the certificate is not trusted, or a firewall blocks the port. Solution — use STARTTLS on 587 or SSL/TLS on 465; for an internal CA either trust it on the node or (insecurely) untick Verify TLS certificate .

docs.h: A device is red but no mail arrived
docs.x: Possible causes - Enable alert dispatch is off, or the Email sink is off, masked, or its severity floor is above the finding. - Device alert floor is Critical only and the device is only degraded. - The finding fired within the Cooldown window. Solution — click Preview now (no send) ; it shows what would fire and the resolved recipients.

docs.h: The webhook URL shows "URL must start with http:// or https://" or "URL has no host"
docs.x: Solution — correct the Endpoint URL and save; the value is kept and flagged until fixed.

Advanced Behaviour worth knowing The bell, email, webhook and hook sinks share the cooldown; the syslog feed has none and is not counted as dispatched . Hooks are counted as queued , never dispatched . A finding no notification sink accepted is not stamped for cooldown, so widening a filter later delivers it on the next run. Mail subjects read [SATOM/<node>] N alert(s) — <first title> . The preview endpoint also returns per-sink counts ( routed ) as JSON; the page itself shows the findings and recipients only.

docs.k: thresholds limits warning critical probes cpu memory sessions roll-up binary facts host disk alert thresholds warn level crit level measurement policy default limits users.manage
docs.s: Declare monitoring limits once per product (and for SATOM and its host) so every probe that has no value of its own inherits them, with the origin of every number shown.

docs.x: Thresholds is the measurement policy : what a number has to reach before it is graded warning or critical. You declare a limit once per scope and every probe that has not been given its own value follows it live. Who is told, and how often, is delivery policy and lives on Email & Alerts .

Offers one scope per product ADOM (from the ADOM registry — normally FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer, FortiAuthenticator), plus SATOM (the application) and SATOM host (the machine) . For a product scope, three sections: Measurement — per probe kind that the product can run (only kinds the product supports are shown). Device roll-up — how the device signals combine into the badge on Fleet health. Binary facts — conditions with no number, each set to crit , warn or off (still shown, never graded) . For SATOM (the application) — six limits of the alert engine; they are the same stored values as
users.manage . Probes to grade (see Probes and Deep monitors ).

Leave a box empty to clear the override (the field falls back to the shipped default and every inheriting probe follows). Type 0 to switch that level off. Click Save this scope . The status line reads "Saved N, cleared M." or lists the errors. To undo everything in the scope, click Revert scope to shipped defaults and confirm "Clear every override in this scope and go back to the shipped defaults?" — "Cleared N override(s)." 1 Probe column used only if someone set

docs.x: Settings → Sentinel → Settings is where Sentinel, SATOM's security-correlation pipeline, is configured. The pane explains what it configures before the form: the pipeline stage by stage, the score bands and live weight table, and ten scenarios you can run against the real engine. Defaults make a fresh installation observant but inert : detection on, actions off, no traffic to any third party. Using Sentinel (incidents, context, response policy, blocklist) is described in Sentinel .

The section has four parts: What Sentinel does, stage by stage — Collect → Normalize + dedup → Route → Correlate → Score → Policy gates → Respond / propose, each with the settings that govern it. The sweep runs every 3 minutes. The score, and what each band permits — the bands observe , investigate , recommend and semi-auto , and the live tables Adds points / Subtracts points read from the scorer. See it happen — ten scenarios against the live engine — each card runs synthetic evidence through the real scorer, bands and policy gates ( simulation — nothing is written, no device is touched ). docs.s: Mint, scope, edit, revoke and delete the bearer tokens that let external systems call the /api/v1 integration API.

docs.x: An API token is a credential for a machine, not a person. External systems (a SIEM, a ticketing workflow, a CMDB) send it in an Authorization: Bearer <token> header to call SATOM's versioned integration API under /api/v1 . Each token is owned by a real SATOM user, bound to one ADOM, limited by a scope and optionally narrowed further by capabilities and an AppID scope . This page is where an administrator issues and manages them; what the API itself offers is described in the API reference .

Create a token and show the full secret exactly once . List every token with its owner, scopes, capabilities, AppID scope, ADOM, status ( active , expired , revoked ) and when it was last used. Edit a live token's name, ADOM, scopes, capabilities, AppID scope and expiry. The secret itself can never be shown or changed again. Revoke a token (it stays in the list, greyed out, and stops working). Delete a token (the row is removed). Every one of these writes an entry to the audit log .

The owner must be an active SATOM user. Only active users are offered in the Owner list. The ADOM you bind the token to must have the API Tokens capability ticked in Settings → ADOMs (see Settings ). Only those ADOMs appear in the ADOM list. On a fresh install every shipped ADOM, including global , has it. To use an AppID scope, the AppIDs must exist and be active under AppIDs , with server policies assigned to them.

🔑 Permission Every route on this page requires users.manage (the legacy user_manage gate) — in practice the Administrator profile. A user without it gets 403 Forbidden if they open /api-tokens/ directly. The sidebar entry is rendered inside the Administrator group of every ADOM whose product has the API Tokens capability; that group is itself hidden from users without users.manage . The token never exceeds its owner's permissions. This is checked twice: when the token is created or edited, a scope whose permission the owner does not hold is refused; and on every API call, the owner must still

1 Create Fill in name, owner, ADOM, scopes; optionally capabilities and AppIDs 2 Copy The full token is shown once — store it in your secret manager 3 Use The external system sends Authorization: Bearer <token> 4 Maintain Edit scope or expiry, revoke or delete when no longer needed

Open Administrator → API Tokens (in the FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer, FortiAuthenticator or Global ADOM, whichever has the API Tokens capability). In the Create a token card, fill in: - Name — a label, e.g. siem-integration (required in the form). - Owner (inherits RBAC) — the user whose permissions cap the token. - ADOM — the product the token is bound to. - Expires (days) — leave empty for a token that never expires. Tick one or more Scopes . read is ticked by default; if you untick all of them the token is saved with read . Optionally open Capabilities ( what kinds of action) and AppID

In Existing tokens , click Edit on the token's row. In the Edit token dialog change any of Name , ADOM , Expiry (days) , Scopes , Capabilities or AppID scope . For Expiry (days) : - leave it blank to keep the current expiry (the hint shows it); - enter a number to set the expiry that many days from today ; - enter -1 to remove the expiry (never expires). Click Save changes . The flash message reads Token “<name>” updated. The owner of a token cannot be changed. To move a token to another owner, create a new token and delete the old one.

Click Revoke on the row and confirm "Revoke token '<name>'? Every client using it stops working immediately." The token stops authenticating immediately, its status badge turns to revoked and the Revoke button disappears. The flash message reads Token “<name>” revoked. A revoked token can still be edited but cannot be reactivated.
Click Delete on the row and confirm "Delete token '<name>'? This cannot be undone." The flash message reads Token deleted.

Send it as a bearer header on every call: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer fmk_<public-id>_<secret>" \ https://satom.example.com/api/v1/ping /api/v1/ping answers with the token's name, owner, scopes, capabilities, AppID scope and ADOM, which is the quickest way to check what a token can do. The full endpoint list is in the API reference .

Yes (form) siem-integration Owner (inherits RBAC) Active user whose permissions cap the token. Shown as username (role) . Yes svc-siem (operator) ADOM Product the token is bound to. A token bound to global may act on any product; any other ADOM restricts it to that product. Yes fortiweb Expires (days) Days from now until the token expires. Empty = never. No 90 Scopes read (GET), write (run actions / config_write), admin . Yes (defaults to read ) read , write Capabilities

Create a user svc-lb with an operator-level profile (it needs config_write for the write scope). Create a token: Name lb-automation , Owner svc-lb , ADOM fortiweb , Expires (days) 180 , Scopes write . Tick only the capability backend_edit . In AppID scope select APP-0042 and APP-0057 . Create a scheduled action Enable / disable a backend (pool member) for each pool member (see Schedule

Last used updates when the token is used (at most about once a minute). docs.h: "Choose a valid owner for the token."
docs.x: Possible causes - No owner was submitted, or the selected user no longer exists. Solution 1. Reload the page so the Owner list is current. 2. Pick an active user and create the token again. Verification - The green New token created banner appears.

docs.h: A scope is refused when creating or editing a token
docs.x: Possible causes - The owner's profile does not contain the permission the scope maps to (see the table under Permissions ), for example write for a read-only owner or admin for an owner without users.manage . Solution 1. Untick that scope, or give the owner the needed permission in Users and profiles , or pick an owner who holds it. Verification - The token is saved and its row lists the intended scopes.

Possible causes - The ADOM chosen is no longer offered for tokens (its API Tokens capability was switched off, or the ADOM was deactivated, after the page was loaded). Solution 1. Reload the page and pick an ADOM from the refreshed list. 2. If the ADOM you need is missing, an administrator must tick its API Tokens capability in Settings → ADOMs. Verification - The ADOM appears in the ADOM drop-down.

Possible causes - The token was revoked, deleted or has expired (status badge revoked or expired , or the row is gone). - The value was copied incompletely; a token always has the shape fmk_<public-id>_<secret> . Solution 1. Check the token's status in Existing tokens . 2. If it expired, edit it and set a new Expiry (days) (or -1 ); if it was revoked or lost, create a new token. Verification - GET /api/v1/ping with the token returns "ok": true .

docs.h: The external system gets 403 owner_disabled or 403 owner_forbidden
docs.x: Possible causes - owner_disabled : the token's owner was deactivated. - owner_forbidden : the owner's profile no longer contains the permission the scope maps to (for example a write token whose owner lost every config-write permission). Solution 1. Re-enable the owner or restore the needed permission in Users and profiles , or 2. Create a new token owned by a suitable user and delete the old one. Verification - GET /api/v1/ping succeeds and the intended call no longer returns 403.

docs.h: The external system gets 403 insufficient_scope or capability_denied
docs.x: Possible causes - The endpoint needs a higher scope than the token holds. - The token has a capability list that does not include the action, or the call is an object write and the explicit capability was never ticked. Solution 1. Edit the token and tick the missing scope or capability. Verification - GET /api/v1/ping lists the new scope or capability.

Advanced How a token is stored and checked The plaintext has the form fmk_<public-id>_<secret> . The 16-character public id is stored in clear (it is what the list shows); the secret is stored only as a scrypt hash and compared on each call. On each /api/v1 call SATOM looks the token up by public id, rejects it if it is revoked or expired, verifies the secret, checks the owner is active, checks the endpoint's scope and that the owner still holds the RBAC permission mapped to that scope, then binds the request to the token's ADOM. docs.s: The read-only trail of who did what, when, from where and against which target — searchable by user, action, text, entry ID and date.

docs.x: The Audit Log is SATOM's record of actions taken in the console and through the API: sign-ins and sign-outs, configuration changes, device actions, token management, theme edits, failures and more. Each entry names the user, the action, the target, a detail payload, the client IP address and the time. The page is read-only — there is no control to edit or delete an entry, for anyone.

Lists entries newest first, 50 per page by default. Filters by free-text search, Username , Action and a date range, and pages through the result with Previous / Next . Exports the entries matching the current filters as a CSV file. Finds a single entry again by its entry ID ( #4821 , 4821 or AUD-004821 ). Opens a detail panel per entry with the full payload and, for failures, the Error reference you can look up in the server log. Scopes entries to the active ADOM.
None. Entries are written automatically by the features that perform actions.

🔑 Permission The page requires audit.view , and the Audit Log sidebar link is shown only to users who hold it. The three system profiles ( Viewer , Operator and Administrator ) all include it. A user whose profile lacks audit.view does not see the link and is refused at /audit/ . ℹ️ Note Changed in 2.11.0: the Audit Log requires audit.view (custom profiles without it lose access), pages with Previous / Next , includes the whole To Date day, and Export CSV downloads the filtered entries.

Open Administrator → Audit Log . The table shows ID , Timestamp , User , Action , Target , Detail and IP Address . Action badges are coloured: red for actions containing delete or error , green for create or login , blue for update or backup , grey otherwise. Click anywhere on a row (except the ID) to open the Audit Entry panel on the right. Close it with the × button, by clicking outside it, or with Esc . Click Refresh to reload the page. Below the table, Page N / M with Previous and Next moves through the result. The filters are kept from page to page.

In the Filters card fill in any of: - Search (user · action · target · detail · error ID) — matches any part of the username, action, target or detail. A value that looks like an entry ID also matches that entry. - Username — the exact username. - Action — one of Login , Logout , Create , Update , Delete , Backup , Error , API Call . This matches any action whose name contains the word, so Create also finds api_token.create . - From Date / To Date . Click Apply . The count line reads Showing N entries (filtered) . Click Clear to remove all filters. The Quick search… box above the table only hi

Set the filters you want (or none) and click Apply . Click Export CSV . The browser downloads audit-log.csv with the entries matching the current filters, newest first, up to 50,000 rows. The columns are id , timestamp_utc , username , action , target , ip_address , product (the ADOM) and extra (the detail). A text cell that starts with = , + , - or @ is prefixed with ' so a spreadsheet does not run it as a formula.

docs.h: Find an entry again by its ID
docs.x: Click the #ID in the first column — it is copied to the clipboard (the label briefly shows copied ✓ ) and the panel does not open. Paste it into Search later and click Apply . 4821 , #4821 and AUD-004821 all find the same entry. A plain number still matches targets and details that contain it, too.

When an entry records an unhandled error, the panel opens with a red Error reference — an eight-character code such as 69881E81 — and a Copy button. Give that code to whoever has shell access to the node: it appears in the application log next to the full traceback. You can also paste the code into Search to find the entry.

Field Description Required Example Search Case-insensitive substring over username, action, target and detail; plus entry-ID match. No api_token Username Exact username of the acting user. No jdoe Action Substring of the action name (see list above). No Delete From Date Entries at or after 00:00 of this date. No 2026-09-01 To Date Entries up to the end of this date (the whole day is included). No 2026-09-30 per_page (URL only) Entries per page, 10–200. No ?per_page=200 page (URL only) Page number. No ?page=2

🧪 Example — Who revoked an API token? Open Administrator → Audit Log . Type api_token.revoke in Search and click Apply . The matching rows show the administrator in User , token:<public-id> in Target and the token's name in Detail . Click the row to see the IP address and the full detail payload.
The log only grows: SATOM has no screen or scheduled task that removes audit entries.

docs.h: Entries near midnight are missing from my date range
docs.x: Possible causes - Dates are compared with the stored UTC time, while the table shows times in the console's configured time zone. Solution 1. Widen the range by one day on the side where entries are missing. Verification - The entries appear.

docs.h: The CSV export has fewer rows than the filter matches
docs.x: Possible causes - One export is capped at 50,000 rows. Solution 1. Narrow the date range and export in several parts. Verification - The last row of each file is older than the first row of the next.

docs.h: An action I know happened is not in the log
docs.x: Possible causes - The entry belongs to another ADOM. A FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer or FortiAuthenticator session sees only that ADOM's entries; FortiWeb sees FortiWeb entries plus unscoped ones; Global sees everything. - The action was taken on an HA standby node, whose database is read-only; audit writes there are dropped silently. - Username is an exact match on an existing user: entries of a deleted user cannot be found with it. Solution 1. Switch to the Global ADOM and search again. 2. Use Search with the username instead of the Username field. Verification - The entry appears.

Advanced What an entry stores Each row in the audit_logs table holds: an auto-increment ID , the user ID and username ( anonymous when nobody is signed in, system outside a request), the action name (e.g. api_token.create , settings.theme.activate , login , ERROR ), a target , a detail text, the IP address , the ADOM the action was performed in, and a UTC timestamp . The detail is written as the text form of a key/value dictionary, not as strict JSON. The IP address is the real client address resolved through the configured reverse proxy, not the proxy's own address. Writing an entry is best-e

docs.s: Issue, import, deploy, rotate and revoke certificates on FortiWeb and FortiADC appliances through ADCS or ACME, and keep the fleet clean with a lifecycle policy.

docs.x: The Certificate Manager runs the whole life of a CA-signed certificate on your appliances: SATOM generates the key and CSR, has your CA sign it (Microsoft ADCS or any ACME CA such as Let's Encrypt), uploads certificate and key to the device, and later swaps, renews and revokes it. It also shows every certificate already on your FortiWeb and FortiADC boxes, with expiry and where each one is bound. ℹ️ Note — Three different certificate questions This page is about certificates on the appliances . Managed certificates — an inventory of the certificates SATOM issued: device, class, SANs, expiry, days left, status and bound policies, with a per-certificate timeline. On-device certificates — a cached, de-duplicated view of the certificate stores on every FortiWeb and FortiADC (Local, SNI, CA, Let's Encrypt on FortiWeb; Local, CA, Intermediate CA, Remote on FortiADC). The same certificate on several boxes is shown once, with every device it lives on. Issuance through a pluggable protocol: ADCS / enterprise CA (a command template, certipy by default) or ACME (RFC 8555, generated lego command

The appliances are registered in SATOM (see Appliances ). FortiWeb deployment uses SSH with the appliance's stored credentials; FortiADC uses its REST API. The signing binary ( certipy by default) must be installed on the SATOM node. For ACME : a directory URL, the CA's Terms of Service accepted, and a validation method that can actually reach this node (webroot path, port, or a DNS provider with its credentials). docs.h: Import a certificate and key made outside SATOM
docs.x: Click Import (or the Import certificate + key tab), choose the appliance and class, then paste the PEM certificate and its key, or upload a PKCS#12 ( .p12 / .pfx ) with its password, and click Import . The key is stored encrypted and the certificate is marked key from outside . To replace an existing certificate with one made outside, use Replace with a certificate + key made outside SATOM on its page instead; it then rotates like a renewal.

Managed certificate: on its detail page, under Swap binding (immediate) , pick the Server policy and click Swap now . The certificate becomes active and the certificate it replaced becomes superseded . The button is disabled when no policy could be read or no private key is stored. Any on-device certificate: in On-device certificates , click the eye icon, then in Swap onto this cert choose Server policy (primary certificate) , SNI member or GUI / admin cert , the target, and click Swap . For a planned change, schedule the swap through a change request instead.

A renewal never replaces a certificate in place, so issuing and switching never cut connections at the same moment: Renew — N days before expiry (or with Renew now / Generate a new CSR now ), the replacement is issued and deployed under a new name, status staged . Swap — on its swap date (N days later), every binding of the old certificate moves to the new one. Swap now does it immediately. Roll back — while the old one is still on the device, Roll back to returns every binding to it. docs.h: "Certificate creation failed: class 'server' has no ADCS template configured (Settings → Certificate Manager)."
docs.x: Possible causes - The active protocol is ADCS and the class's ADCS template field is empty. (Under ACME the field is not checked.) Solution 1. Settings → Certificate Manager → the class card → enter your ADCS template name in ADCS template . 2. Save Settings and issue again. Verification — the new certificate's timeline shows a generate and a sign event.

docs.h: "signing binary not found" / "signer produced no certificate (rc=…)"
docs.x: Possible causes - {bin} points to a client that is not installed on this node. - The CA refused the request (wrong template, credentials, challenge failure); the message ends with the redacted command output. Solution 1. Read the error event on the certificate's timeline or on Renewals ; secrets are shown as ******** . 2. For ACME, test on a staging directory; check the webroot is served on port 80 or the DNS credentials are correct. 3. satom diagnose acme on the node checks the client, account key, webroot and provider credentials. Verification — a new issuance records a sign event with the s

Possible causes — a required variable of the selected provider has no stored value. Solution — open the provider in DNS provider credentials (dns-01) , fill the fields named in the missing: badge, Save credentials . Verification — the missing: badge disappears.

Possible causes — the client waited too long (DNS propagation through an internal resolver, an unreachable CA). Solution — set Resolvers to a public resolver, lower Propagation wait (s) , or check outbound access to the CA.

docs.h: "Certificate creation failed: signed but deploy failed: …"
docs.x: Possible causes — SSH (FortiWeb) or REST (FortiADC) to the appliance failed, or the generated name is not valid on the device (letters, digits, . , - , _ , at most 63 characters). Solution — fix connectivity or credentials on the appliance record; the certificate is signed and kept, so open its detail page and use Renew now to issue and deploy again.

docs.h: "Revoked at the CA, but NOT deleted from the device — still bound to: …"
docs.x: Possible causes — the certificate is still used by a server policy, SNI member or the GUI. Solution — swap the bindings to another certificate, then remove it from the on-device detail page or let the lifecycle sweep delete it.

docs.h: "Not removed: could not fully verify bindings (a device read failed); refusing to remove"
docs.x: Possible causes — one of the binding reads (server policies, SNI, global settings) failed, so SATOM cannot prove the certificate is unused. Removal fails closed. Solution — check the appliance is reachable and retry.

docs.h: "Built-in providers cannot be deleted — disable them instead."
docs.x: Shipped providers are re-seeded at boot, so they can only be disabled: open Add or edit a DNS provider , enter the same slug, untick Enabled , Save provider .
A certificate is due for revocation or deletion but is still bound in SATOM's records. Swap the binding first; the sweep also re-checks bindings live and skips anything it cannot prove unbound.

Advanced Secrets, environment and redaction Private keys are generated in SATOM and stored Fernet-encrypted on the certificate record. The ADCS password, the EAB HMAC key and every DNS-provider field marked secret are stored encrypted and never returned to the browser. The signer runs with a minimal environment: a fixed passthrough ( PATH , locale, TZ , CA-bundle and proxy variables) plus the provider's variables. DNS credentials travel only in that environment, never in the command line. HOME is the provider's ACME account directory when one is set, otherwise the private temporary directory c

docs.x: Possible causes — the new certificate does not verify on the other node (it chains to neither the system trust store nor the internal CA), so the peer refuses its requests instead of sending them unverified. The peer's log reads peer TLS refused for <host>: peer TLS certificate did not verify … . Solution — install a certificate the other node trusts. SATOM_PEER_TLS_ALLOW_UNVERIFIED=1 in .env restores an encrypted-but-unverified retry as a temporary emergency override only; remove it once the certificate is fixed. Verification — on High Availability , the peer's Health is up again.

docs.x: System Backup & Restore is the page that protects SATOM itself — not the appliances. From it you take and restore whole-instance database bundles, see every backup stream at a glance, browse the device-config versions SATOM has recorded, roll the application code back to an earlier commit, and reach the external backup server where appliances push their own configuration archives and where firmware images are kept. Per-appliance configuration backups (the device vault ) are a different feature: see Device backups .

Backup coverage — everything, at a glance. One table listing every backup stream (application code, live database, database bundles, device-config source of truth, git repository, device-config vault, appliance-pushed configs, firmware) with its format, where it lives, how often it is taken and a live state badge. Database bundles. Create backup now writes a single .tar.gz containing a pg_dump of the database plus, optionally, the per-device JSON tree and the versioned source-of-truth store, and can push it to the backup server. Bundles can be downloaded, restored or deleted. Restore. Replaces

docs.h: Browse device-pushed backups on the external backup server
docs.x: In External backup server , click Browse on a device row. The dialog lists every archive the appliance pushed. Pick A and B . Use Compare A → B , type a term and press the search button ( search in B… ), What's inside B (sections, with encrypted or binary ones listed separately), View B (or click a file name) to read the extracted configuration text, or Download B for the raw archive. These archives are written by the appliances themselves on their own schedule; SATOM only reads them.

In Firmware on the backup server , click Pull on an image. It is copied into Infrastructure → Firmware (sha256-verified), where the per-appliance Upgrade / Downgrade actions can use it. Images already present show in console instead. See Firmware .

🧪 Example — Nightly bundle plus a pre-change manual bundle Before a risky maintenance window, an administrator opens System Backup & Restore, leaves Include per-device JSON ticked and clicks Create backup now . The flash reports fmw-backup-20261003-081500.tar.gz with reports/ included; sot/ included; recovery-seal included . She downloads it to her workstation. The maintenance goes wrong; she clicks Restore on that bundle, types RESTORE , and SATOM first writes a safety bundle of the broken state, then restores the morning's database.

A database bundle is a file named fmw-backup-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar.gz (UTC timestamp) in the node's data/system_backups/ directory, mode 0600 in a 0700 directory: only the service account can read it. On a pair, the standby receives a copy with the next data sync. A restore leaves an additional safety bundle (manifest label pre-restore-safety ). A code rollback appears in Recent updates on the Software Update page. Git bundles are named satom-repo-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.bundle in data/git-bundles/ . docs.x: Possible causes - The confirmation box was empty or not exactly RESTORE (upper case). Solution 1. Click Restore again and type RESTORE . Verification - The flash starts with Restored … .

Possible causes - pg_dump is not installed or cannot reach the database. - The database credentials in the application configuration are wrong. Solution 1. Read the error text after pg_dump failed: — it is the tool's own message. 2. Fix the connection or install the PostgreSQL client tools, then retry. Verification - Backup created: … and a new row in the bundles table.

docs.h: Restore message warns about a different FERNET_KEY
docs.x: Possible causes - The bundle was taken on a node with a different FERNET_KEY , or this node has none. The message begins This bundle was taken under a DIFFERENT FERNET_KEY … or This node has no FERNET_KEY, so the restored encrypted columns cannot be read. Solution 1. Put the matching key into the node's .env and restart the service before relying on any stored credential. 2. Bundles deliberately do not contain the key. Run satom diagnose recovery to check that someone holds it. Verification - Appliance connections that use stored credentials work again.

docs.h: "This node is the standby — delete bundles on the primary; the datasync mirrors the deletion here within 5 minutes."
docs.x: Possible causes - You tried to delete a database or git bundle on the standby. Solution 1. Open this page on the primary and delete it there. Verification - Within 5 minutes the bundle is gone from the standby too.

docs.h: "Rollback not confirmed — type ROLLBACK to proceed." / "Pick a commit to roll back to."
docs.x: Solution 1. Click the rollback icon on a commit row, then type ROLLBACK exactly. If the flash says Already running that revision. , the selected commit is the one already running.

docs.h: "Blocked by the staged-rollout safeguard: roll the STANDBY back to this revision and let it pass its health check first, then the PRIMARY unlocks."
docs.x: Possible causes - You queued a code rollback on the primary of a pair, and the standby does not run that commit yet (or has not passed its health check on it). Solution 1. Open this page on the standby and roll it back to the same commit. 2. When the standby is healthy on it, repeat the rollback on the primary. Verification - The primary's flash reads Code rollback to … queued … .

docs.h: "Peer <host> unreachable — off-box bundle copy cannot be verified right now."
docs.x: Possible causes - The registered peer is down or does not answer on its health endpoint. Solution 1. Check the peer on High Availability . Verification - The Backup server (standby) card shows a per-bundle comparison table.

docs.h: A bundle reported on the backup server is missing from the table
docs.x: Possible causes - After a verified upload, the nightly run removes local copies the backup server holds byte-for-byte (default: keep none). The Database backups table lists only bundles physically on this node; the coverage table shows how many the backup server holds and names the newest one. Solution 1. Opening /system-backup/download/<bundle name> fetches an evicted bundle back from the backup server (size-checked) before sending it. 2. To keep some bundles locally, raise the local retention in Settings → Backup Server .

docs.h: satom diagnose data reports bundles or vault entries "too open"
docs.x: Possible causes — the node was installed by a release that left data/ 0755 and its files 0644 , and has not had the repair applied yet. Solution — on the node, run sudo satom execute repair data to see the plan, then sudo satom execute repair data --yes to apply it. It only removes permission bits and never follows a link. Verification — sudo satom diagnose data reports readable by other accounts: none .

Possible causes - The file is not a .out image ( only .out firmware images can be pulled ). - The backup server is unreachable. Solution 1. Check the External backup server card for an unreachable message and the backup server settings.

Advanced What a database bundle contains db.dump — pg_dump -Fc of the whole database. reports/ and sot/ — the per-device JSON tree and the content-addressed source-of-truth store (when Include per-device JSON is ticked). The database only holds the version index; the blobs must travel with it. recovery-seal.json — the sealed recovery envelope, if this node has one. It is ciphertext; the detail reports recovery-seal ABSENT (no off-node custody) when there is none. config/ — the node's publication overlay, if present. manifest.txt — label, timestamp, database name and host, and key fingerprints

docs.t: Deploy clone — copy one SATOM installation into another
docs.x: A deploy clone copies the configuration of one SATOM installation into another one — a lab into production, an old pair into a new pair. It is not a restore: a system backup bundle puts the same deploy back the way it was and carries that deploy's ciphertext. A clone moves configuration between two installations that each keep their own FERNET_KEY , their own identity and their own HA pair.

docs.t: Deploy clone — copy one SATOM installation into another
docs.x: Exports the configuration only into one .tar.gz : appliances and their credentials, users, profiles and settings, scheduled action definitions, templates, exceptions, probes, dashboards, the wiki and the API library, Script Library scripts and schedules, integration hooks, WAF artifacts and branding. Leaves behind everything that is not configuration: backups (the device vault and the system bundles), config history (the SoT store and the live config tree), the device cache, runs, logs, samples, incidents, notifications and firmware images. docs.x: External vault. A credential kept in the external vault travels as its vault marker. The target reaches it through the same vault configuration, which travels with the bundle; the export says how many such credentials there are. What stays behind on purpose: queued Script Library and hook requests (the target would run them a second time), the node's leases, and its signature store, which every node fetches for itself. Partial clones (by category or by appliance, merged into a deploy that keeps its own data) are not available yet.

docs.s: What 3.0 changes underneath the normal update — pack schema /2, one key per use, release notes only from signed packs, knowledge packs outside the update — and what online and air-gapped nodes must do, how to verify, and how to roll back.

docs.x: SATOM 3.0 is applied like any update ( Software update ). What changes is where vendor knowledge comes from and which key may sign it : release notes, the Upgrade Advisory (called the Scout advisory at the time), upgrade paths, the API knowledge of builds you do not run, and signature metadata now arrive only in signed packs , in two lanes — the API pack pinned to each release and the rolling knowledge pack — each with its own key.

Change What it means for you Pack schema satom.api-pack/2 3.0 packs carry a lane, a minimum SATOM version, the harvester snapshot and a kind on every item. SATOM 2.13 and older refuse them ( unsupported pack schema ). 3.0 still imports 2.x packs. One key, one use Update packages: the update trust store, unchanged. Packs: only the key of their lane ( api_pack or knowledge ), shipped with the release. See Pack trust . No vendor crawler SATOM no longer contacts any vendor documentation site; the Scan from Fortinet panel and its routes are gone. See Release notes . Knowledge packs are not inside t

Update (Software Update → Check / Apply , or an offline package). On a pair, update each node. Seed the two new scheduled actions once, on the primary. docs.x: Software Update updates SATOM itself: the application code and its Python dependencies, never operating-system packages. There are two delivery paths — from the git remote (check, then apply) and from a signed offline package for nodes with no route to the remote. In both cases the web application only enqueues a request; a separate privileged runner performs the update, restarts the service, health-checks it and rolls back automatically if the check fails.

Possible causes - A release trust anchor is installed, and deploy/ changed since the last signed release. docs.s: Run SATOM as a primary/standby pair — see both nodes and their replication live, register the peer, switch between HA and standalone mode, and fail over by hand.

docs.x: SATOM can run as two nodes: a primary whose database is read-write and a standby that follows it. The High Availability page is the cluster's own view: which nodes exist, which one is primary, whether the standby is actually receiving data, and — when the primary is lost — a guarded, manual way to promote the standby. Loading the page never contacts an appliance: it reads the local database and probes the peer over HTTPS. This page is about SATOM's own nodes. HA pairs of FortiWeb or FortiADC appliances are registered on Appliances .

Cluster architecture — one card per registered node (name, host, role, running code revision, database state and lag, when it last reported), with an arrow from each primary to each standby. In HA mode the arrow is labelled streaming ▸ / WAL replication + staged deploy ; in Standalone mode it reads standalone / no replication . The lag itself is on the node cards. Click a card to load it into the node editor; Add node clears the editor. Node-to-node architecture — a fixed reference table of the channels the nodes use and what each carries. Deployment mode — switches between HA — two-node clust

users.manage and the Global ADOM. Two SATOM nodes installed as a cluster, with PostgreSQL streaming replication between them. The deployment-mode switch does not build or remove replication; it only changes SATOM's behaviour. The data-sync timer and its SSH key on the standby (set up at installation time in cluster mode — see Installation ). The node certificate for the 8443 channel, trusted by the peer (the system trust store or the internal CA): Node TLS . Both nodes' clocks NTP-synchronised : a peer request whose signature timestamp is more than 120 seconds off is refused. Both nodes on the

All routes — viewing the page, changing the mode, editing the registry and promoting — require users.manage (legacy coarse key user_manage ); in the default profiles only Administrator has it. 🔑 Permission Without users.manage the Administrator menu is hidden and /high-availability/ returns 403 Forbidden . Role restrictions: Save mode is disabled on the standby — the mode lives in the replicated settings and can only be written on the primary. Promote this node to PRIMARY is shown only on a node that is a standby and in HA mode.

Open Administrator → High Availability on the primary. Click Add node (or click an existing card to edit it). Fill in Node name (hostname) , Host / LAN IP and optionally Label (optional) . Click Save node . The flash reads HA node '<name>' (<host>) saved. It propagates to the peer on the next data sync; its live state is probed on this page. The node you are on is always kept in the registry. To remove the peer, click Remove on its row in HA nodes ; the current node has no Remove button.

On the primary , in Deployment mode , pick HA — two-node cluster or Standalone — single node . Click Save mode . The flash reads Deployment mode set to HA. (or STANDALONE ). In Standalone , the staged-update safeguard, peer probing, failover and the data sync are all off, and updates apply directly to the node. If no mode was ever saved, SATOM uses HA when a peer is registered and Standalone otherwise.

Possible causes - The two clocks differ by more than 120 seconds, so the peer refuses the request signature. - One node is not yet updated to the release that signs peer requests (during an update this lasts about a minute, until the standby catches up). - The identity key is not configured. Solution 1. Synchronise both nodes with NTP and check the offset ( timedatectl on each node). 2. Finish the update on both nodes. Verification - /healthz called by the peer reports peer_authenticated: true , and the peer views show the peer's details again.

docs.h: "This node is PRIMARY but no replica is connected"
docs.x: Possible causes - PostgreSQL replication on the standby is stopped or cannot connect. Solution 1. Fix replication in PostgreSQL on the standby (outside SATOM). Verification - A replica row in state streaming appears on the primary.

Possible causes - The data sync timer is stopped, the SSH key is missing, or the registry lists no peer. The sync logs a reason and exits non-zero when it cannot query its role or find the peer. Solution 1. Check satom-ha-datasync.timer on the standby (see Services and timers ).

Advanced Roles and probes A node's role is read live from PostgreSQL ( pg_is_in_recovery() ), never stored. The standby cannot write the replicated settings, so the page probes the peer's /healthz/primary and /healthz endpoints instead of trusting a stored report. If the probe fails but the primary sees a streaming replica from the peer's address, the peer is shown as standby with replicating (app unreachable) . /healthz/primary returns 200 on the primary and 503 on a standby — use it as the load-balancer health check so traffic only reaches the read-write node. docs.x: Appearance is the Settings pane where an administrator chooses how the SATOM console looks. A theme is a named set of overrides for the stylesheet's 34 design tokens (sidebar, top bar, surfaces, accent, brand gradients, text, status colours, shadows, layout sizes and font), plus an optional brand logo and favicon. One theme is active at a time and applies to every user, every ADOM and the sign-in pages.

Ships four built-in themes: SATOM Aurora (the default look), SATOM Classic , SATOM Slate and SATOM Graphite . Built-ins cannot be edited or deleted. Lets you create, edit, Duplicate , Apply , Export , import and Delete your own themes. Import from a site… builds a theme from a website's brand colours, icon and favicon, or copies a theme (logo and favicon included) from another SATOM node. Previews edits live on the page before anything is saved. Audits text contrast (WCAG 2.1) and asks for confirmation before saving an unreadable palette. Replaces the top-bar logo and the browser favicon while
None. A fresh install already has the four built-ins, with SATOM Aurora active.

🔑 Permission Every Appearance action requires users.manage (the Administrator profile). For other users the User Interface group, and with it the Appearance pane, is not rendered at all; the theme routes return 403 Forbidden if called directly. The active theme's logo and favicon are served without a sign-in, because they also appear on the sign-in, forgot-password, reset-password and two-factor pages.

Open Settings , then User Interface → Appearance . The pane has three cards: Themes (the list), Theme editor , and What a theme can and cannot repaint . Import from a site… in the Themes footer opens a fourth, Import from a site .

In Themes , find the theme. The active one carries an active badge and its name is shown next to Active: in the card header. Click Apply on its row. The flash message reads Theme '<name>' applied. Every user sees the new look on their next page load (other server workers pick it up within about 15 seconds).

Update the other node if it predates the endpoint.

docs.x: Possible causes - The name resolves to an address this node never fetches from. Solution 1. Use the site's public or internal (RFC 1918) address instead.

docs.x: Possible causes - This node has no route to the site, or the site is down or slow. Solution 1. Check the node's outbound access to that host, or import from another node that can reach it and copy the theme across.

docs.x: Possible causes - The site styles itself from script, is monochrome, and publishes no icons. Solution 1. Build the theme by hand in the editor: Accent and Sidebar → Background carry most of a brand.

docs.h: "Unsupported logo type (use PNG, JPG, WEBP, GIF, ICO or SVG)." / "SVG too large (max 512 KB)." / "Image could not be processed: …"
docs.x: Possible causes - The upload has an unsupported extension, an SVG is over 512 KB, or a raster file is not a readable image. Solution 1. Export the logo as PNG or a smaller SVG and upload again.

docs.x: Solution 1. If you can still click: Settings → User Interface → Appearance → Revert to the shipped look , or Apply on any built-in theme. 2. Otherwise, on the SATOM node as root run: satom execute reset theme It activates SATOM Aurora (see CLI ). Verification - After a reload the console shows the default blue/gold look and Active: reads SATOM Aurora .

There is no supported dark theme. Status badges and some decorative tints still use fixed colours in the stylesheet, so a dark page background would leave those elements light. Light-background palettes are fully supported.

Advanced How themes are stored and applied Themes live in the ui_themes table. A row stores only the tokens that differ from the stylesheet default; a value equal to the default is dropped when saving. Exactly one row is active. Activation clears the flag on all rows and sets it on one; if no row is active, SATOM Aurora is used. The active theme is cached per server worker for 15 seconds. The token list is generated from the stylesheet, so the editor always offers every token the stylesheet exposes. docs.s: How a SATOM node is put together — reverse proxy, gunicorn, the Flask application, PostgreSQL, the metrics store and the background services — and how two nodes form a primary/standby pair.

docs.x: SATOM is a server-side web application. Browsers never talk to a Fortinet appliance directly: every request goes to the SATOM node, which reads its local database and, when an action needs it, calls the appliance's REST API (or SSH, for a few operations) on the user's behalf. A node consists of one web application and a handful of small background services that share the same code base in /opt/satom and the same PostgreSQL database. Component What it is Listens on Article Reverse proxy nginx, terminates TLS and forwards to gunicorn :443 (and :80 → redirect) Installation Web application gunicor

1 Browser HTTPS to satom.example.com 2 nginx TLS termination, HSTS, proxy_pass to 127.0.0.1:8000 with Host $http_host and X-Forwarded-* 3 gunicorn 4 worker processes, 600 s timeout (satom.service) 4 Flask before_request gates product (ADOM) gate → access gate (IP allow-list) → device gate → CSP nonce 5 View (app/views) thin handler: parameters → service call → template or JSON 6 Service (app/services) business logic; resolves REST paths through the endpoint registry 7 Client / database REST call to the appliance, or a read from the local PostgreSQL cache 8 after_request security headers, CSP,

The installer writes the nginx vhost itself (via deploy/tls-bootstrap.sh ); deploy/nginx-vhost.conf is a reviewable sample of the same layout. The proxy must forward the browser's original Host header including the port ( proxy_set_header Host $http_host; , never $host ). See Security model for why.

The shipped unit deploy/satom.service starts: gunicorn --workers 4 --bind 127.0.0.1:8000 --timeout 600 \ --access-logfile /var/log/satom/access.log \ --error-logfile /var/log/satom/error.log wsgi:app The unit binds to loopback, so only nginx can reach the application port, and a software update that re-copies the unit no longer re-opens 0.0.0.0:8000 . The installer ( installers/install-satom.sh ) pins the service account through a systemd drop-in (see Services and timers ). ℹ️ Note Changed in 2.11.0: the shipped unit itself binds gunicorn to 127.0.0.1:8000 (before, only the installer's rewrite

wsgi:app calls create_app() in app/__init__.py , which: loads the configuration class selected by FLASK_ENV ( production refuses to start without SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI ); initialises SQLAlchemy, Flask-Migrate, Flask-Login, CSRF protection (Flask-WTF), the rate limiter (Flask-Limiter) and Babel (UI language); registers about 95 blueprints; FortiWeb-scoped blueprints are mounted under /web , and a missing blueprint module is skipped instead of stopping start-up; installs the request gates, the security headers and the error handlers; exposes unauthenticated health probes: /healthz , /healthz/p

Gate Effect Product (ADOM) gate Works out the effective product for the request ( global , fortiweb , fortiadc , fortianalyzer , fortiauthenticator ) and redirects away from pages that do not belong to it. Access gate Applies the IP allow-list from Settings → Access Control . Users holding user_manage are exempt; an unreadable allow-list returns 503 instead of admitting everyone. Device gate In the FortiWeb ADOM, per-device pages need a selected device; without one the user is sent to the Architecture view. CSP nonce A nonce, stable for the session, is attached to every inline script and style

app/views/*.py HTTP handlers (Flask blueprints) app/services/*.py business logic, importable without a request context app/clients/ REST clients per product + client_for(appliance) app/registry/ endpoint registry loader (DB first, shipped JSON baseline fallback) app/models*.py SQLAlchemy models, one file per domain app/api_v1/ the token-authenticated public REST API app/api/ internal JSON endpoints used by the UI app/templates, app/static Jinja templates, Turbo Drive, vendored JS/CSS Dependencies point one way: views → services → clients / registry / models. Services never assume a browser req

docs.h: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: SATOM is mapped to the NAF Framework (Network Automation Forum, commit da82b12 ), the vendor-neutral reference model of six functional building blocks around the network infrastructure. Read against that model, the layers above sort into blocks: the Template Library, bindings and baselines are the Intent ; the Source of Truth, the metrics store, the health engine and Sentinel are the Observability (the "Source of Truth" name predates the mapping — it holds the actual state, not the desired one); device sync, deep capture, the scrape targets, SNMP polling and the syslog receiver are the Collect

Principle What it means in practice Database-first reads Pages render from the local device cache in PostgreSQL; contacting an appliance is an explicit action (refresh, sync, save). Preview before write Device changes are computed as a diff and shown before they are applied; applied changes are audited. Registry-resolved URLs Code asks the endpoint registry for a logical endpoint name; the REST path for the product and API version comes from the registry, not from hard-coded strings. Fail closed on partial knowledge For example, a configuration sync that returns zero objects is treated as an e

Long operations (firmware upload, upgrades, bulk pushes, discovery…) run as jobs : a daemon thread inside the gunicorn worker that started it, with its state kept as a JSON file in data/jobs/<id>.json . Any worker can read the state, so progress polling works no matter which worker answers. Stop and pause are cooperative: the request sets a flag in the job file and the job stops at its next safe checkpoint. See Jobs and Statuses . POST requests on the device-facing pages are wrapped the same way: the request is replayed inside a job thread (with the same login, CSRF, ADOM and permission checks

Scheduled Actions are fired by a separate process, never by the web workers (four workers would fire every action four times). satom-scheduler.service runs deploy/scheduler_guard.sh , which asks the local PostgreSQL whether it is a primary and only then starts app.scheduler_runtime ; on a standby it waits and re-checks every 30 seconds. The scheduler ticks every 45 seconds, claims due actions with a database lease and runs each exactly once. An overdue action without catch-up is rolled forward and marked missed instead of being run late. See Scheduled actions .

satom-reconciler.service runs on both nodes of a pair, ticking every 60 seconds. It does not start the Flask application; it reads the two settings it needs with psql and otherwise uses git and the update request queue. In MANUAL mode (the default) it only records drift; in AUTO mode it drives the staged self-update — standby first, then the primary, health-gated. See Software update .

The web application runs as an unprivileged account. Anything that needs root (installing units, upgrading libraries, restarting services, applying the PostgreSQL TLS protocol and cipher settings, promoting a standby) is written as a request file into data/update-requests/ ; the satom-updater.path unit notices it and starts the root-owned satom-updater.service , which re-validates the request against its own allow-list. See Security model .

Fleet metrics are written to a local VictoriaMetrics instance ( satom-metrics.service ), bound to 127.0.0.1:8428 with a retention of 396 days. It has no authentication of its own, which is why it only listens on loopback and all queries go through the application. Configuration (boards, panels, targets, reports) stays in PostgreSQL. If the binary is missing, the rest of SATOM works and store-backed panels show a query error. See Metrics .

Two nodes form a primary + standby pair. Failover is manual by design. Concern How it is handled Database PostgreSQL streaming replication; the standby is a read-only replica. Scheduled actions Fire only where pg_is_in_recovery() is false (the primary). Load balancer /healthz/primary returns 200 on the primary and 503 on a standby. docs.s: How SATOM maps onto the Network Automation Forum's reference framework — which of its six functional blocks each SATOM feature belongs to, where SATOM's own names differ from the framework's, and where the conformance matrix lives.

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: The Network Automation Forum (NAF) publishes a vendor-neutral reference framework for network automation systems. It describes six functional building blocks — Intent , Executor , Collector , Observability , Orchestrator and Presentation — "besides the actual network infrastructure", and states for each block what a system MUST, SHOULD or MAY do. SATOM is mapped to the NAF Framework : every feature in the console has a place in one of those blocks, and the gaps between what the framework asks for and what SATOM does are written down, not implied. Source: Network Automation Forum, The NAF Frame

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: It is vendor-neutral and community-maintained. Nobody's product is the yardstick. MUST / SHOULD / MAY make conformance checkable. Each requirement is a row with a state, not an opinion. It gives a shared vocabulary with customers, auditors and integrators: "SATOM is your Executor and Observability for the Fortinet estate" is a sentence everyone can place. It lets SATOM sit as one block in a customer's stack — their NetBox as Intent, their SIEM as Observability, SATOM as the Fortinet-specific Collector / Executor / Orchestrator — because the blocks talk through documented APIs. It is a yardstic

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.h: The six blocks, in SATOM's words
docs.x: SATOM predates its mapping, so several features carry names of their own. The table says what SATOM calls each block's contents; the framework's name is the one to use when talking to someone who knows the framework. NAF block What SATOM calls it Intent (desired state) Templates, Template bindings, Baselines (template combos), the Exception Library, Change types and the secret vault Observability (history of the actual state, insight, events) Source of Truth (configuration history), Monitoring and the metrics store, the health engine and its alerts, Drift, Sentinel, Scout, the Release Advisor

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: Five SATOM names mean something else in the framework. Keep them apart: "Source of Truth" is Observability, not Intent. SATOM's Source of Truth stores the actual configuration of every appliance, version by version — the framework calls history of the actual state Observability . The framework's Intent — the desired state — is what SATOM calls Templates and Baselines . See Data and storage and the Template library . The Knowledge Harvester is not the Collector. It harvests vendor knowledge (which fields a firmware build serves, release notes); the NAF Collector reads the network's state. See A

docs.h: What each block looks like in SATOM today
docs.x: Since release 3.4.0 every block has both a console face and an API face.

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: Desired state is the versioned Template library with its approval workflow, the bindings that tie a template to an appliance with per-device variables, and the baselines that group templates by classification. The REST API reads all three ( /templates , /bindings , /baselines ) and, with the explicit capabilities template_draft and template_apply , creates, edits, binds, approves and applies them through the console's own dry-run and canary path — never a direct write to a device. The model is Fortinet-specific by design; the framework's "vendor-neutral representation" is a documented deviatio

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: The Source of Truth keeps every configuration version; the metrics store keeps 396 days of readings; the health engine evaluates checks every 15 minutes and routes findings to five sinks ( Alerting ). The API exposes configuration history and diffs ( /appliances/<id>/config-history , config-diff ), the current findings ( /findings ) and a read-only MetricsQL query ( /metrics/query ) over SATOM's own satom_* series. The framework's "event when the actual state differs from the intended one" is the Intent deviation check: a bound device that no longer matches its template is a finding, a Complia

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: Device sync and deep capture read the appliances' REST and CLI; the scrape targets of Metrics collection read their counters; FortiAnalyzer supplies logs. Beyond the device APIs, an opt-in SNMP v2c collector polls uptime, interfaces, CPU, memory and disk, and a syslog receiver inside the scheduler takes messages from known senders. Stated exclusions: SNMPv3, SNMP traps, flow telemetry (NetFlow, sFlow) and packet capture. Normalisation is across firmware builds and channels of one vendor, not across vendors.

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: Every write goes through the CLI writer or the REST clients, behind a diff shown before it is applied, a transactional CLI session that aborts on the first error, and a read-back that verifies the write ( Object editor , Policy cloning , Provisioning , Firmware upgrade ).

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: Processes coordinate the other blocks without touching a device themselves: they can now start from an event (an alert, a failed upgrade, an approved change), from the Walk a process scheduled action, or from the API ( /processes/<id>/run , rehearsal unless the token holds process_arm ), and a Compensate step undoes what a walk wrote. Change requests and Integration hooks are the other two doors of the same block.

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: The console, the satom command line, the Documentation Center and the notification sinks; and for machines, API v1 with an OpenAPI 3.0 document built at request time from the live routes ( GET /api/v1/openapi.json ), so a route added tomorrow is documented the moment it is registered.

docs.t: Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework
docs.x: The matrix page lists every requirement of the framework as a row: block, level (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), the requirement in the framework's words, the state — met , partial , gap , accepted-gap with its reason, or n/a — and the file in SATOM that is the evidence. A test in SATOM's own suite parses the page, checks that every evidence file exists, counts the MUST rows that are not met and allows exactly one verdict sentence for that count.
