docs.x: One interactive installer, two modes — connected (online) and air-gapped (offline bundle). It asks for the IP, the port, the admin password and standalone or cluster, and handles everything else: packages, PostgreSQL, the internal PKI, the systemd services and nginx TLS. Every installation path ends in the same state: the console on https:// , plain http:// answering with a 301 redirect, the application running as an unprivileged service account, and the background services enabled. 💡 Tip — Step-by-step on GitHub The installation manual ( docs/INSTALL.md , also shipped inside every offline bun

A Linux distribution with systemd as PID 1 . Alpine/musl is not supported. Supported families (package manager detected automatically): Debian / Ubuntu ( apt ), RHEL / Rocky / Alma / Fedora ( dnf / yum ), openSUSE / SLES ( zypper ), Arch ( pacman ). Debian 12 is the reference platform. Python 3.10 or later; the installer installs the distribution's own if it is missing. Root, or an account allowed by sudo to run the installer (see Security model ). The installer installs, from the distribution's repositories only: Python, PostgreSQL, nginx, rsync, OpenSSL, CA certificates, curl, sudo and git (

sudo bash install-satom.sh --preflight # or --check; changes nothing sudo bash satom-setup.sh --check The preflight verifies writable system paths, free space, busy ports (and which process holds them), required tools, the bundle (offline) and whether SATOM is already running. It refuses to install over an active node unless SATOM_ALLOW_REINSTALL=1 is set, because a reinstall writes a new .env ; use Software update to upgrade instead.

The same install-satom.sh serves both modes: it installs online when it runs on its own, and offline when it finds a bundle/ directory beside it. Online Any distro family 🌐 Connected install Fetches OS packages from the distribution mirrors and Python wheels from PyPI as it goes, and clones the project's public repository (the URL can be changed at the prompt). It detects apt , dnf / yum , zypper or pacman and maps package names per family; PostgreSQL's data directory, configuration file and pg_hba.conf are queried from the running engine itself, so the Debian, RHEL, SUSE and Arch layouts all

Arch has no offline bundle; install it online. Besides the packages, a bundle carries the application, the ACME client, the metrics-store binary, the release's API library pack, the sudo and SSH packages and the sysadmin manual INSTALL.md . Verify it with the .sha256 file shipped beside it. To read the version a bundle contains before installing it: bash tar xzOf satom-offline-<version>-*.tar.gz --wildcards '*/bundle/app.tar.gz' | tar xzO VERSION - Bundles are built with installers/build-offline-bundle.sh (on Debian 12), build-offline-bundle-rhel.sh (on Rocky 9) and build-offline-bundle-suse.s

A name left out here produces a browser name-mismatch warning and means reissuing the certificate later, so give every name operators will type. cd deploy/docker cp env.example .env ./satom-docker.sh gen-secrets ./satom-docker.sh build satom:<version> ./satom-docker.sh up The stack runs the application, PostgreSQL, Redis, the metrics store and an nginx proxy; web , scheduler and cron are the same image. satom-setup.sh can also perform a Docker install (secrets in /opt/satom-docker/satom.env , mode 0600 — back it up). A container does not administer its host, so Software Update, service control, certificate activation and systemd unit health are refused in the console with a message naming the alternative — unless the optional operation

A production pair is a primary and a standby , not two halves of a load balancer: the standby's PostgreSQL is a streaming replica, its scheduler and cron services idle until the database is promoted (so two nodes never fire the same action), and your reverse proxy should carry it as a backup server that takes traffic only when the primary stops answering /healthz . On the primary, set SATOM_NODE_ROLE=primary and an immutable SATOM_IMAGE tag in .env , then run SATOM_ENV=prod ./satom-docker.sh up . Copy the same .env to the standby — SECRET_KEY , FERNET_KEY and the database passwords must match,

Move the image as a file, the same way the offline bundles travel: ./satom-docker.sh export satom:<version> /tmp/satom-<version>.tar.gz # writes a .sha256 beside it # copy the tarball AND its .sha256 to the target, then ./satom-docker.sh import /tmp/satom-<version>.tar.gz import checks the .sha256 before loading the image, so a truncated copy is reported as a checksum failure rather than as a layer error inside docker load . Without the .sha256 beside the tarball it only warns that it cannot verify.

docs.h: What a container backup must cover
docs.x: The image is disposable; the satom-data volume is not. It holds the device backup vault, the system backup bundles, the configuration-history object store and the reports. Back it up together with a database dump: the history index lives in PostgreSQL while its objects live in the volume, so a database dump restored alone leaves rows pointing at nothing.

The installer writes the nginx vhost for you (TLS 1.2/1.3, HSTS, client_max_body_size 400M , proxy_read_timeout 120s ). If you put SATOM behind your own proxy or load balancer, it must pass: proxy_set_header Host $http_host; # NOT $host proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; $host drops the port: behind a non-standard port every form, including the sign-in form, then fails with a "session expired" message. Also add the proxy's address to TRUSTED_PROXIES so rate limits and the audit log see the real client address. See Security m

Installed with admin password install-satom.sh the one you typed at the prompt satom-setup.sh typed (12 to 1024 characters, no character-class rule) or, if left empty, generated into /root/satom-admin-password.txt (0600) Application start-up on an empty database SATOM_ADMIN_PASSWORD , or a random password written to /opt/satom/initial-admin-password (0600) There is no default password. See First login . ℹ️ Note Changed in 2.11.0: both installers apply the console's single password rule (at least 12 characters, at most 1024, no character classes); before, install-satom.sh accepted 8 characters

docs.h: Finishing the install: arm the protections
docs.x: The safeguards travel with the code; the coverage does not — and this is the most common way an installation ends up unprotected. Required 🗓️ Nothing is scheduled until the first appliance Schedules are database rows, the seeds are insert-only and an operator's edit always wins over them. A brand-new node has no scheduled actions and no alert recipient . When it gets its first appliance, SATOM creates the default System Automations (the plan below) — only while the node has none at all; rows you deleted are not re-created. The alert recipient is never created for you: without it, signals are c

Arm the protections as described above. Remove the installer permission: rm /etc/sudoers.d/satom-installer . Restrict the console port to the operations networks. Check the privilege model: bash systemctl show satom.service -p User --value # the service account, not root sudo -u satom sudo -n nginx -t # allowed sudo -u satom sudo -n systemctl restart satom # must fail Replace the self-signed certificate when ready, in Node TLS or with deploy/tls-bootstrap.sh import-cert --cert FILE --key FILE . Secure the recovery secrets ( sudo satom execute seal recovery ). See Security model . Logs: /var/lo

docs.x: A SATOM node runs one web service and several small helpers. All of them share the code in /opt/satom and read /opt/satom/.env . The unit templates ship in /opt/satom/deploy/ ; the installer copies them to /etc/systemd/system/ and adds drop-ins for the service account. Unit Type When it runs Account HA role satom.service long-running always service account both nodes satom-scheduler.service long-running always (fires only on primary) service account primary fires, standby waits satom-reconciler.service long-running tick every 60 s service account both nodes satom-metrics.service long-running a

Runs: gunicorn --workers 4 --bind 127.0.0.1:8000 --timeout 600 with access and error logs in /var/log/satom/access.log and /var/log/satom/error.log . Bind: the shipped unit listens on loopback only, so only nginx reaches it; a software update no longer re-opens 0.0.0.0:8000 . Restart: Restart=always , 5 s delay. Restart it after any Python or template change; static JS/CSS do not need a restart. ℹ️ Note Changed in 2.11.0: the shipped satom.service binds gunicorn to 127.0.0.1:8000 (existing nodes receive the corrected unit at their next update), and with a custom SATOM_APP_USER the installer no

Runs: deploy/scheduler_guard.sh , which loops on deploy/satom-node-role.sh . When the local PostgreSQL answers "primary" it exec s python -m app.scheduler_runtime ; otherwise it sleeps 30 s and asks again. A promotion therefore starts the scheduler with no extra step. What it does: every 45 s it releases stale leases, then claims due scheduled actions and runs each one once. Overdue actions without catch-up are moved to their next run and marked missed . Wall-clock schedules use the time zone configured in Settings. Why separate: the four web workers would otherwise fire every action four time

Runs: python -m app.reconciler_runtime , ticking every 60 s; Restart=always , 15 s delay. What it does: compares this node's code with the expected revision. In MANUAL mode (default) it only records the drift. In AUTO mode it drives the staged self-update: standby first, then the primary, health-gated. It does not boot the Flask application, so it runs on the read-only standby too. Its status is shown on the Software update and High availability pages.

Runs: /usr/local/bin/victoria-metrics with -storageDataPath=/var/lib/satom-metrics , -httpListenAddr=127.0.0.1:8428 , -retentionPeriod=396d , -memory.allowedBytes=512MiB , -search.maxQueryDuration=30s . Installed and enabled only if the binary is present (the installer places it from the offline bundle or downloads the pinned release). Each node keeps its own store; it is not replicated. See Metrics .

Schedule: OnCalendar=*:0/15 (every 15 minutes), 3 min after boot, randomised by up to 60 s, Persistent=true . Runs: deploy/satom-alerts.sh → flask alerts-run , which evaluates the proactive checks (certificates, device reachability, git lag, backups…) and dispatches new alerts by e-mail and the in-app bell. See Alerting . On a standby: findings are evaluated and sent to syslog, but in-app notifications and e-mail are skipped ("read-only replica — notification is primary-only"). A promoted standby starts dispatching automatically. Exit status: a run that found new alerts but reached no channel

Schedule: daily at 03:30, randomised by up to 30 min, Persistent=true . Runs: deploy/satom-cert-renew.sh → flask cert-renew . Renews the node's service certificate when it was issued by the internal CA and is within the renewal threshold; does nothing for imported or bootstrap certificates. If the renewal mode is autopull , it also fetches the renewed certificate from the configured source. Every run is recorded in the renewal journal. See Node TLS .

Schedule: every 60 s ( OnUnitActiveSec=60s ), 90 s after boot. Runs: python -m app.cli_sentinel responder-tick as the service account, with a 300 s start timeout. What it does: executes queued Sentinel response actions and expires blocks whose time-to-live has passed. Gates are re-evaluated at execution time. The timer is enabled even though the response engine ships disarmed, because it is also what lifts expired blocks. See Sentinel .

Written by the installer only in cluster mode: 2 min after boot, then every 5 min. Runs: deploy/satom-ha-datasync.sh . Exits immediately unless this node's PostgreSQL is a standby and the HA mode is not standalone . Finds the peer in data/ha_nodes.json and pulls the primary's data/ with rsync -az --delete over SSH (key /opt/satom/.ssh/id_ha_rsync , strict host key checking), excluding jobs/ , tmp/ , update-requests/ , update-status/ , logs/ , diagnostics/ and deep_jobs/ .

Trigger: DirectoryNotEmpty=/opt/satom/data/update-requests . Runs: the privileged update runner self_update_runner.py (start timeout 1800 s). The installer redirects ExecStart through a drop-in to a root-owned copy in /usr/local/lib/satom-runner/ using a system Python, so the service account cannot alter what root executes. What it does: code update (git), pip install , flask db upgrade , refreshed unit files and service restarts, with automatic rollback when the post-restart health check ( /healthz , 90 s) fails. It also carries the other root-only requests (for example an nginx reload, the P

Trigger: DirectoryNotEmpty=/opt/satom/data/integrations/queue . Runs: python -m app.services.hook_runner as the service account, 900 s timeout, with extra hardening ( ProtectSystem=strict , ProtectHome , NoNewPrivileges , write access only to data/integrations ). What it does: runs integration hooks in a child process that cannot import the application, does not inherit its environment and receives only the secrets the hook declared. A timeout kills the whole process group. See Integrations .

The installer writes /opt/satom/.env once: SECRET_KEY=<random> FERNET_KEY=<random Fernet key> SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI=postgresql+psycopg://satom:<password>@127.0.0.1/satom FLASK_ENV=production NODE_IP=192.0.2.10 WEB_PORT=443 Owner root , group = service account, mode 0640 . The application and the timers read it; nothing in the application writes it. systemd loads it with EnvironmentFile= for every unit; wsgi.py additionally loads the .env that sits next to it (without overriding values systemd already set), so manual runs from another directory still see it. systemd reads EnvironmentFile only
Only variables the code actually reads are listed. "—" means unset by default.

Variable Meaning Default Read in TRUSTED_PROXIES Comma-separated proxy addresses whose X-Forwarded-For is trusted for rate limiting and audit 127.0.0.1,::1 app/extensions.py LINK_HOSTS Comma-separated extra host names that absolute links mailed out of a request (the password-reset link) may use. docs.x: Fortinet firmware builds differ in which REST endpoints and fields they serve — even builds of the same API version. The API library records, per product and per exact build , which endpoints and fields exist, their types and options, by which channel (REST, CLI or both), and the evidence each claim came from. It lives in the database ( api_lib_* tables) and only ever grows: evidence outlives the appliance that produced it. docs.h: How a pack is built and signed
docs.x: The SATOM team's Knowledge Harvester builds one snapshot of everything it knows. An approved snapshot is re-manifested per lane and signed with that lane's key: the knowledge key whenever the knowledge changes, the API-pack key at every SATOM release. The signature is Ed25519 over the exact bytes of manifest.json ; the manifest holds the sha256 of every file in the pack. Verification on the node checks the signature first, then every file's hash, then the schema — before anything is read.

docs.x: satom is a console tool for the people who run a SATOM node. It is separate from the web interface on purpose: it has to keep working when the web application, its database or the network is broken. Install location: /usr/local/sbin/satom , with its code in /usr/local/lib/satom-cli/ . Both are a root-owned copy; the CLI never runs code from /opt/satom . Runs on the system Python (3.10 or later), never on the application's virtual environment, and needs only the standard library to start — so satom diagnose still answers when the virtual environment is broken. Installed by deploy/install-cli.sh

Print the sudoers rule for an operator account (needs no privilege): satom show sudoers alice The rule it prints is alice ALL=(root) /usr/local/sbin/satom , to be installed as /etc/sudoers.d/satom-operator with mode 0440 after visudo -cf . Without an account name it uses satomadmin . It also states what the rule grants: everything under execute (service control, venv and unit reinstall, queued code and pip updates, promotion, certificate operations), but no shell. When an unprivileged user runs a root command, the CLI refuses with permission denied: <command> , shows who you are running as and

docs.s: The catalog of protections that stop SATOM from losing data, locking you out or writing something nobody approved — the six design rules every guard follows and a map of the guard groups.

docs.x: SATOM writes to production appliances, rewrites its own installation, installs its own dependencies and reloads its own web server. Every one of those is a way to lose data or lock yourself out. The safeguards are the guards that make those operations survivable. Every guard described in this section ships in the product today. Most of them are invisible while they hold: you only see one when it refuses something, rolls something back or raises an alert. ❗ Important — The failure this product defends against hardest Not a missing guard, but a guard that silently takes the wrong branch and repo

docs.h: The six rules every guard follows
docs.x: Every guard in this section is built to the same six rules — each one a direct answer to a guard that could otherwise report success while doing nothing: 📣 Fail loud A guard that cannot do its job aborts the operation . No step is allowed to report success while doing nothing. For example: an update aborts if local commits cannot be parked first, and publishing a manual stops the build on any leak-scan hit. 📸 Snapshot first Nothing destructive runs before the previous state is parked somewhere that survives the destruction. docs.h: How to read the group articles
docs.x: Each group article starts with a short explanation of the risk, followed by a Guard | What it prevents table. docs.x: The repository carries the application code. Device configuration is not kept in git: since 2026-08-05 it lives in a local, content-addressed history that is replicated to the standby and carried in every backup bundle (see Source of truth ). The git remote is a distribution point, not a place of custody — and the dangerous moment is not a remote outage, it is the moment the remote comes back and an update resets the checkout. Guard What it prevents Commit preservation before a hard reset Losing commits that exist only on this node. Before an update resets the checkout, local commits are parke

The web process never changes the installation itself. It writes a request; a privileged runner picks the request up and does the work. The update path therefore cannot be reached by whatever reaches the web application (see Privilege boundary and operator console ). Every update — code or dependency — follows the same sequence: 1 Snapshot The current revision or installed package version is recorded 2 Apply The code is updated or the pinned version is installed 3 Smoke test The application must still import 4 Health check The service is restarted, then checked over real HTTP 5 Revert Any fail
The Unpushed commits , Behind / diverged and Backup missing / stale / error signals in the alert catalog are the alerting half of these guards.

docs.h: Why divergence is the expensive failure
docs.x: A cluster multiplies the ways state can diverge. Each guard here exists because divergence — two nodes that disagree — costs more than downtime. The common thread is the one writer rule: the primary owns every write that replicates, and the standby refuses rather than producing state its own synchronization would undo.

docs.x: Writing to an appliance is the part of SATOM that can take a customer offline, so it carries more gates than anything else.

Guard What it prevents Read-only means read-only A write hidden behind a read. Every line of a read-only device command is validated, not just the first, so a pasted read followed by a write cannot slip past a legitimate opening line. Only the read verbs get , show and diagnose ( diag ) are accepted, and a diagnose command containing a state-changing word (kill, clear, reset, delete, failover, sysrq/crash, set…, abbreviations included) is refused. docs.t: Safeguards — fresh installs and known limits
docs.x: The guards travel with the code. A node installed from the connected path or from an air-gapped bundle has these from its first boot: the history guard that parks local commits before a reset; the dependency allowlist; the pinned unprivileged service account; the restricted peer channel (forced command on the peer key); the certificate validate-and-rollback; the read-only check on appliance commands.

docs.t: Safeguards — fresh installs and known limits
docs.x: Everything that lives in the database. Seeds are insert-only and operator edits outrank them. A brand-new install has no scheduled actions and no alert recipient . When the node gets its first appliance, SATOM creates the default System Automations (sync, backup, monitoring sweeps, reports) — only while the node has none at all; rows you deleted are not re-created. Until then, or if those rows are deleted: its source of truth is never refreshed; no repository or database backup is ever produced. The alert recipient is never created for you: without it, alert signals are computed and delivered

docs.t: Safeguards — fresh installs and known limits
docs.x: An air-gapped bundle is a snapshot of the product at build time, so the guards inside it are the ones that existed then. The bundle records its own version — check it before assuming a fix is present. The bundle also carries the ACME client and the privilege-escalation (sudo) and SSH packages, because a host with no network cannot fetch them. A missing one used to abort the install after the service account had been created — exactly the half-applied state the verify, then commit rule exists to prevent. See Installation and Offline updates .

Certificates issued by the internal CA do renew automatically. See C

docs.s: The most common problems across SATOM — sign-in, forms, permissions, appliances, jobs, scheduling, alerts, metrics, updates, HA and start-up — each with likely causes, a fix and how to confirm it, plus links to the detailed article.

docs.x: Most server-side problems are diagnosed with two commands on the node (any user): satom get system health # units, /healthz, disk — one roll-up satom diagnose all # every check, one exit code A page that failed with Something went wrong shows an Error reference ; an administrator finds the full failure with grep <reference> /opt/satom/data/logs/satom.log . Message texts are listed in Error messages ; status values in Statuses .

docs.h: "Invalid username or password." although the password is right
docs.x: Possible causes - The account is local and the password differs from the directory one (local accounts never fall back to the directory). - A directory account was imported but not approved, or is disabled. - The node is reached over plain http:// (see the next problem). Solution 1. Try another known-good account. 2. For directory users, test the source in Settings → Authentication . 3. An administrator can reset a password on the node: sudo satom execute admin reset-password <username> (audited as user cli/root ). 4. Check the audit log: every failed local sign-in is recorded as login.fail ,

docs.h: Every password is refused and the page says the site is served over HTTP
docs.x: Possible causes - The browser reached SATOM over http:// . The session cookie is marked Secure , so the browser never returns it and no sign-in can succeed. Solution 1. Use https://satom.example.com/ . 2. If HTTPS is broken, restore the TLS proxy ( deploy/tls-bootstrap.sh ), see Installation . Verification — the sign-in form accepts the password over https:// .

docs.h: "Too many failed attempts — account temporarily locked. Try again later."
docs.x: Possible causes — 10 consecutive failed sign-ins on that account. Solution — wait 15 minutes, or on the node: sudo satom execute admin unlock <username> (the password is unchanged). Verification — the next correct sign-in works.

docs.h: Every form says the session expired
docs.x: The message is "Your session expired or the form was stale — please try again." , on every POST including sign-in. Possible causes - The reverse proxy sends proxy_set_header Host $host; and SATOM is reached on a non-standard port (or through NAT). $host drops the port, so the CSRF check compares the browser's Referer (with port) against a host without it and rejects every form. - A genuinely old form (the CSRF token lives one hour) — then it happens once, not every time. Solution 1. In the proxy configuration use proxy_set_header Host $http_host; . 2. On a node whose vhost the installer wrote:

docs.h: "Your session was locked after N minutes of inactivity."
docs.x: Possible causes — the browser session was idle for longer than Settings → General → Session Lock (minutes) . Background refreshes (notification bell, job dock, status badges) do not count as activity, so a tab left open still locks. Solution — sign in again; you return to the page you asked for. An administrator can change the timeout (5 to 1440 minutes, default 60). Verification — the audit log shows session.idle_lock for the sign-out.

docs.h: Rate limit on the sign-in page (429)
docs.x: Possible causes — more than 5 sign-in attempts per minute from one address. Behind an extra proxy that is not listed in TRUSTED_PROXIES , all users share the proxy's address and therefore one limit. Solution — wait a minute; add the proxy address to TRUSTED_PROXIES in /opt/satom/.env and restart satom.service . See Configuration files . Verification — the audit log shows real client addresses, not the proxy's.

Possible causes - Your profile lacks the permission the page or button needs. Every page that shows device content needs a read permission too: the Audit Log needs View audit log ( audit.view ); appliance list, detail and datasheet pages need View appliances ( appliances.view ); the FortiWeb workspace, protection, exceptions, artifacts, server objects, object editor, wizard and fleet objects need View protection ( protection.view ); Device Provisioning needs View operations ( operations.view ); the API-Registry Explorer and the FortiADC / FortiAnalyzer / FortiAuthenticator API consoles need Vi

docs.h: A page sends me to another place or to a different ADOM
docs.x: Possible causes - Pages belong to an ADOM (FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer, FortiAuthenticator, Global). Opening a page that does not exist in the current ADOM redirects to that ADOM's home. - FortiWeb device pages need a selected appliance; without one you land on the Architecture view. Solution — switch ADOM with the ADOM picker or select an appliance first. See ADOMs and products .

Possible causes — the IP allow-list setting cannot be read (for example a damaged value after a restore). SATOM refuses rather than admit everyone. Solution — an administrator (not affected) opens Settings → Access Control and saves a valid list. Verification — non-administrators can open pages again.

docs.h: A new appliance never syncs and stays unknown or offline
docs.x: Possible causes - Verify SSL Certificate is on for an appliance with a self-signed certificate: the TLS check fails before authentication. - Wrong host, port or credentials; the appliance's admin account is locked. - Network path from the node to the appliance is blocked. Solution 1. Add the appliance's CA to the Trust store (preferred), or turn off Verify SSL Certificate on the appliance. 2. Check credentials and reachability on the appliance page ( Appliances ). Verification — the status badge turns online and a sync completes.

docs.h: A red banner "device error -20010 … license not valid"
docs.x: Possible causes — the appliance's licence is expired or flapping. Solution — fix the licence on the appliance, then refresh. Pages keep working from the cache meanwhile.

docs.h: "This object is locked by another user."
docs.x: Possible causes — another editor holds the edit lease. Solution — wait: an abandoned lease expires after about two minutes, or take over the lock explicitly. See Locks .

docs.h: A job stays "running" after a restart
docs.x: Possible causes — the service restarted while the job's worker thread was running. Solution — nothing: at start-up and then at most every two minutes SATOM marks such jobs error with "Orphaned — the service restarted while this job was running." Check the appliance and run the action again. To clean old entries: sudo satom execute repair jobs --yes . Verification — the Job Manager no longer lists it as active.

Possible causes - No scheduled actions exist: the node has no appliance yet (the default set is created with the first one), or the rows were deleted. - This node is a standby : the scheduler only fires on the primary. - satom-scheduler.service is stopped, or cannot reach the database. - The action is disabled, or all its targets are in maintenance ( skipped ). Solution 1. satom diagnose scheduler . 2. Create the recommended set: sudo satom execute seed actions --yes . 3. sudo satom execute restart scheduler . Verification — satom get scheduler status shows recent runs. See Scheduled actions a

Possible causes — the scheduler was not running at the due time (or found the action overdue) and catch-up is off, so the run was skipped and the action was moved to its next run. The yellow missed badge explains this on hover. Solution — check that satom-scheduler.service runs on the primary, and enable catch-up on the action if a late run is better than none, or run it manually.

docs.h: A device is red but no e-mail arrived
docs.x: Possible causes - The appliance is in maintenance (alerts suppressed by design). - Alerts are disabled or no recipient is set; SMTP delivery fails. - This node is the standby (notifications are primary-only). Solution — check Settings → Email & Alerts and use Preview now (no send) ; run sudo satom execute alerts run --dry-run . A run that found alerts but reached nobody leaves satom-alerts.service in failed . If satom get alerts status shows last email: REFUSED , the alerts are being found and the mail transport is turning them away — fix the relay or switch the transport to an SMTP provider.

docs.h: Metrics panels show a query error or stay empty
docs.x: Possible causes - satom-metrics.service is not installed or not running (the binary was not available at install time). - Nothing collects: the metrics_scrape scheduled action does not exist. Solution 1. sudo satom execute reinstall metrics-store . 2. sudo satom execute seed actions --yes (includes the 3-minute metrics scrape). Verification — satom diagnose all reports the store as live; panels draw data after a few minutes. See Metrics .

Possible causes — satom-updater.path is disabled on this node, so requests stay queued . Solution — sudo satom execute enable updater (on both nodes). Verification — satom get update history shows the runner picked it up.

Possible causes — the preflight blocks it: untrusted signing key, wrong Python, missing wheels, too little disk, or a version below the package's minimum. Solution — read the named checks on the Software Update page; install the release key with sudo satom execute trust add-key <key>.pub . See Offline updates .

Possible causes — in a pair, the primary may only take a revision the standby has already validated. Solution — update the standby first, wait for its health check, then the primary. See Software update .

Possible causes — the node has a signed-release trust anchor, and deploy/ changed since the last signed release. The application was updated; the unit files, install scripts, operator CLI and runner copies were not. Solution — on the primary, run sudo satom execute sign-release (a dry run that shows the deploy/ diff), then sudo satom execute sign-release --yes , and update again, standby first. Verification — sudo satom get release trust shows that HEAD 's deploy/ matches the newest signed commit. See Signed releases .

docs.h: Settings will not save on the second node
docs.x: Possible causes — that node is the standby ; its database is a read-only replica. Solution — make the change on the primary; it replicates. Files in data/ reach the standby within 5 minutes. Verification — satom get node status shows which node is primary. See High availability .

docs.h: The standby's replication lag keeps growing
docs.x: Possible causes — replication is not keeping up or is stalled. Solution — read the replication card on the High Availability page. Do not promote a lagging standby; promotion is for a primary that is confirmed down.

Possible causes — the two nodes' clocks differ by more than 120 seconds, so each refuses the other's request signatures; or one node is not yet updated to the release that signs peer requests (expect about a minute of this while the standby catches up during an update). Solution — synchronise both clocks with NTP, and finish the update on both nodes. Verification — the peer's card on the High Availability page shows its role, revision and up again. See High availability .

docs.h: The service does not start after editing .env
docs.x: Possible causes - SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI missing with FLASK_ENV=production . - FERNET_KEY missing. Solution — restore the values; satom diagnose config checks the file. Restart with sudo satom execute restart web . Verification — curl -k https://satom.example.com/healthz returns 200.

docs.h: Stored appliance passwords no longer work after a rebuild
docs.x: Possible causes — the database was restored on a node with a different FERNET_KEY . Backup bundles never contain the key. Solution — restore the original key from the sealed envelope ( sudo satom execute unseal recovery ) or from your exported copy, put it in .env , restart. If the key is lost, re-enter every appliance password. Verification — satom diagnose recovery ; appliances sync again. See Security model .

Possible causes — growth of data/ , the metrics store or bundles; a full disk stops PostgreSQL while /healthz may still answer 200. Solution — satom get system disk shows what grows; sudo satom execute repair tmp --yes removes aged scratch files; configure the backup server so verified bundles leave the node. Verification — free space above max(15 % of the volume, 3 GB) .

docs.s: Short answers to the questions people ask most about SATOM — passwords and sign-in, permissions, what SATOM changes on appliances, data and backups, updates, high availability, the API and the CLI.

docs.h: What is the default admin password?
docs.x: There is none. The first admin password is the one typed during installation, or the value of SATOM_ADMIN_PASSWORD ; if neither was given, a random password is written to /opt/satom/initial-admin-password (mode 0600, never to a log). See First login and Installation .

docs.h: How many failed sign-ins lock an account, and for how long?
docs.x: 10 consecutive failures lock the account for 15 minutes. Separately, each client address may try to sign in 5 times per minute. An administrator can unlock with sudo satom execute admin unlock <username> . See Security model .

docs.h: Can I use Active Directory, LDAP or RADIUS?
docs.x: Yes. Configure the sources in Settings → Authentication . They are tried in the configured order; local accounts always keep working and never fall through to a directory.
Yes, TOTP with one-time backup codes, for local accounts. Directory accounts do their MFA at the directory.

docs.h: Is there an idle session timeout?
docs.x: Yes. Settings → General → Session Lock (minutes) (5 to 1440, default 60) is an idle timeout: a browser session with no page load, navigation or form submission for longer than that is signed out on its next request, with "Your session was locked after N minutes of inactivity." Background refreshes such as the notification bell do not keep a session alive. API tokens are not affected. Separately, forms carry a CSRF token valid for one hour; an expired form is simply re-submitted.

docs.h: How long must a password be?
docs.x: 12 to 1024 characters, with no character-class rule. The same rule applies on every path that sets a password: Change Password, Add User, administrator reset, the reset link, the CLI and both installers. Existing passwords are not re-checked until they are changed. ℹ️ Note Changed in 2.11.0: Session Lock is enforced as an idle timeout (before, the setting had no effect), the password minimum is 12 characters everywhere, and the sidebar only shows pages the user can open.

docs.h: What can the built-in profiles do?
docs.x: Profile Can readonly View every section, change nothing operator View, plus manage appliances, protection, network, backups, operations and templates, and use Scout, the AI assistant admin Everything, including users, profiles, the registry and settings Create your own profiles from granular permissions; see Users and profiles and Permissions .

docs.h: Why is a menu entry missing for some users?
docs.x: The sidebar shows a link only when the user's profile can open that page. Pages that show device content need a read permission (for example protection.view for the FortiWeb protection pages, registry.view for the API Explorer, monitoring.view for Sentinel), and the Global home lists appliances only to holders of appliances.view . The seeded profiles hold every read key.

docs.h: Why can't some users see an appliance?
docs.x: Appliances in maintenance mode are hidden from users without appliances.view_maintenance , and each ADOM only shows its own product's appliances.

docs.h: Which Fortinet products does SATOM manage?
docs.x: FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer, FortiAuthenticator and, read-only since 3.0, FortiGate, each in its own ADOM, plus a Global ADOM that sees all of them. See ADOMs and products .

docs.h: Does SATOM change an appliance without showing me first?
docs.x: Structured configuration writes go through one writer whose default is a dry-run: it computes the request without contacting the appliance. A real apply takes a before/after snapshot and writes change history and an audit entry. Exceptions are tools that are explicitly raw, such as the API-Registry Explorer and the operator console. Destructive actions (firmware upgrade, reboot) need an approved change request inside its window.
In the SATOM database, encrypted with the node's FERNET_KEY . Optionally an external vault can hold them instead ( Settings → Vault ). See Security model .

docs.h: Do pages read live from the appliance?
docs.x: No — pages render from SATOM's local copy of each appliance's configuration. Contacting the appliance is an explicit action (refresh, sync, save).

docs.h: Why does a fresh installation do nothing automatically?
docs.x: Scheduled actions are seeded only when the node gets its first appliance (and only if it has no System Automation yet). Before that, or to fill gaps, run sudo satom execute seed actions to see the recommended set (hourly sync, nightly inspection and system backup, monitoring sweeps, reports, Sentinel jobs) and add --yes to create it. See Scheduled actions .

docs.h: Do scheduled actions run twice in a two-node pair?
docs.x: No. The scheduler only fires on the node whose database is the primary; on the standby it waits and checks again every 30 seconds.

docs.h: A long action is still running — can I close the browser?
docs.x: Yes. Device actions run as background jobs on the server; follow them in the Job Manager . Stop and pause take effect at the next safe point.

docs.h: What does a system backup contain?
docs.x: A pg_dump of the database, the per-device configuration files and versions, the sealed recovery envelope if one exists, and the documentation redaction rules. It never contains FERNET_KEY or the internal CA key. See System backup and Data and storage .
396 days, in the node-local metrics store. See Metrics .

docs.h: Can I update a node with no Internet access?
docs.x: Yes, with a signed offline update package uploaded on the Software Update page or applied with sudo satom execute update package <file> --yes . See Offline updates .

docs.h: What happens on the standby node?
docs.x: Its database is a read-only replica, scheduled actions do not fire, alert notifications are not sent, and data/ is copied from the primary every 5 minutes. Changes must be made on the primary. Failover is manual. See High availability .

docs.h: Can I run SATOM in Docker?
docs.x: Yes. The container stack runs the application, PostgreSQL, Redis, the metrics store and an nginx proxy. Host-level actions (software update, service control, certificate activation, unit health) are refused unless the optional operations agent is enabled. See Installation .

docs.h: Does the browser need Internet access?
docs.x: No. Every script, stylesheet and font is served by the SATOM node; the Content-Security-Policy allows no other origin.

docs.h: Which languages does the interface support?
docs.x: English, Español, Deutsch, Français and Italiano. Each user chooses a language; administrators choose which are offered.

docs.h: How big should the server be?
docs.x: From 2 vCPU / 4 GB / 20 GB for up to 10 appliances to 8 vCPU / 8 GB / 120 GB for about 110. Beyond that, split the fleet across installations. See Installation .

Yes: a token-authenticated REST API at /api/v1 , for inventory, triggering non-destructive scheduled actions, firmware checks and WAF/FortiADC carve-outs. It can never upgrade, flash or reboot an appliance. See REST API v1 .

docs.h: Can a token do more than the user who owns it?
docs.x: No. A token cannot be created or edited with a scope its owner's permissions do not cover, every call checks that the owner still holds the matching permission, and a disabled owner disables all their tokens.
A console tool on the node for diagnostics, repairs, updates and recovery, which works even when the web interface is down. Read commands work for any user; changes need sudo . See CLI .

docs.x: Released: 2026-10-21 · All releases

SATOM is now mapped to the Network Automation Forum's reference framework — six functional blocks around the network infrastructure — and this release closes the gaps that mapping exposed. The REST API describes itself with an OpenAPI document and gains three families of endpoints: desired state (templates, bindings, baselines — read, and written with explicit capabilities), what SATOM has observed (configuration history and diffs, the current findings, a read-only metrics query) and processes . A device bound to a template that no longer matches it is a finding. Processes start from events, f

Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework : the six blocks in SATOM's words, the five names that collide (the "Source of Truth" is the framework's Observability , not its Intent ), and why SATOM aligns with it. The conformance matrix — every requirement, its state and the file that is the evidence — is published with the product documentation ( docs/naf-alignment.html ; on a node, /manual/docs/naf-alignment.html ), pinned to the framework's commit da82b12 , and a test derives from it the only verdict the documentation may state.

docs.x: GET /api/v1/openapi.json — an OpenAPI 3.0 document built at request time from the live routes, the scope each one enforces and its summary. A route added tomorrow is documented the moment it is registered. Intent : GET /templates , /templates/<id> , /bindings , /baselines , scoped to the token's ADOM like a console session. docs.x: The health engine's new Intent deviation check (on by default, its own toggle, sink family intent ) renders each binding's template with the device's variables and compares it field by field with the cached device objects — the key-subset comparison the approval modal already uses, never equality against a raw snapshot, because an appliance fills in what the template never set. Measured on a FortiWeb 7.6.8 and an 8.0.6: the box answers "4" to a 4 , counts its own sub-table rows and renumbers internal handles; those are ignored, and sub-table rows are reported unmeasured rather than guessed at.

The upgrade merges them and keeps every article's audience. A FortiWeb template body may name its collection as the registry logical name, the cmdb tail or the full REST path; all three resolve to the same cached object. Device findings and the alert.fired payload carry appliance_id , so a hook or a process trigger can address the device.

docs.s: A documentation release — the API SATOM exposes to your systems is named and presented as the SATOM API, with its own manual title, its own section on the Features page, its own place in the site navigation and its own category in the Documentation Center, so it can no longer be confused with the Fortinet device APIs SATOM drives internally.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-21 · All releases

SATOM has two kinds of API, and the documentation did not tell them apart clearly enough. One is the set of Fortinet device APIs SATOM uses internally to read and write FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiGate, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator. The other is SATOM's own REST API at /api/v1 , the one your systems use to talk to SATOM. This release names the second one for what it is — the SATOM API — everywhere it is documented. No code path, schema or behaviour changes.

The integration manual is the "SATOM API v1 — Integration Manual" , and it opens by stating that it is SATOM's own API and not the device API. The base URL is written as https://<your-satom-host>/api/v1 , the address of your own SATOM server; the examples used to name three different hosts. The site navigation says "SATOM API" on every page of the manual a node serves at /manual/ , and the Features page has a SATOM API section of its own: what a token is, what it can read, what it can act on, what it can author, what no token can ever do, and the OpenAPI document the API serves about itself. docs.s: A fix release — every connection SATOM opens to an address you configure in Settings now verifies against the trust store, so an internal service signed by your company CA no longer fails with "unable to get local issuer certificate".
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-21 · All releases

The trust store used to reach only appliances, hypervisors and a few readers. Everything else you point at an address in Settings built its own TLS connection on the public roots, so an internal service signed by your company CA failed with certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate — even with that CA in the store. From 3.4.2 every one of those connections verifies against the public roots plus the trust store.

Settings → General → Update sources: an internal update feed or Python package index signed by your CA now passes Test , the update check, the download and the pip the updater runs. The same for every other configured service: the git remote, SMTP, alert webhooks, LDAP / Active Directory, the secret vault (unless it names its own CA), NetBox, ticket trackers, DNS / IPAM providers, the AI and Sentinel endpoints, App-ID sources and integrations. A verify switch you turned off stays off. The store widens what a verified connection accepts; it never changes whether a connection is verified.

docs.k: release 3.0.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: SATOM stops reading Fortinet's website itself and gets its vendor knowledge from signed knowledge packs, warns when a FortiWeb's signature database goes stale, and adds a read-only FortiGate workspace.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-08 · All releases

SATOM 3.0 changes where its vendor knowledge comes from. Release notes, the Scout advisory and upgrade paths no longer depend on SATOM reading Fortinet's documentation website: they come from signed knowledge packs that SATOM can fetch every day by itself, or that you upload on an air-gapped node. The release also watches the age of each FortiWeb's signature database and opens a new, read-only FortiGate workspace. Administrators will notice the new Knowledge packs card and the stricter pack signing rules; everyone will see a "Knowledge from…" freshness line on release notes, Scout and the Migr

docs.h: Knowledge packs on the Software Update page
docs.x: Under Software Update → Knowledge packs you now see, for each kind of pack, which one is installed, its date and its age: the API pack , which is tied to the SATOM release you run; the rolling knowledge pack , which is refreshed independently of releases. A stale badge appears once a pack is more than 30 days old, and the card shows what the knowledge feed currently offers. Three buttons do the work: Check now asks the feed what is available. Download fetches the pack. Its size and checksum must match what the feed announced; if they do not, nothing is kept. Import loads the pack as a backgrou

A new scheduled action, knowledge fetch , runs once a day. A setting decides how far it goes: off — do nothing; notify — only tell you a newer pack exists; download — download it, but leave the import to you; download and import — the default: download and import it. By default it reads the public SATOM knowledge feed, but you can point it at any HTTPS mirror. It uses the same connection settings, proxy and certificate checking as the software-update feed. A standby node does nothing and says why. The result of the last run (status, message, time and pack) is kept so you can see what happened.

docs.h: "Knowledge from…" on the pages that use it
docs.x: The Release Notes window, the Scout advisory and the Migration Report now show which pack their knowledge came from and its date. You get a warning when that pack is older than 30 days, or when no knowledge pack was ever imported, so you know how much to trust the advice.

A new daily scheduled action, signature check , reads only the signature database version of each FortiWeb and records when it last changed. It refreshes SATOM's cached signature catalog only when a version actually changed. The alert engine raises a device alert when a FortiWeb's signature database is older than a set number of days (7 by default), has never been updated, or cannot be read. Administrator → Signatures lists the signature database state per device. When a knowledge pack carries it, signature search and signature details also show public FortiGuard information: the signature nam

Knowledge packs can now carry more kinds of content. Each item is checked on its own: a malformed item is rejected with its reason, and the rest of the pack still imports. A section your SATOM does not know yet is skipped with a visible warning instead of failing the import. Predefined protection profiles go into the factory catalog , never over a profile SATOM captured from one of your own appliances. Field rename suggestions are shown with a badge. They are never applied for you and never replace a field mapping you made. Baselines are stored for a firmware build that has no baseline of your

When a pack wrote something earlier — release notes for a version, the field list of an object, other reference rows — and a newer pack carries a different version of it, the newer one now replaces it. The rules are simple: your own local data always wins and is never replaced; between two packs, the one built from the newer snapshot wins. Data that a 2.x SATOM imported from a pack is recognised as pack data, so it can be corrected too. The 3.0 API pack replaces the 2.x release packs: a shipped pack whose content an imported pack already carries is no longer reported as pending.

SATOM now has a sixth workspace, for FortiGate . You register a FortiGate with a REST API administrator token in the password field, because FortiOS 8.0 no longer accepts a password on its REST API. A dashboard with a device picker and the live status of the unit. 30 read-only pages in 7 areas that follow the FortiOS 8.0 menu. SATOM only reads: it never sends a change to the FortiGate. When the FortiGate refuses a request, you see an error, never an empty table. An "unauthorised" answer names the usual cause: an unlicensed virtual machine. Secret fields and encrypted values are removed before

SATOM no longer reads Fortinet's documentation website. The Scan from Fortinet panel on the release notes pages is gone. Release notes, the Scout advisory and upgrade paths read only what signed packs imported. Collecting from the vendor's website is now done by a separate tool that builds the packs. See The Knowledge Harvester . One key, one use. Each signing key now serves one purpose only. Software update packages are checked only against the update keys; a new-format pack only against the keys for its own kind (API pack or knowledge pack). A pack signed with the wrong kind of key is refuse
In the FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator workspaces, the Schema builds and Build compatibility links that appeared in the sidebar since 2.13.0 opened a refusal page. They now open.

New pack format. Packs published from 3.0 on use a new format. SATOM 2.13 and older refuse them with an "unsupported pack schema" error, so update SATOM before importing a 3.0-era pack. SATOM 3.0 still imports the older 2.x packs. Version requirement in packs. A pack can name the minimum SATOM version it needs. If it is newer than the SATOM you run, the whole pack is refused and the message tells you which version is needed. Add the two new scheduled actions. On an existing node, run the operator CLI's seed command ( satom execute seed actions --yes ) so the daily knowledge fetch and signature

An automatic check keeps any part of the application from contacting a Fortinet website again. Each pack records who published it, what it was built from and a fingerprint of its content, which is what allows the "newer snapshot wins" correction rule. Signature metadata from FortiGuard is supported but ships empty for now, because FortiGuard's terms do not allow redistributing it.

docs.k: release 2.13.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: SATOM learns what each firmware build really supports, over both the REST API and the CLI, and uses it to check every write, predict whether a configuration survives an upgrade, and write fields only the CLI can set.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-07 · All releases

2.13.0 is about firmware builds. SATOM now reads what each build of an appliance offers through both channels — the REST API it already used, and the appliance's own command line — and keeps that knowledge per build. On top of it come four things you can use: a Build compatibility check on every write and a page to explore it, a Migration Report that tells you whether an appliance's configuration will survive a move to another build, a CLI writer for the fields only the command line can set, and a new-build watch that warns administrators when an appliance runs a build SATOM has not studied ye

Before SATOM writes to an appliance, it now checks the change against that appliance's exact firmware build: Fields the build does not have are removed for that device and listed, for example "Applies, but on 8.0.6 this field does not exist: it will be skipped on 3 appliances". When SATOM knows the field's new name, it says so. Fields that only the command line can set are flagged, because a REST write cannot set them. A value outside the allowed options or range, or an object the build does not have, blocks the write. A build SATOM has never measured reads "not measured — cannot be guaranteed

A new Build compatibility page, reached from the API library, shows: a field × build matrix that says for each field whether a build serves it over both channels, the CLI only, hidden in the full configuration only, REST only, or is unknown — with filters and paging; a comparison of two builds : objects and fields added and removed, changed options, types, ranges and defaults, rename candidates and fields that moved; the history of one field across builds. See Build compatibility .

docs.h: Migration Report: will this configuration survive build X?
docs.x: The new Migration Report page (Automation, next to Upgrade Flow; also reachable from the appliance page) answers one question before an upgrade. You pick an appliance and a target build; SATOM takes the appliance's newest full configuration from the backup vault (or a backup you choose) and checks every object and field it uses against the target build. Each finding is classified: Block — an object or field the device uses is removed, a value is no longer accepted, a value is out of range, or a type change the value does not satisfy. Translate — a rename your field mappings already cover. Warn

docs.h: CLI writer: fields only the CLI serves
docs.x: Some fields can only be set from the appliance's command line. The object editor now handles them: Each field of a save is routed by what the appliance's exact build supports: CLI-only and hidden fields go through the command line, the others through REST as before. A field the build does not have, or one SATOM never measured, is refused with the reason. The Save preview shows the CLI script for the command-line part next to the usual REST request. The change to one object runs as a single CLI transaction. SATOM stops at the first error the appliance prints and cancels the pending change, so n

docs.h: Harvest the CLI schema of a build
docs.x: The API library now also learns from the appliance's command line: the full command tree of the running build (objects, fields, types, options) and the field names its full configuration shows, hidden ones included. Only names are collected, never values. You start it with Harvest CLI schema in the API Explorer (it runs as a device job and only reads from the appliance), from a scheduled action, or from the operator CLI. Comparing two builds now also covers the CLI side: fields that changed channel, options added and removed, type and range changes, and rename candidates — which are reported b

docs.h: Schema builds page and the new-build watch
docs.x: When an appliance runs a build SATOM has no schema for, administrators get one bell notification per product and build: "New build X on Y: schema not harvested". It comes from the firmware check and from a new scheduled action. The new Schema builds page (sidebar) lists each product's schema reader and whether it has been verified, the builds waiting to be harvested with a one-click harvest , and — after a harvest — what is new or changed compared with the closest known build, marked "to verify" where the REST side is not yet measured. Schema reading now works per product. FortiWeb, FortiAuthe

docs.h: A knowledge pack ships with each release
docs.x: Next to the release packs, each release now carries one knowledge pack built by the separate SATOM Harvester tool and signed with the release key. Installing or updating SATOM imports every pending shipped pack : the newest release pack, then the newest knowledge pack, each only if this node has not fully imported it yet. Older packs of the same series are superseded and skipped. A run with a failed item, or where you imported only some items, leaves the pack pending, so the next update tries again. The import history now records such runs as partial . Software Update lists knowledge packs wit

docs.h: Release notes for FortiAuthenticator, FortiAnalyzer and FortiGate
docs.x: Release notes now cover FortiAuthenticator (6.6 and 8.0), FortiAnalyzer and FortiGate. Their special notices feed the upgrade notes the advisor reads. The Release Notes window is offered in the FortiAuthenticator and FortiAnalyzer workspaces too. FortiGate notes travel in API packs. A build your appliances run that has no notes on this node is listed in the version pickers. Picking it while the vendor's website is unreachable says "No release notes for this build (offline: import a newer API pack)" instead of showing an empty list. See Release notes .

Every WAF and signature exception, and its fleet library copy, now records the firmware build and REST API version it was written for. Copies on other appliances keep the original build; editing the content updates it; rollback and restore bring back the build of the old version. No existing history gains an extra version because of this. Inject to device and the Attack ID insert check the exception against the target's build with the same rules as templates: discarded, renamed or unsupported fields block the push. An approver can override with a reason, and the override is audited. Exception

The CLI-coverage badges are more honest. Many blocks marked "CLI only" are in fact served by REST and just missing from the catalog. A block SATOM measured as served is now a catalog gap ; the others read Not in catalog , and the REST column says CLI only only when REST was measured absent. The release-notes scan lost its Firecrawl option. The endpoint and key fields and the "Direct" switch are gone from the scan panel; the scan only downloads directly from the vendor. A node without Internet gets the same notes from an API pack. An old browser tab or script that still sends those fields is no

Build compatibility in the Global workspace answered with an error page. It now opens. False "CLI only" fields. On a node where a table was empty, the channel view could mark hundreds of fields "CLI only" just because the vendor documentation did not list them (242 on FortiWeb 7.6.8). Only a real measurement can now say a field is missing; documentation alone leaves it unknown. Lab evidence from knowledge packs was skipped when the node had measured the same build itself, so tables that are empty in production stayed unknown. Lab evidence is now imported alongside your own; it can only add, ne

The API library stores both channels per build and keeps the REST-only pages (versions page, preflights, baselines, matrix export) reading REST evidence only. The command used to read the CLI tree is allowed only as an exact match behind its own safeguard; the read-only console rules are unchanged. API packs carry the new CLI evidence, and a row carrying a configuration value is refused both at export and at import. An unused Web Protection side menu that was rebuilt on every request was removed; the visible sidebar is unchanged.

docs.k: release 2.12.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: Templates now know which firmware build they were written for and are checked against every target build, predefined protection profiles are cached in a factory catalog, and deep rediscovery is much faster.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-06 · All releases

2.12.0 closes a quiet gap: a FortiWeb accepts a write containing a field its build does not know, reports success and simply drops the field. Templates now record the firmware build they belong to and are checked against each target's build before they are applied. The release also introduces the factory catalog , which stops SATOM from re-reading the same vendor-written protection profiles on every sweep, and makes a deep rediscovery with the CLI capture much faster. Anyone who applies templates or runs rediscoveries will notice the change. Administrators should read Before you upgrade : appr

Templates now store the firmware build their content was written for, the REST API version, where they came from (captured from an appliance, written by hand, or adapted) and, for captures, the source appliance. Save as template (from a Web Protection Profile or a configuration object) records the appliance's running build. New Template , the New template form on section pages and System Provisioning now ask you to choose a build SATOM knows. System profiles no longer default to a fixed "8.0" line. When you save , the template is compared with its own build through the API library, and the Tem

docs.h: Every apply is checked against the target's build
docs.x: Every way of applying a template — the Template Library, section pages, System Provisioning, baselines, and the automatic fleet deploy after a Web Protection Profile is approved — now shows a verdict per device: fields the build would discard, renamed fields and endpoints the build does not serve block the apply; missing evidence is a warning , never a pass; an approver can override with a reason, and the override is audited.
Approving a template now records the builds it was validated for. Rolling it out to the fleet on another build needs Revalidate first.

Adapt to firmware saves a new pending version of a template rewritten for a target build: known renames are carried over, fields the build does not serve are removed, and every change is listed in the version note. See Template library .

docs.h: Factory catalog for predefined protection profiles
docs.x: Every FortiWeb ships the same twenty or so predefined Web Protection Profiles, and the deep pass used to read all of them in full on every appliance, on every sweep — up to about 125 device reads each, most of the sweep's work. SATOM now keeps them in a factory catalog , one entry per profile per firmware version, build number and REST API version. The first deep pass on a build reads the predefined profiles in full and stores them. Later deep passes rebuild a predefined profile from the catalog, but only when the appliance's own rows match the stored entry. Anything that does not match is rea

docs.h: Deep rediscovery with the CLI capture is much faster
docs.x: A deep rediscovery with protection profiles and the CLI capture was reported as extremely slow. The captured configuration is the same; how it is read changed: Each device read happens once per sweep. A protection profile shared by 30 policies used to be read 31 times; repeated reads are now answered from memory. The finished sweep reports how many device reads it made and how many were reused. The CLI capture runs alongside the deep pass , so the sweep takes as long as the longer of the two instead of their sum. If you press Stop during the deep pass, a capture already running is allowed to f

Templates saved before this release show no firmware . Approved templates have no validated builds yet. Their fleet rollouts and baseline applies are refused until an approver clicks Revalidate for fleet builds (in the template's View dialog), once per template. Single-device applies are only checked field by field and keep working. The factory catalog and the parallel reads can be tuned or switched off by your administrator in the node configuration; see Configuration files and environment variables .

docs.k: release 2.11.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: A large security and consistency release — every page and action now enforces its own permission, passwords and idle sessions follow one policy, privileged actions are audited, and a long list of everyday problems is fixed.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-03 · All releases

2.11.0 is a hardening and clean-up release. Its main theme is that what you see is what you may do : every page, button and menu entry now checks the same permission, pages that used to open for any signed-in user now ask for a view permission, and rows hidden from a list can no longer be reached by typing their address. Passwords follow one rule everywhere, the Session Lock setting finally signs idle browsers out, and privileged node actions now leave an audit trail. Alongside the security work come a few new tools (external change approval, secret values for integration hooks, store snapshot

Record an external approval. A change request in External approval mode could never run, because nothing recorded the outside verdict. Your integrations can now send the verdict to SATOM through the REST API (with an administrator-scope token; changes outside the token's workspace are not found; manual-mode and closed changes are refused; every call is audited). An Administrator can also record or withdraw the verdict by hand on the change's External change record card. See Change requests . Change ticket reference from a hook. When a hook that runs on a new change request succeeds and returns
The Notifications page has a Clear all button. After you confirm, it permanently deletes all your notifications. The bell's Clear still only marks them read. See Notifications .

Peer replication status on the Collection page: whether this node's samples are also written to the peer node, which peer, the last success and the number of failures in a row. Store snapshots and nodes : a new card shows the state of each node's metrics store and lists its snapshots. Users with edit rights can take or delete a snapshot; deleting one is audited. See Metrics collection . Unmute is now available on muted probes in Deep monitors and Service Monitor. Analytics boards can be created from the page and open straight away, and custom boards gain an Edit board form for the title, descr

Users page actions. Each user row now offers Reset password (local accounts, with confirmation), Clear 2FA (when enabled) and Unlock (when the account has failed sign-ins or is locked out). All three are audited. Unlock clears the lockout and nothing else: a disabled account stays disabled. Holders of View users now get a read-only user list and a Users entry in the sidebar. See Users and permission profiles . Node TLS renewal. Settings → Node TLS has a new Renewal of an imported certificate card: choose Alert only or Automatic pull , enter where to fetch the certificate from, and press Test n

False-positive explainer: two optional fields — a Web Protection Profile, now named in the "where on the device" path under each carve-out, and a payload decoder that peels encoding layers off a value you paste without a log entry. See False-positive explainer . Certificate inspector: the Paste tab has a passphrase field for encrypted private keys, and the Probe tab an optional SNI / host name field. See Certificate inspector .

There is now one rule everywhere: at least 12 and at most 1024 characters , length only, with no rule about character classes. It applies to Add User, an administrator's password reset, Change Password, the reset link, the operator CLI's password reset, the installer and the guided setup. Before, each of these had its own rule, and the web forms accepted any non-empty password while saying "at least 8 characters". Existing passwords are not checked again; the rule applies the next time a password is set.

docs.h: Session Lock now signs idle browsers out
docs.x: Settings → General → Session Lock (minutes) was saved but never applied, so a browser could stay signed in for weeks. It is now an idle timeout: a browser with no activity for that long is signed out on its next click with "Your session was locked after N minutes of inactivity.", and the lock is written to the audit log. Background refreshes (the notification bell, job progress, status badges, edit-lock heartbeats and timed panel reloads) do not count as activity, so a tab left open still locks. API tokens are not affected. See General settings .

docs.h: Pages and actions ask for the right permission
docs.x: Read pages need a view permission. About 80 pages only checked that you were signed in. Now the audit trail needs View audit log ; the API consoles of FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator need View registry ; the appliance list and detail pages need View appliances ; Device Provisioning needs View operations ; and the Monitoring pages need any read permission. The Audit Log menu entry follows its page's permission. Device-content pages need a view permission. The FortiWeb workspace, protection pages, exceptions, WAF artifacts, server objects, the other product workspaces, the API reg

View backups now opens the Device Backups list (details only), so read-only users can see which backups exist. Creating, uploading and deleting still need a backup create or restore permission; downloading a backup (the full device configuration) needs Create backups . The appliance Restore page needs both Manage users and Restore backups ; Import Backup needs Restore backups . Operators and administrators keep their access. Upgrade Preparation is granted by Run appliance actions . A live restore is aborted when the automatic pre-restore backup fails , so a restore never runs without a rollbac

The Schedule for later card on the single-appliance Upgrade page is gone: the action it created could never run. Use Upgrade Flow , which raises a change request with its window and schedules the upgrade once approved. Existing scheduled entries are left as they are. Upgrade Flow now covers FortiWeb only , because SATOM cannot flash FortiADC; FortiADC pre-upgrade checks are still on the appliance page. See Upgrade Flow .

Every message that leaves the node is redacted. Before, only the newest message was; up to 19 earlier turns went out verbatim. Every turn sent is now redacted, counted in the export log and in the pre-send review, which says how many earlier messages go with the new one. Local means a local address. docs.k: release 2.10.1 what's new changelog
docs.s: Stop now really stops a rediscovery during its deep capture, and keeps your previous deep capture intact.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-03 · All releases
A small fix release for operators who run rediscoveries with the deep capture option turned on. Pressing Stop during the deep capture now actually stops it, instead of carrying on to the end.

docs.h: Stop did not stop a running deep capture
docs.x: When a rediscovery was in its deep pass ( Capture full WPP + policy depth ), pressing Stop said "stopping after the current step" but then went on to walk every remaining server policy and web protection profile anyway. Now: The deep pass checks for Stop before each object, finishes the object it is working on, and ends as Stopped . The result tells you where it stopped, for example at object 5/23 and the name of the profile it was on. What the deep pass had read so far is thrown away and your previous deep capture is kept . A half-finished capture would make the objects it never reached look
Two internal checks that had been failing since 2.6.0 were repaired. The product itself behaved correctly.

docs.k: release 2.10.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: Job notices can be minimised, the deep capture shows real progress, and Device health is filled in right after a rediscovery.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-03 · All releases

This release answers three requests from people using SATOM every day. Job notices can now be folded down to a single line, the deep capture of a rediscovery shows what it is doing instead of sitting at 100 %, and Device health no longer claims a device was "never harvested" just after you rediscovered it.

Each notice in the jobs dock (the stack of job toasts on screen) now has a − button. A minimised notice is one line: the job title, its percent and a thin progress bar. Click □ or the title to bring it back to full size, with its message and its Stop button. Your choice is remembered when you move to another page or reload, for the rest of the browser session. Dismissing a notice forgets the choice. This keeps long-running jobs visible without covering the page you are working on.

docs.h: Deep capture sat at "running…" at 100 % with no count
docs.x: With Capture full WPP + policy depth turned on, the rediscovery bar reached 100 % and then showed only "Deep capture (WPP + policy graph) running…" for as long as the deep pass took. Now: The deep pass first lists the server policies and web protection profiles it will read, then reports each one as it starts. The bar switches to the deep pass's own percent, and the line reads, for example, Deep capture 5/23 · 8 server policies, 14 WPPs · WPP 3/12 followed by the profile name. The job notice in the dock and the Jobs page show the same line and percent. The finished summary says how many server

docs.h: Device health said "never harvested" right after a rediscovery
docs.x: After a rediscovery, Device health could show no cached configuration on this node , never harvested and 4 probes have never run . Two things changed: A rediscovery now fills the local cache. Until now only the hourly harvest updated the cache that Device health, the section pages and the inventory read. A successful rediscovery now does it too, and it is recorded as a harvest run started by a rediscovery. A rediscovery and an hourly harvest of the same configuration count as one version, not two. If the cache cannot be updated, the rediscovery still finishes as done and its summary says local

docs.k: release 2.9.1 what's new changelog
docs.s: A discovery with wrong credentials no longer locks the FortiWeb admin account or wipes the last good snapshot.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-02 · All releases

An important fix for anyone running discovery or rediscovery. If the appliance refused SATOM's credentials, the sweep used to keep trying on every endpoint, which locked the FortiWeb admin account and then replaced the device's configuration snapshot with an empty one. Both problems are gone.

docs.h: Refused credentials locked the admin account and left an empty snapshot
docs.x: In the reported case, a rediscovery got "unauthorised" (HTTP 401) on all of its endpoints, and afterwards the appliance showed no configuration at all, not even its time settings. On FortiWeb, every refused request counts as a failed admin login, and after a few of them (three by default) the account is locked. A locked account refuses everything, including the right password, so SATOM kept the admin locked out for itself and for anyone trying to use the FortiWeb GUI. The empty result was then saved as the latest snapshot, replacing the last good one. What happens now: A refused login stops di
