docs.k: release 2.9.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: Every action you take on a device now runs as a background job that shows its progress, and writes to the same device queue instead of colliding.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-02 · All releases

This release changes how SATOM carries out anything you do to an appliance. Instead of a button that freezes until a slow device answers (or times out half-way through a change), every device action now runs as a background job that shows where it is, step by step. Writes to the same device line up behind each other. Operators who work on many devices or slow appliances will notice it most. It also fixes a large number of buttons that looked like plain text.

docs.h: Every device action runs as a job
docs.x: The request was simple: every action inside a device should create a job, run in the background and show how far it has got. Until now, an action that talked to an appliance ran while your browser waited. A slow appliance meant a frozen button and no feedback, and if it took too long the request was cut off with the device possibly half-changed. Only a handful of device actions used jobs. Now almost every action in the device areas runs as a job, including: appliances, Workspace, the object editor and the server policy wizard; Web Protection, Server Objects, Exceptions and the Certificate Mana

SATOM waits about two seconds for the action to finish. If it finishes in that time, you get the normal result, as before. If it takes longer, the action is handed to a job right away. On pages that update in place, the job notice follows it and the page gets its normal result when it is done. On classic forms you are taken to a progress page that switches to the action's own result page when it finishes. Confirmation messages are kept.

Each call SATOM makes to the appliance, and each SSH command, is one step of the job, shown with its result and how long it took. You can follow the steps in the job notice, on the progress page and in the job's details on the Jobs page.

docs.h: Writes to the same device wait their turn
docs.x: Two changes to the same device run one after the other. The second one shows Queued — waiting for the first action, and you can stop it while it waits. Once a change has started on the device it can no longer be stopped: stopping between two calls would leave the device half-changed. Read-only actions never queue, and can be stopped between calls.
The appliance page now lists the running and recent jobs for that device, and refreshes as soon as one starts or ends.

docs.h: Discovery and rediscovery are jobs too
docs.x: A discovery or rediscovery now appears in the jobs dock and on the Jobs page with its progress. You can stop it from either place, or from the Discovery page as before.

Device actions that take more than a moment now show progress instead of a frozen button. The Jobs page stays readable: an action that never reached a device (for example a form error, or an edit that only changes SATOM's own database) does not leave a job behind. Some things deliberately work as before: calls made with API tokens, actions on the standby node, and the actions that were already jobs (firmware upgrade and downgrade, backups, signature sync, monitor sweeps). Administrators can turn the new behaviour off with a node setting.

93 buttons looked like plain text. Buttons such as Edit , Analysis / FortiView and most quick actions on the appliance page had no background or border. They now look like buttons again, and a new check stops this from coming back. The update package builder could not be run directly. On a fresh copy of the source, running the script that builds an offline update package failed with Permission denied unless you started it through the shell explicitly. It now runs directly. Nothing inside an update package or an installed node changes.
Jobs Appliances Discovery and rediscovery Offline updates

docs.k: release 2.8.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: Rediscovery finally uses your imported CAs, rediscovery gets a Stop button, and Node TLS certificate changes show each step and warn about the web server reload.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-02 · All releases

This release is about certificates and about control over long sweeps. Rediscovery now trusts the private CAs you imported in the TLS trust store, the trust store page is easier to use, a rediscovery can be stopped, and changing the console's own certificate under Node TLS now shows what is happening and tells you clearly what to expect when the web server reloads.

A Stop button appears while a sweep is running. Anyone allowed to start a rediscovery can stop it. The sweep stops once the request it is waiting on returns, and saves no snapshot, so the previous complete snapshot is kept. Stopping during the sweep also skips the deep capture and CLI capture. If one of those passes has already started, it runs to its end. A stopped sweep ends in a new Stopped state that records who stopped it. A sweep marked as running whose worker has already gone is closed right away. A sweep run by the other cluster node cannot be stopped from here. A leftover stop request

docs.h: Content view in the TLS trust store
docs.x: A new Content action opens the decoded certificate: subject, issuer, serial number, validity, key, signature algorithm, SHA-256 and SHA-1 fingerprints and every extension, plus the PEM text, with Copy and Download buttons.

docs.h: TLS trust store: one Save button per slot
docs.x: Save root CA and Save intermediate CA replace the single Import button. Each one saves only its own box (plus the name and note). The reply tells you which role every certificate was filed under, so if you paste a certificate in the wrong box you are told, instead of it being silently re-labelled. The row and test buttons on the trust store page now look the same as the other buttons in Settings.

docs.h: Node TLS: certificate activation shows each step
docs.x: Under Settings → Node TLS , importing a certificate (pasted or uploaded), issuing one from the internal CA and renewing now run as jobs. A progress panel on the tab shows each step: check (or create) the certificate; write the files; test the web server configuration; reload the web server; check that the web server now serves the new certificate. If something fails and the previous certificate is put back, that step is shown too. Mistakes in what you entered are still reported immediately. If the node has to hand the work over to its privileged update service, the panel says so and shows how

docs.h: A clear warning about the web server reload
docs.x: Changing the certificate reloads the web server that serves the console. You are now always told so: in a confirmation before you start, in a warning in the panel, and in a reminder after success. Open connections move to the new certificate. If the page stops responding or the browser shows a certificate warning, close every browser window and open SATOM again. If the page loses contact with the node right after the switch, the panel explains that this is expected, keeps retrying for three minutes, and points you to the Jobs page, where the outcome is kept.

After the reload, SATOM connects to itself and compares the certificate it is actually serving with the one it just installed. If they differ, the job ends with a warning (nothing is rolled back, because the web server accepted the files). This check runs only when you change the certificate from the console; the nightly automatic renewal does not run it.

docs.h: Rediscovery ignored the TLS trust store
docs.x: Even with the root and intermediate CAs saved under Settings → TLS trust store , a rediscovery could fail with certificate verify failed , while Test TLS on the same page said the device was verified. Sweeps, jobs and scheduled actions were checking devices against public CAs only. They now use your imported CAs too. If the trust store cannot be read at all, SATOM still falls back to public CAs, never to no verification.

docs.k: release 2.7.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: A node can now fetch its own signed update package online, updates bring the new API pack with them, and Node TLS can generate certificate requests.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-02 · All releases

This release makes updating easier and gives administrators more control over the console's certificate. A node can check for and download the newest signed update package by itself, an update now also brings the API library up to date, and Node TLS can create a certificate signing request for an outside CA. It also fixes the sudo satom command on openSUSE and RHEL, and certificate issuing on hosts with a managed sudo setup.

docs.h: Download the newest update package from the console
docs.x: Every release's signed update package is now listed in a public index (the "system-upgrade feed") with its version, download link, size, checksum and signing key. Under Software Update → Offline update package , use Check for a newer package online and Download & stage . The check and download run as a background job; then you go through the usual preflight and Apply . The same is available from the command line: a new update command reads the feed, downloads the newest package, checks its size and checksum, and applies it the same way as a package you uploaded (the signature is checked twice)

docs.h: Node TLS: generate a certificate signing request (CSR)
docs.x: Under Settings → Node TLS → Certificate signing request (CSR) you can have the node create a private key and a CSR, so another CA can issue the console's certificate. Fill in the common name (the node's host name by default), extra names or IP addresses, and optionally organisation, unit, city, state and country. Choose the key: RSA 2048, 3072 or 4096, or ECDSA P-256 or P-384. The private key never leaves the node. Copy or download the CSR. When the certificate comes back, import it with the private key left empty: it is paired automatically with the waiting key.

docs.h: Node TLS: paste a certificate as text
docs.x: Import certificate (PEM) now accepts pasted text as well as files, with a Paste PEM / Upload files switch. Line endings and indentation from a paste are cleaned up. Giving the same item both as a file and as text is refused.

docs.h: Updates bring the API pack with them
docs.x: Every release's API pack is now kept, not just the latest one. "Shipped pack" means the newest by version. After a successful update on a primary or standalone node, the update imports the newest shipped API pack as one of its steps. A problem with this step never fails the update; it is skipped on a standby node and can be turned off. Before, an update put the new pack on disk but left the API library on the old one. Software Update shows a notice while the newest shipped pack has never been imported on this node. A full import that finds nothing new now counts, so the notice clears.

sudo satom said "command not found" on openSUSE and RHEL. On those systems sudo does not look in the folder where the SATOM command lives, so every sudo satom … command printed by the installer, the command line and the documentation failed outside Debian. Installs, updates and a reinstall of the command now add a link where sudo finds it (never replacing an unrelated command of the same name), and the privilege check reports the link. The offline update guide gave commands that did not work on hosts where sudo only allows root. The instructions now use commands that work there too. "Issue fro
Before any restart or reload of the web server, the privileged update service now tests the web server configuration first.
Software update Offline updates Node TLS API library Command line

docs.k: release 2.6.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: API packs carry SATOM's knowledge of vendor APIs to offline nodes, and a running update now shows the step it is on.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-02 · All releases

This release introduces API packs : a signed file that moves what one SATOM installation has learned about vendor APIs to another, so nodes without Internet access, or without an appliance of a given firmware, still know it. Every release now ships its own pack and the installers import it. Updates also become easier to watch: the update screen and the command line show the step in progress instead of looking frozen.

docs.h: API packs: the API library for offline nodes
docs.x: An API pack is one signed file that contains what a SATOM installation knows about vendor APIs: the API library evidence (which endpoints and fields each firmware build serves); the release notes, with the full vendor text; the field definitions read from appliances; the summary of which CLI settings are and are not reachable through the API. A node that is offline, or that has never seen an appliance running a given firmware, has no other way to learn this. Nothing identifying leaves the node. Only field names and types are exported, never configuration values. Device names are replaced by st

The pack travels with the product: in the online installation, in every offline bundle, in the update package and in the public source. It is also attached to the release on its own, for a node that only needs the pack.

On a standalone node or a cluster primary, the installer imports the pack once the console is up, online or offline. If the import fails you get a warning with the command to try again; the installation itself does not fail. Installer settings let you skip the pack, import a different one, or limit it to certain products. Existing answer files keep working.

docs.h: Settings → Software Update → API library packs
docs.x: Lists the release's pack and any packs you uploaded. Shows every item as new , present or local (measured by this node). Filter by product and section, tick what you want, and import it as a background job with progress per item. A failed item turns the job red and tells you which items were imported. On a standby node the page is read-only. The same can be done from the command line, as the service account: one command shows the pack, another imports a pack file or the shipped pack, optionally limited to a product or section. Without confirmation it only shows what it would do.

docs.h: The CLI coverage card uses imported data
docs.x: When this node has no CLI capture for the firmware you are asking about, the CLI coverage card now reads the imported pack and names it as its source. It never borrows data from a different firmware version.

docs.h: Updates show what they are doing
docs.x: The slow steps of an update (database backup, installing software components offline, database changes, restart, health check) can take minutes. Until now nothing changed on screen while they ran, so a working update looked stuck. Settings → Software Update: the live panel shows Running: and the current step with a timer. While the request waits to be picked up it says waiting for the update runner (and after 30 seconds points to what to check). During the restart it says the service is restarting — reconnecting instead of going silent. If you reopen the page while an update runs, the live pan
The Switch Product icon showed as a broken image on the Line profiles page.
The release process now builds and verifies each release's API pack automatically, and scans its contents with the same redaction rules as the public source.
API library Software update Offline updates Command line Line profiles

docs.k: release 2.5.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: Every release now ships a signed offline update package, offline-installed nodes can finally apply it, and the console no longer reaches out to the Internet.
docs.x: Released: 2026-10-01 · All releases

This release makes offline updates real. Every release now publishes a signed update package, and nodes that were installed offline can apply it for the first time. Database updates now run properly on installed nodes, the console no longer waits for Internet resources on isolated networks, and dialogs work again on servers with animations turned off. Behind the scenes, SATOM now picks API endpoint names per firmware build.

docs.h: A signed offline update package with every release
docs.x: Each release now publishes an update package next to the offline bundles and the container image, with its checksum and the public key that signs it. The package contains the application and all of its pinned software components, but no operating system packages. An existing node applies it from Settings → Software Update or from the command line. Before anything is published, the package is built from the same redacted content as the bundles, signed, and checked against the key the product ships. New installations trust the new release key automatically. Older nodes need to trust it once (see

docs.h: Endpoint names follow each appliance's firmware build
docs.x: When SATOM talks to a FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer, FortiAuthenticator or FortiWeb, it now picks the API endpoint name that matches that appliance's exact build. This applies to backups, exception injection, cloning (using the target's build), write-through, the FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator configuration sweeps and the API explorer consoles. The order of preference is: an endpoint an operator edited in the registry, then what the API library measured on that build, then the registry default. If the build does not serve an endpoint you get a readable "not served by" message instead of "unkno

docs.h: The FortiWeb baseline drops 31 endpoints that do not exist
docs.x: The FortiWeb endpoint list was refreshed against firmware 7.6.8 and went from 517 to 486 entries. The 31 removed names were measured absent on every measured build: FortiWeb answered each of them with "The REST API has invalid URL". Some of their objects actually live under other names. A refresh no longer drops an endpoint that another measured build still serves; it is kept and marked as carried over from that build. Without this, 8 endpoints added in FortiWeb 8.0.5 would have been lost and never read on a fresh install. Per-build selection keeps them away from a 7.6.8 appliance.

docs.h: Docker: console updates download the published image
docs.x: When you update a Docker installation from the console, the operations agent now downloads the published container image, checks its checksum and that it really is the requested version, and loads it, instead of building it for 5–15 minutes. It still builds when the release has no image, the host is not x86_64, or building is requested. A failed or mismatching download fails the update and leaves the running stack untouched. An agent started from 2.4.1 or earlier keeps building until the stack is brought up again with the Docker helper.

An offline-installed node could never apply an update package. Every package was refused at the step that counts local changes, with "not a git repository", so no node installed from an offline bundle could be updated from Software Update . The installer now records a starting point the update needs, and the update adopts an installation that does not have one. Database updates never ran on installed nodes. The first update tried to recreate the database from the beginning, failed on a table that already existed, and still reported success. Simple additions arrived anyway, but a database chang

Nodes installed before 2.5.0 must trust the new release key once before they accept the update package. The steps are in Offline updates . Nodes installed offline before 2.5.0 still apply their first package with the old update service, so they need a one-time preparation step first, also described in Offline updates .

Every third-party file the browser loads is now listed with its version, licence, source and checksum, and a check fails the build if anything would be loaded from another site. Unattended package signing never puts the passphrase on a command line. The update package builder now picks software components for the nodes, not for the machine that builds it.
Offline updates Software update Pack trust API registry Container operations Installation

docs.k: release 2.4.1 what's new changelog
docs.s: Docker installs from the published source work again, and every release now publishes a ready-made container image.

A release for people who install SATOM with Docker. The public source of 2.4.0 could not start under Docker; 2.4.1 fixes that. Each release now also publishes a ready-made container image, so the guided installer downloads it instead of building one.

docs.h: The container image is published with every release
docs.x: Each release now carries a ready-made SATOM container image (for 64-bit x86 hosts) and its checksum, built from the same redacted code as the offline bundles. The 2.4.0 release received its image after it was published. The guided installer, in Docker mode, now downloads this image, stops if the checksum does not match, and loads it, instead of building the image for 5–15 minutes. It still builds when the release has no image, on a host that is not x86_64, or when you ask it to build. docs.k: release 2.3.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: Never published on its own — its Docker operations agent and Docker fixes reached users in 2.4.0.
docs.x: Released: 2026-09-26 · never published · All releases

This version was never published. Its release run stopped before anything was tagged or packaged, so no installation ever ran 2.3.0. Everything below reached users in SATOM 2.4.0 . The main addition is an optional Docker operations agent : on a Docker installation, the console can now restart the stack's services, switch to another release and install the proxy certificate, things the container setup could not do before. Several Docker problems were also fixed.

The web console itself still never touches the Docker engine. It leaves a request for the agent, a separate and optional service that is the only container with access to Docker. The agent checks each request against a short, fixed list of allowed operations and carries it out. The agent is off by default , because access to Docker is equivalent to full control of the host.

A new page, shown only on a container node, for users allowed to manage users. It has these cards: Operations agent: whether it is live, not answering or not enabled, its versions and layout; Capabilities: what the console can do on this node; Services of this stack: the services and their state; Update: switch to another release, confirmed by typing UPDATE ; Proxy certificate: install a new certificate; Recent agent requests.

Only three kinds of request; anything else is refused: Restart a service. The web, proxy, database, cache and metrics services can only be restarted; the scheduler and cron services can also be started and stopped. The agent itself and the certificate set-up service are never touched. Switch to a release (given as a version number). Install a certificate (certificate, private key and optional chain). A request that is more than 10 minutes old when the agent picks it up is refused rather than carried out late.

Installing a certificate reloads the proxy instead of restarting it, so open connections, including your own, survive. The new certificate is tested first; if it is rejected, the previous one is put back and nothing is reloaded. The page and the import result then show the certificate actually being served.

The agent downloads the release if it is not already on the host, refuses a release with invalid network settings, builds the image, recreates every service except itself, reloads the proxy and waits up to 7 minutes for the web service to become healthy. If it does not, the release, the image and the stack settings are rolled back. Things to know: It takes no backup and does not roll back the database. It never updates itself: the agent moves to the new version the next time the stack is brought up with the Docker helper, and the page shows the difference until then. Release switches need the

docs.h: When the console uses the agent
docs.x: The console only hands work to the agent when the agent has been declared for this stack and has reported in within the last minute. A silent agent is treated as absent, with the message "The operations agent is enabled but not answering" , and nothing is queued behind it. The services card, container health and the node certificate now read their information from the agent.

The guided installer can enable the agent when the release includes it, and in update mode it offers to add it to an existing installation. Disabling it later is a one-line change in the stack's settings. Switching from the console to a release without the agent is refused. On manual checkouts the agent is enabled with a new setting in the environment file, off by default.

Failover to the standby on a container node remains a manual database procedure: the agent never does it. The built-in update methods for native installations still refuse to run in a container, and now point you to System → Container operations .

The Docker health check checked the application again. It had stopped with an error before showing the runtime summary. Promoting the standby is refused in a container. Before, the console queued a failover that nothing would ever carry out, and reported it as queued. Version numbers with a trailing line break were accepted when asking for a release switch. Both the agent and the console now reject them. Docker: the console answered with error 502 after the web service was recreated , until the proxy was restarted (every Docker install before this version). The proxy now looks up the web servi

docs.k: release 2.2.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: SATOM now keeps a versioned API library for every product, and firmware answers, pre-flights and the API explorer are based on it.
docs.x: Released: 2026-09-26 · All releases

This release introduces the API library : a permanent record of which API endpoints and fields each firmware build of each product serves, with every fact traced back to where it came from. The firmware matrix, the clone and upgrade pre-flights, the API versions page and the API explorer now all rely on it. Anyone who clones configuration between appliances, plans firmware upgrades or uses the API explorer will notice more precise answers.

docs.h: A versioned API library for every product
docs.x: The library is stored in SATOM's database and is never rewritten: each piece of evidence is stored once, and seeing the same content again only confirms it. Facts are kept per field, per firmware build and per source, so the library grows with the number of builds, not with the number of sweeps. Five products are covered: FortiWeb — from sweeps and field definitions read from appliances; FortiADC — from sweeps and the earlier firmware matrix; FortiAuthenticator — from its own API description, read live and read-only (58 resources and 316 fields on 8.0.3); FortiAnalyzer — from the vendor's publ

docs.h: The API versions page covers every product
docs.x: A product selector now reaches FortiAuthenticator, FortiAnalyzer and FortiGate. The new Library comparison compares any two builds: endpoints and fields added, removed, changed in type or renamed, with unknowns kept separate. The new Endpoint drill-down lists the fields of an endpoint on a build and tells you since which build any field has existed.

A new page lets operators with registry editing rights record that a firmware renamed a field. Comparisons and pre-flights then report a rename instead of one field lost and another added. Mappings are retired, never deleted.

docs.h: The API explorer knows the firmware build
docs.x: It identifies the selected appliance's exact build and shows it, with its evidence, in a banner. Every endpoint in the menu is marked served , absent or unknown for that build. It lists the fields the endpoint serves on that build. For a build nobody has measured yet, it offers Harvest this appliance now .

docs.h: The clone dialog offers the destination's new fields
docs.x: When you clone to an appliance on a newer build, fields that the destination serves and the source lacks are listed with their type, options and evidence. Nothing is added unless you fill in a value, and every value is checked again on the server.

Every rediscovery files its snapshot in the library. When the firmware check sees that an appliance changed build, it queues one background harvest. This is on by default and can be turned off. A new scheduled action harvests every appliance whose build has no evidence yet. It is available but not scheduled by default.

The firmware matrix, the clone and upgrade pre-flights and the API versions page now read the library. Rebuild still writes an export file so that the command-line version and pre-flight reports keep working when the database is down; the console itself no longer reads it. The clone and upgrade pre-flights look up both appliances' exact builds and say what kind of evidence each answer is based on. If only the vendor's documentation says an endpoint is missing, you get a warning; only an appliance that actually rejected the endpoint blocks the operation. The API explorer refuses to send a reque

Deleting or retiring an appliance deleted the evidence for its firmware build. It no longer does. One build measured only on appliances since retired had disappeared this way; it was restored from archived snapshots. A rediscovery run as a job could write into the wrong database. It now always writes to the database of the SATOM instance running it. A rediscovery after a firmware check replaced the appliance's full firmware string , including its build number, with the bare version. It no longer does.

2.1.0 is a large release built mostly from operators' requests. It touches four areas: Firmware upgrades — Scout reads Fortinet's upgrade instructions and tells you, on the upgrade page itself, if the version you are about to install has a known reason not to go ahead. Change requests — an open change can now be corrected instead of being cancelled and retyped. Before, this needed the full edit form. Maintenance mode is more than a label: it hides the device from operators and read-only users and stops scheduled probes and metric collection. So: you need the same permissions as in the edit form: permission to edit the device and permission to see devices in mai

A status check no longer counts as an edit. The time a device was last changed now really means the last configuration change, not the last time its status was polled. A device's firmware read during a sweep now carries t

SATOM still contains nothing that can write to a FortiGate, and holds no credential that could.

docs.h: Nothing is listed without border confirmation
docs.x: An address can only reach the list after passing the border check introduced in 1.18.0. FortiWeb sometimes reports a CDN's address instead of the real client, and listing such an address would block every legitimate visitor behind that CDN. That is why this feature was released only after the border check. You can set the border check aside for one listing, but only as a recorded action with a written reason . The never-block list can never be overridden.

docs.h: Release an address with one click, and keep the record
docs.x: One click takes an address off the feed immediately. This works whether or not the feed is switched on, the audit mirror is working, or the border is answering. A release is not a deletion: the entry stays, with who released it and why, so that false positives can be reviewed later. Deleting an old incident does not release an address that is still within its listing period.

FortiWeb blocks expire on the appliance itself. A threat feed has no such timer, so SATOM builds the feed fresh from its database on every request and leaves out expired entries. Nothing depends on a background job staying alive to remove them. One limitation remains and is stated openly: a FortiGate that cannot reach SATOM keeps the last list it downloaded. Every feed therefore says when it was generated and when it should be considered stale, and the console reports staleness.

You can keep an audit copy of the blocklist in a git repository. It is off by default and has no default destination . Use a separate, private repository. A blocklist reveals which addresses attacked which customer and must never be placed where it could become public. If the mirror cannot reach its repository, listing and releasing still work.

A new settings group, Border blocklist feed , covers: switching the feed on or off (off by default); the feed token that forms part of the feed's address; how long an entry stays listed (24 hours by default, never more than 720 hours); the maximum number of entries (500 by default); after how many minutes the feed counts as stale (30 by default); the git audit mirror: remote, branch, token, and whether to update it automatically (empty and off by default).

docs.h: A new scheduled action and a new response action
docs.x: A scheduled action publishes feed bookkeeping and history; every 15 minutes is suggested. It is not what keeps the feed current, since the feed is always built on request. A new response action for blocking an address at the border appears in Sentinel's catalog of actions. It is permanently limited to a recommendation because it affects every FortiGate and VDOM that reads the feed, and every service behind them. SATOM refuses to run it automatically.

docs.h: The border verdict is kept on the incident
docs.x: The border check's result is now saved on the incident as evidence. A reviewer can see on what grounds an address was listed, without SATOM asking the border a second time.
The Sentinel menu now has six entries. Border blocklist is the last of the four configuration pages, because it is the one read by something outside SATOM.
The check that keeps unsuitable addresses off the list let multicast addresses through. Multicast, reserved and unspecified addresses are now all refused.

The feed is reachable without a login , because a FortiGate threat-feed connector cannot log in. It is protected by its token instead: while no token is set, the feed answers nothing; a wrong token and a feed that does not exist give the same "not found" answer; the feed is never cached; when you change the token, the old one stops working immediately. Update your FortiGate connectors at the same time. Nothing is listed while the never-block list contains a line SATOM cannot read. A broken protection list is treated as a reason to stop, not as an empty list. Fix any invalid entry first. When t

docs.k: release 1.18.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: Sentinel can now ask the firewall in front of an appliance, through FortiAnalyzer, whether an attacking address is a real peer, and uses the answer as evidence and as a safety veto.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-23 · All releases

Sentinel gains border corroboration : for each protected appliance it can ask a FortiAnalyzer whether the FortiGate in front of it logged the same source address at the same time. A confirmed source scores higher, and an unconfirmed one cannot be put on a border blocklist. Administrators who set up Sentinel, and especially sites behind a CDN, will want to read this.

Under Sentinel → Context → Border map you can now tie each protected appliance to a FortiAnalyzer, an ADOM, a FortiGate and a VDOM. Sentinel then asks that FortiAnalyzer whether the FortiGate logged the same source in the same time window. Every field is typed in by you. Nothing is guessed from a host name or picked from an ADOM listing, because a wrong guess would not fail: it would query someone else's traffic and still return an answer that looks valid.

Two new scoring factors raise an incident's score: Border corroboration (+12) — the border firewall independently logged the source. Border multi-target (+10) — the border saw that source reach more different destinations than your scanning threshold. These matter because they come from a second device. Every other positive factor ultimately comes from the same FortiWeb's view of the same traffic. They are especially useful for installations with no hypervisor access, which can never earn the up to 18 points that virtual-machine and host anomalies contribute, but usually do have a FortiGate.

docs.h: The answer also works as a veto
docs.x: FortiWeb reports the real client address when a policy reads the forwarded-for header, and the CDN's own address when it does not, and the attack log cannot tell the two apart. Blocking the second kind at the border would cut off every client behind that CDN. So, while Require border corroboration is switched on (the default), an address the border never confirmed cannot be added to a border blocklist. There is deliberately no penalty when the border has not seen a source. Silence at the border says something about addressing, not about hostility, and penalising it would under-score every cust

docs.h: Seven new settings and a Test lookup button
docs.x: A new Border corroboration group in the Sentinel settings holds seven settings, each with its "?" explanation. Two deserve special care because they fail silently: Collector clock offset from UTC — if it is wrong, every lookup returns nothing, which looks exactly like a source the border never saw; Require border corroboration — the veto described above. Every mapped appliance has a Test lookup button. It runs one real query against the FortiAnalyzer and shows any refusal exactly as the device returned it. This exists because a wrong ADOM, a wrong device name, a wrong clock offset and a genuin
The Context pane in the Admin Console could miss information that the stand-alone Context page showed. Both now always show the same thing.

This feature has not yet been proven against a live FortiAnalyzer , and the console says so. If a lookup fails for any reason, Sentinel treats the border layer as not evaluated , never as "the border says no". Sentinel only reads from FortiAnalyzer. It never writes to a FortiAnalyzer or a FortiGate; the only request it creates on FortiAnalyzer is a log search.

docs.k: release 1.12.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: Policy cloning now copies SNI policies, certificates and profile settings it used to miss, and a declined section is finally left exactly as the destination had it.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-22 · All releases

This release is about policy cloning . A clone or migration now carries several things it used to leave behind — SNI policies, certificate material, references to trigger policies and custom responses — and it compares a profile's own settings, not just its lists. It also fixes an important flaw: when you declined a section, the profile that pointed at it could still be written with the source's value. Operators who clone or migrate server policies will notice the difference most; administrators get a new sizing guide and a clearer message when a node runs out of disk.

docs.h: Cloning: things that are now copied
docs.x: SNI policies. An SNI policy used to be treated like a certificate and skipped, so its member rows were skipped too and the copy arrived pointing at an SNI table the destination had never seen. SNI policies and their rows are now created at the destination like any other object. Certificate material. Certificates and their private keys cannot be read through the appliance's web API, so SATOM now carries them over its SSH connection as part of the clone. They are copied before the first write , because a certificate is something other objects depend on. Discovering a missing certificate halfway

docs.h: Cloning: compare a profile and decide
docs.x: There is a third choice for how a clone treats a profile: New, compare and decide . Until now SATOM compared the rows inside a profile's lists but never the profile's own switches, so a profile whose lists matched but whose settings differed looked identical when it was not. With this choice the profile itself is compared, and you decide what happens. Nothing is pre-ticked.

docs.h: Cloning: reuse a destination profile, or create one only if missing
docs.x: Two new options, available both in the single-policy clone dialog and in bulk jobs: Reuse a profile that already exists on the destination instead of creating a new one. Create the profile only if it is missing on the destination. In a bulk run each profile is handled once per pair of source profile and landing profile, so the same profile is not created repeatedly.

docs.h: Cloning: rows the destination already has are updated, not duplicated
docs.x: The appliance treats some rows as duplicates when a few key values match, even if the rest of the row differs. SATOM used to see such a row as missing and plan to create it; the appliance then refused the duplicate and kept serving the old value. Matching rows are now reconciled — updated in place — instead of re-created.

A pre-flight check can now test whether the backend servers are reachable, from two places that are always reported separately: from the destination appliance, and from the SATOM node itself. A result that could not be determined is shown as unknown , never folded into "reachable" (which would hide a real outage) or "down" (which would invent one). The check is off by default .
Pre-flight analysis of several policies now runs in parallel. In a measured run of 10 policies it went from about 51 seconds to about 21 seconds, with the same plan.

The manual has a new sizing guide. The old requirement tables only stated the minimum the installer needs; they never said how large a node must be for the number of devices it manages. Key points: Device polling is the limit, not storage. A node spends a little under a second per device in each 3-minute collection cycle, which puts about 110 devices on one installation at a 50 % load. Configuration history grows faster than metrics — roughly twice as fast — because metric samples are extremely compact. The installation guide now says its table is a minimum and links to the sizing tiers, and t

docs.h: A clearer message when a node runs out of disk
docs.x: The alert engine records and sends every finding through the database, so it can never warn you about a full disk that has taken the database down. When it now fails, it writes the node's disk, memory and load figures to the system log, so the cause is visible there. This makes the failure readable; it does not prevent it — free disk space still has to be watched from outside the node.

Declining a section now really keeps the destination's version. Previously, declining a section removed it from the plan, but the profile that pointed at it was still written with the source's value. The destination then pointed at something it did not have, and the appliance replaced it with a default of its own — so you got neither the source's nor the destination's setting. Now: if the item that points at the declined section already exists on the destination, that reference is put back to the value the destination has today; if that item would be newly created, there is nothing to keep, so

Saving an FTP server policy was always refused. Every valid FTP server-policy save came back saying the firmware has no FTP protection profile collection. Collections the appliance's web API cannot read now produce an "unverified" warning instead of a refusal. Certificate import failed on appliances with ADOMs enabled. On an ADOM-enabled appliance the first step of the certificate import was rejected, and the rest of the import was then sent to whatever prompt happened to be active. The import now enters the right place on both kinds of appliance. The Sentinel button that arms an automatic blo

Internal device names were removed from comments in shipped files. Sample private-key text in a placeholder and in test files is now assembled at runtime, so the release publisher's secret scanner no longer stops on it. The manual's counts were corrected: Settings has 26 panels (Vault and Sentinel were missing from the count), and the Concept Map maps 88 pages and excludes 112.

A large release with four big themes. Sentinel is a new security module that groups attack events, traffic outcomes, appliance and infrastructure metrics and vulnerability data into scored incidents, and can carry out a small, tightly controlled set of responses. Credentials can now be kept in an external vault instead of in SATOM itself. A new WAF Artifacts store lets clones and migrations copy file-based WAF objects (schemas, API definitions, Lua scripts) with their content, not just their name. And SATOM now understands that several ADOM rows can be one physical appliance , which changes th

Sentinel is a new module that correlates FortiWeb attack signatures, HTTP response outcomes, appliance counters, virtual machine and hypervisor metrics and vulnerability intelligence into incidents . Each incident explains itself from the evidence it was built on. Pages: a console, an incident page, a Context page, a documentation page and a response-policy page, plus a Sentinel section in Settings. Background work: three scheduled actions — the sweep, the baseline calculation and the vulnerability data sync. A fresh installation sets them up automatically, and the installation diagnosis repor

Sentinel can propose responses and, for verified actions, carry them out. Every proposal passes through thirteen gates , checked in a fixed order. Block an IP address is the first action that can actually run. It was tested end to end on a live FortiWeb. A separate runner, which checks once a minute, re-checks every gate at the moment it acts and asks the appliance whether it can enforce the block before writing. A block is only marked applied after SATOM reads it back from the appliance. Whether it actually helped is judged separately: an action that landed but changed nothing returns its inc

A clone used to create them empty at the destination: a rule bound to an empty object was refused, or, worse, if the rule already existed the policy silently ran with that protection off. docs.x: Released: 2026-08-17 · All releases

A small follow-up to SATOM 1.10.0 released the same day. It fixes three buttons that could never be submitted, and it tidies up the three diagnostic tools that 1.10.0 added to the Tools menu so they look and behave like the older tools beside them.

docs.h: Three buttons that always failed with "session expired"
docs.x: Three buttons answered every click with "Your session expired or the form was stale — please try again." Your session was fine; the button itself was broken and retrying never helped. They now work: Rebuild on the API versions page of the API registry. Revoke in the section-template catalog. Scan devices in the certificate manager.

docs.h: The new diagnostic tools now match the rest of the Tools menu
docs.x: The certificate inspector , the false-positive explainer and the transaction tracer were drawn differently from the older tools in the same menu (such as the Network Calculator): ten of their buttons appeared as plain grey browser buttons instead of SATOM's styled buttons; their cards had no tinted header and tighter spacing; their window titles were larger, and their form fields were full-size next to small buttons; their tabs behaved like links rather than buttons. They now use the same buttons, cards, titles, field sizes and tabs as every other tool, so opening one tool after another no lon

The database library SATOM uses is now pinned to one exact version, so two offline bundles built on different days ship the same software. New automatic checks catch a button that cannot be submitted, and a tool button whose style does not exist, before a release is made.
Certificate inspector False-positive explainer Transaction tracer API registry Certificates Previous release: SATOM 1.10.0 · Next release: SATOM 1.11.0

docs.k: release 1.10.0 what's new changelog upgrade flow bookmarks alerting
docs.s: Adds Upgrade Flow for whole maintenance windows, three diagnostic tools, the bookmarks rail and Concept Map, alert routing with syslog and webhook delivery, issue-tracker tickets, and an external API for WAF exceptions.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-17 · All releases

One of the largest releases so far. Maintenance windows become one staged workflow ( Upgrade Flow ), backed by change requests that carry evidence for every appliance they cover. Three new diagnostic tools — a certificate inspector, a false-positive explainer and a transaction tracer — join the Tools menu. The console gains a bookmarks rail and a Concept Map , the Admin Console menu moves to a grouped side column, and alerts can now be routed per channel and sent to a SIEM, a signed webhook, chat tools or an issue tracker. External teams can file their own WAF exceptions through the API. A lon

Automation → Upgrade Flow turns a maintenance window into one staged workflow: run the pre-flight on every appliance in the window in one sweep, raise a single change request that cites all of that evidence, export the combined customer impact, then execute. Each step existed before, but one device at a time, so upgrading sixty appliances meant walking the path sixty times and still ending up with a change document whose evidence covered one box. Live progress per appliance. A change request now shows every appliance it covers and what has happened to it: pending, running, ok, failed — and int

docs.h: Change requests: evidence for every appliance
docs.x: A change request now cites one pre-upgrade run per device it covers . Previously it could rest on the evidence of a single appliance even when it covered twenty. The change request page lists each appliance with the run that covers it , and names the appliances that have no baseline. The customer-impact spreadsheet is built from all the runs together, without counting a service twice and without merging two appliances that publish a policy with the same name. The pre-upgrade scheduled action now does the full pre-flight — backup, health checks, maintenance permission and a baseline of every pu

docs.h: Command line: reboot or upgrade a device by name
docs.x: For operators on SSH during a maintenance window when the web interface is not available, the command line can now reboot or upgrade an appliance by name . It only selects the one scheduled action that is already tied to an approved change request and runs it through the same approval check as the scheduler — it can never allow something the web console would refuse. When it refuses, it says exactly why: no such action, no change request, change not approved or its window closed, the action also targets other devices or the whole fleet, or more than one possible action. The command line can al

Open them from the header Tools menu. Certificate inspector . Paste a certificate chain (or the output of a TLS connection test) or probe a live address and port. It shows the chain from the server certificate upwards and verifies every link by checking the signature , plus expiry, key size, signature hash, whether the hostname is covered, and whether a pasted private key matches. When the chain cannot be checked on this node, completeness is shown as unknown , not as incomplete. False-positive explainer . Paste an attack-log entry (syslog, JSON or a raw HTTP request). It tells you which modul

A collapsible bookmarks panel on the right of every page, like a browser sidebar: folders, nested groups that collapse, and a search box. Three stores are always there — Favourites , Folders and Shared — plus an inventory view that lists the live fleet, so the panel is useful before you bookmark anything and new devices appear automatically. Starring or filing a device turns it into a bookmark. Everything starts collapsed ; SATOM remembers what you opened. What you see depends on your own permissions , never on those of the person who shared a bookmark — sharing cannot hand anyone a device the

A new Concept Map page shows every page of the console as a mind map — SATOM in the centre, one card per topic, every page inside its card and clickable. One search box matches a page's name, purpose, address and the words people type under pressure, such as "certificate", "rollback" or "who changed it". A list view shows the same set for reading and printing. It is linked from the footer of every page and reachable from all five ADOMs. Pages you are not allowed to open are not shown, and the page tells you how complete its own coverage is.

docs.h: Alerting: per-channel routing and new delivery channels
docs.x: Until now alerts had a single on/off switch, and every finding — even the informational ones — went to email and to the in-app bell. Each delivery channel now has its own minimum severity and its own set of alert families. Defaults match the previous behaviour exactly (bell and email on, every severity, every family), so nothing narrows on upgrade. Failures of the alert engine itself, and findings it does not recognise, always get through. Settings → Email & Alerts gains a Delivery sinks table (on/off, minimum severity and the seven family boxes) and a Syslog collector block. Preview now also

docs.h: Issue tracker tickets (Jira Cloud, OpenProject, Vikunja)
docs.x: Settings → Integrations gains a built-in ticketing connection. Raising the change ticket on a change request now opens a real ticket and writes its reference and link back onto the change — no custom script needed. The ticket lists the appliances by name, the affected services, the stored pre-upgrade evidence, and the appliances that have none. A change that already has a ticket reference is never given a second ticket , even after a double-click, a browser retry or a second operator. Test connection checks the configured project, not just the credentials, and reports who it signed in as, whet

docs.h: External API: WAF exceptions and FortiADC rules
docs.x: Security and application teams can now file their own FortiWeb WAF exceptions — and, when trusted, apply them — through the integration API, along with FortiADC rules. Only exception types from SATOM's curated catalog can be written. The API cannot write arbitrary appliance configuration, and signature changes stay with operators. Filing for approval and applying directly are separate token permissions, both of which must be granted explicitly. Existing tokens get neither. A token that may only file and asks to apply is told so rather than silently downgraded. A token can only withdraw what it

docs.h: Firmware lines: API versions and registry reconcile
docs.x: A new API versions page in each product's API hub compares what each firmware line (for example 7.6 and 8.0) actually serves, field by field, from evidence SATOM already collects. A command-line preflight tells you whether a payload would be understood on a line before you write it. One of its answers is unmeasured — "no evidence", which is never the same as "yes". A new Registry reconcile page on both API hubs shows, per endpoint, what the fleet's appliances report: endpoints no live appliance serves (proposed for disabling), endpoints that differ between firmware lines (never proposed), and

Settings → Languages. Choose which of SATOM's five languages users may pick. A withdrawn language disappears from the profile picker, from the change-document language choice and from browser language detection. English cannot be switched off. Withdrawing deletes nothing: users keep their choice (their profile explains it is not honoured right now) and translations stay, and the page shows how many users picked each language before you switch it off. Classification catalogs (zones, lines, departments) are edited one value at a time. Each value shows how many appliances, combos and segments use

The Admin Console menu is a side column grouped by theme : System, Access & Identity, Certificates & Trust, Monitoring & Alerts, Network & DNS, Fleet & Devices, User Interface and My Account. It starts fully collapsed , keeps one group open at a time, and remembers the open group per browser. A section reached from a link or after saving opens its group. The sections, their icons and their links are unchanged. Admin Console panes use a single column — cards, tables and banners stack at full width instead of sitting side by side. Hovering or focusing a bookmark row lights it in your own banner

Config drift on devices that had not changed. Fields the appliance changes by itself — its clock, internal counters, list order — triggered a new version and an alert every hour. They are now ignored when deciding whether a configuration changed; the stored snapshot still keeps them. "Host degraded — CPU load" on an idle node. The figure divided the host's load by the node's own cores. CPU is now measured for the node itself; the host's load is still shown, labelled as the host's. "ALL backends down" for servers the appliance reported as up. A pool member with no health check configured is now

After an update, every page on a standby returned an error for hours while the update reported success. Updates now restore whatever the node was running and check it over HTTP, standby included. An update now fails — instead of a page breaking afterwards — when a page links to something that does not exist. Regex Lab names the engine that judged the pattern and points out where it can disagree with the appliance; patterns the appliance accepts were sometimes reported invalid. Renaming a classification value no longer leaves appliances in "(no zone)", baselines with an empty scope, or a duplic

Stored script links blocked in bookmarks. A team bookmark could hold a script link that ran in every colleague's browser. Links are now checked when saved and again when shown, including rows restored from a backup or replica. Unauthenticated API calls get a JSON error, every applied exception leaves an audit record naming the token and its owner, and refused calls are recorded. A boot-time database update had been silently skipping three columns; this can no longer happen unnoticed. The user guide now has sections for Bookmarks, Concept Map, Upgrade Flow and Languages, and describes the group

docs.k: release 1.9.3 what's new changelog
docs.s: SATOM speaks your language, change requests become a complete, signable change process for every Forti product, and directory sign-in gains RADIUS import, an approval gate and several sources in order.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-10 · All releases

1.9.3 is a large release with three themes. The whole console can now be shown in Spanish, German, French or Italian, chosen from your profile. Change requests grow into a full change process: a guided form that proposes the wording, a formal change document in several languages, saved pre-flight evidence, maintenance windows on your own clock, NetBox and external approval, and a notice to affected users when the window closes. And sign-in through a directory gains RADIUS user import, an approval gate for new accounts and support for several sign-in sources at once. Operators who raise changes

The menus, buttons and pages of the console are now translated into Spanish, German, French and Italian , not only English. SATOM picks the language in this order: the language saved in your profile, then your browser's language (if SATOM ships it), then English. Translations are prepared in advance and stored with the product. Pages never wait for an AI model to translate them, the same button always has the same name, and an installation without access to an AI service still shows its menus in your language. A wrong translation can be corrected in the translation files without a new release.

docs.h: Your language is a profile setting
docs.x: Profile → Language stores the language you work in against your own account. It is not shared with other users and does not depend on a browser cookie. The user menu in the top bar shows your current choice next to the entry that changes it. "No preference" and "English" are kept apart. If you have no preference, the change request form asks you which language to use and tells you where to set a preference so it stops asking. If you chose English on purpose, it is not asked again. If you pick a language the change document cannot yet be produced in, your choice is kept, and the change request

The formal change document can now be produced in English, German, Spanish, French and Italian. A language is only offered when every sentence the document can print exists for it and is up to date. If even one is missing, the whole language is withdrawn from the picker, so you never get a document that is half in one language and half in another under an approver's signature.

Every change request can now be viewed or downloaded as a formal change document (Markdown). It has thirteen numbered sections: general information, purpose, affected systems, justification, impact, risk, rollback, prerequisites, work to be performed, post-change validation, communication plan, approvals and outcome. Purpose, impact, risk, work and validation are written specifically for each of the change-controlled actions. A firmware upgrade is described as what it is on a Fortinet appliance (uploading a firmware image and rebooting into it), never as operating-system patching, so the appro

New Change Request now asks two questions first, in this order: The document language . The type of change . From those two answers, plus the pre-flight run the change cites, SATOM proposes the title, reason, rollback plan, change owner and notification recipients. The language comes first because all proposed text is written in it. The device list and the maintenance window are not proposed: those are decisions for you, and a guessed window is worse than an empty one. The proposed wording describes this change: the action, the devices, and the cited run's number, time, verdict, firmware and c

A new page, Administration → Change Types , controls the options in the type of change picker and every sentence a type contributes: the proposed title, reason and rollback plan, and the eight paragraphs the printed document quotes (purpose, justification, impact, downtime, risk, rollback steps, work and validation). Built-in types can be reworded. Overrides are per field: correcting one paragraph keeps the product's wording for the others, and future product corrections still reach the fields you did not change. Leaving a box empty keeps the product's wording; it does not blank that section.

docs.h: Change requests for every Forti product
docs.x: Change requests are no longer limited to FortiWeb. FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator appliances can now be named in a change window, and the page is reachable from every ADOM. Each ADOM shows only the change requests for its own devices, including when you open one directly by its link. More actions are now under change control: enabling and disabling policies and back-end servers, changing back-end configuration, swapping certificates, the certificate lifecycle sweep and custom API calls join the firmware upgrade. The list is now built automatically from the actions marked as dan

docs.h: The Automation section in every ADOM
docs.x: Scheduled Actions , Device Provisioning and Change Requests now appear in the Global, FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator consoles, and in any ADOM added later. Each ADOM shows only its own scheduled actions, also when you edit, toggle, delete, run or view the history of one directly. The scheduled-action editor offers only the actions that apply to this ADOM, and its device picker lists the devices of this ADOM (it used to be empty outside FortiWeb). System Provisioning stays FortiWeb-only on purpose : its profiles are made of FortiWeb configuration objects that other pro

docs.h: Upgrade preparation leads to a change request
docs.x: Each pre-flight ("Upgrade preparation") run is now saved . Every stored run is listed on the page with its verdict, and a finished run offers Raise change request with the appliance, the action and the run already filled in. Saved runs cannot be changed afterwards, so the run an approved change cites is exactly the run that was taken. The verdict only grades the checks you asked for. A published service that was already unreachable before the change is recorded as the baseline , not as a failure. View result on every row of the runs table opens the full saved run: the health checks, the backup

docs.h: The affected services are frozen onto the change
docs.x: When a change request is raised, the list of affected services is captured and stored with it. The detail page, the document and the export all use that snapshot, so the document that was approved and the record of what ran are the same. You can ask to compare the snapshot with the devices as they are now. Any difference is reported, never merged in silently. Export the inventory as Excel (.xlsx) or CSV with the columns you choose. Columns always appear in the same order, and choosing none exports the five default columns. The column names match what you see on screen.

docs.h: Change requests on your local clock
docs.x: Window start and end are now read in the timezone set under Settings → General , and the window fields name that timezone. Before, times were shown in local time but saved as if typed in UTC, so a window entered as 22:00 could open hours later than announced. Daily, weekly and monthly scheduled actions now also run at the local time you set. "Every night at 02:00" means 02:00 local time, all year round. Scheduling a firmware upgrade from the appliance page also uses the configured timezone.

Settings → Integrations can now connect SATOM to NetBox (address, an encrypted token, TLS verification, a timeout and a mapping of appliances to NetBox devices). When a change request starts running, SATOM opens a maintenance window in NetBox, and closes it with the outcome when the run ends. It works with any NetBox, with or without plugins. You choose how the window is recorded: a journal entry, a device tag, or device custom fields. Window times are always sent with an explicit timezone, so NetBox cannot shift them by hours.

You can now add small Python scripts that SATOM runs when something happens: a change is requested or approved, a window opens or closes, or an upgrade finishes or fails. For example, a hook can open a ticket in your own system and hand the ticket reference back to the change request. Hooks never run inside the web console. A separate, restricted runner executes them with a time limit and only the secrets the hook declares. A script with a syntax error is refused when you save it, with the error message, instead of failing during a maintenance window. Output is shortened and any declared secre

A change request can be bound to an external change authority ( Approval → External ). It then only runs once that authority has explicitly approved it. No answer, a slow answer, an unclear answer or never having asked all count as "not approved". Withdrawing an approval clears it, so it can no longer open a window. Existing change requests default to Manual approval and behave as before. The change request page shows the external ticket reference and link, the state of the window in NetBox and an integration log. "None requested" and "error" are shown as different states.

docs.h: Affected users are told when the window closes
docs.x: When a window closes, success or failure, SATOM emails the people on the change request's Notify on completion list, with the reason. If that list is empty it uses the default recipients from Settings → Email ; if neither is set, nothing is sent and the change request records why. The notice is sent once and is separate from the warning sent before the window. If the email cannot be sent, the change keeps its real outcome and the notice can be retried.

docs.h: Directory sign-in: RADIUS import, approval gate, several sources
docs.x: Import users from FortiAuthenticator / RADIUS. Settings → Authentication → Sync directory users now works for RADIUS too, not only AD/LDAP. Because RADIUS cannot list users, SATOM reads the group members from a FortiAuthenticator already registered under Appliances, using its existing API key. Sign-in itself still goes over RADIUS. Pick the appliance and the group in the RADIUS section. Several import groups, each with its own profile. For example, one group can be imported as operators and another as read-only users in a single run. A user in two groups gets the profile of the first row; a bl

New directory accounts start as read-only , not operator. Giving more rights is an explicit administrator action. An unknown profile name always falls back to fewer rights, never more. A live firmware upgrade now needs an approved, open change window. This applies to the upgrade button on the appliance page as well as to scheduled upgrades. Dry runs are not gated, because they send nothing to the appliance. An authorised upgrade moves its change request to in progress and closes it with the real outcome. The per-username allowlist is removed (Settings → Access Control → Allowed Users). Profile

Deleting an object that others still use is refused. SATOM now checks the appliance's own reference count before deleting and, when it can, names the objects that still point at it. The check also runs on Preview , so the refusal appears before the confirmation prompt. An object whose references cannot be read is not deleted; an administrator can force the delete when the firmware's count is wrong, and the audit log records that it was forced. A change request could never finish. After its action ran, it stayed at scheduled forever. It now moves to in progress and then to completed or failed .

Firmware upgrades started by hand now need an approved change request with an open window. Plan to raise and approve one before your next live upgrade. New directory users default to read-only. If you relied on new directory users getting operator rights, set a profile per import group or adjust each user under Users. The per-username allowlist no longer applies. Review who can sign in through your directory groups and, if prompted on the Access Control page, clear the old list. Consider turning on the approval gate for directory users if you allow sign-in from several sources.

Integration hooks run in a separate, locked-down service, never inside the web console. A setup problem that made queued hooks silently never run was fixed before release. The Excel export is built into SATOM, so offline installations need no extra software. The vendor's logo file is no longer served from SATOM; only the product-type icons that label each appliance remain. A software dependency needed for translations is now part of the standard install, so a reinstall cannot remove it.

docs.k: release 1.9.2 what's new changelog
docs.s: The object editor now offers a dropdown wherever a field must name an existing object, and checks those names on the appliance before saving.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-09 · All releases

A small release for anyone who edits FortiWeb objects in SATOM. Fields that must name an existing object now behave like their neighbours, and a save that names an object the appliance does not have is stopped with a clear message instead of an unhelpful appliance error.

docs.h: Names are checked on the appliance before saving
docs.x: When you save or create an object, SATOM now checks every field that refers to another object and asks the appliance whether that object exists. This happens on Preview as well as when you apply. If a name does not exist, the message names the field, the value you entered, the kind of object it should be, and the names that do exist. SATOM tells apart "there are no objects of this kind", "this firmware does not have this kind of object" and "SATOM could not ask the appliance". If the appliance cannot be read, the save is not blocked; the affected fields are simply reported as not verified.

Twenty reference fields showed a free text box instead of a dropdown — eighteen on the Web Protection Profile and two on the Server Policy. A value typed there was rejected by FortiWeb with "Invalid input value", which named neither the field nor the value, and the other changes in the same save were lost too. These fields are now dropdowns. Each one was verified on a real appliance first; fields that could not be verified were left as they were, so a dropdown never lists the wrong kind of object.
