docs.k: release 1.9.1 what's new changelog
docs.s: Cloning and migrating FortiWeb configuration now copies everything an object needs, the clone shows what it will and will not copy, and every audit entry shows its ID.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-09 · All releases

This release makes copying FortiWeb configuration trustworthy. Migrated Custom Access Rules now arrive with their conditions, a cloned Web Protection Profile really is a separate copy, and the clone tells you up front what it cannot copy. Anyone who searches the audit log also gets a visible ID for every entry.

docs.h: The clone tells you what it cannot copy, before it writes
docs.x: The Exceptions page now shows a preview of the clone before you authorise it, listing what will be copied and what will stay shared with the original. Three kinds of objects are never copied silently: FortiWeb's own predefined objects. Objects governed by an approved template. Objects whose parent stays shared, because changing them would also change every profile that uses that parent. You can override the first two object by object; the third is a consequence and is not offered as a choice. Applying a plan that leaves anything shared requires an explicit acknowledgement.

docs.h: Capacity is checked for the whole clone
docs.x: Before the first write, the clone now adds up how many objects of each limited type it will create and checks them against the appliance's limits, instead of only checking room for one more profile. This prevents a clone that stops half-way. Object types without a configured limit are shown as unchecked .

docs.h: Every audit entry shows its ID
docs.x: The audit log list has a new ID column at the start. Click an ID to copy it without opening the entry. The detail panel shows the ID with its own copy button. The search box finds an entry by its ID, whether you type 4821 , #4821 or AUD-004821 . A number still also matches entries whose text contains it. Searching by ID respects ADOM scoping: you only find entries you are allowed to see.

A migrated Custom Access Rule lost its conditions. Cloning or migrating a rule copied its name but not the conditions it matches on (URL, source address, rate limit). The job reported success and the rule appeared on the destination, but it matched no traffic. All the rule's conditions are now copied with it, and SATOM no longer creates bogus condition rows on firmware that does not have a given condition type. A cloned Web Protection Profile still shared its sub-policies with the original. The clone was effectively the original renamed, with around forty sub-policies still shared, so a change
Cloning server policies Exceptions and signatures Web protection profiles Audit log Previous release: SATOM 1.9.0 · Next release: SATOM 1.9.2

docs.k: release 1.9.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: The Attack ID page becomes a full investigation and exception workbench — field-by-field explanations, AI questions per field, exceptions built from the fields you tick and inserted from the same page.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-08 · All releases

1.9.0 turns the FortiWeb Attack ID search into the place where you investigate a block and fix it. Each field of an attack-log entry is explained, you can ask the AI Advisor about any single field, and you can build a narrowly scoped exception from the fields you tick and insert it into the appliance without leaving the page. It also stops exceptions from silently landing on profiles shared by several sites, and makes the audit log record who really made each change.

Every field of an attack-log entry now explains what it is, how this value is classified and what to check next. For example: Whether a source address is private, shared, a documentation range or public, with a reminder that a private source usually means the real client is in the forwarded-for header. URLs shown decoded, with the decoded form judged rather than the raw one, and query parameters broken out. What the port, method and user agent mean, and what the signature class is made of. How often the same value appears in the last 100 entries on that appliance. All of this is worked out ins

docs.h: Ask the AI about one field
docs.x: Each row of the entry has a second icon next to the explain icon. Clicking it sends the question straight away and shows the AI Advisor's answer under the local explanation of that field, with a box below for follow-up questions (press Ctrl+Enter to send). Follow-ups continue the same conversation. SATOM sends only which entry and which field; the value is read again from the appliance, so a browser cannot supply made-up evidence. This path explains only. It does not draft exceptions, and any draft the model produces anyway is discarded. Every question and answer is recorded in the audit log,

docs.h: Every analysis shows what it cost
docs.x: Each result on the panel shows which engine produced it, how long it took and how many tokens it used, including failed calls. The local field explanation says "no tokens"; a provider that did not report its usage shows "tokens not reported", never zero. While a call is running, a clock shows how long you have been waiting.

docs.h: Build an exception from the fields you tick
docs.x: The Advisor only drafts an exception for a false positive at acceptable risk. Now you can also build one yourself, for example when a genuine attack pattern must still be allowed from one known caller: Tick the fields the exception should be limited to and pick the kind of exception. SATOM builds a valid FortiWeb exception from the entry exactly as the appliance reported it. An exception that goes against the Advisor's conclusion is allowed, but needs a written justification, stored with the rule and in the audit log.

docs.h: The field picker suggests the scope
docs.x: The field picker no longer opens empty. It pre-selects a recommended scope and explains each box: Required fields are always ticked. A signature exception gets exactly one element, the most precise one the entry has, because FortiWeb matches one per row. The source address is left unticked when the request can be described by URL or host, because an exception tied to an address stops working when that caller moves. The reason is shown, and it is one click away. The suggestion is checked against the real exception builder, so a default that would not be valid says so straight away. Everything s

docs.h: SATOM suggests the right kind of exception
docs.x: A block by a protocol constraint is not fixed by a signature exception, and the log entry does not say that. SATOM now ranks the possible exception types for the entry, narrowest first, each with its reason.

A draft exception is now shown in plain terms: where it lands (Server Policy → profile → module → type, and which FortiWeb object holds it), how wide it reaches, what stops being inspected and what stays enforced. The raw content is still one click away for editing. Breadth is judged from the actual content: a signature exception with nothing to match is reported as wider than its type suggests.

docs.h: Insert the exception from this page
docs.x: Inserting is now two steps on the same page: a preview that shows exactly what will be sent and writes nothing, then the write. You no longer have to go to another screen to push the draft.

docs.h: See which profile each policy uses, and whether it is shared
docs.x: The results table now shows the Web Protection Profile behind each Server Policy and whether other policies share it, naming them. This tells you before you start whether an exception is one click or a profile clone. If SATOM cannot read the appliance, the cell says unknown rather than staying blank.

Required scope is ticked for you. For Allow Method and HTTP-constraint exceptions, which FortiWeb keys on a URL pattern, the panel now ticks the URL box itself, visibly in the table. Only fields that narrow an exception are ever pre-ticked, so the default can never widen it. If you untick it, the explanation of what is missing comes back. A required field the entry does not have is reported as absent. Asking the AI about a field answers on the click , instead of opening an empty box and waiting for you to type. Exceptions on shared profiles are refused. A Web Protection Profile applies its exc

A carve-out on a shared profile reported an error after succeeding. The profile was correctly cloned and the policy re-bound on the appliance, but SATOM then showed "An unexpected error occurred" and threw away your draft. It now completes normally, and a failing bookkeeping step can no longer break the work it records. docs.h: Control the standby's services from the primary

The primary asks the standby to act, and the standby checks the request against its own list of allowed services before doing anything. An unreachable standby is shown as unreachable, never as "queued" or as an empty list. A standby that answers as if the feature does not exist is identified as probably running an older release. docs.k: release 1.7.1 what's new changelog
docs.s: Fixes the sealed recovery envelope introduced in 1.7.0, which could not reach the standby or any backup, and documents recovery custody in the operator manual.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-07 · All releases

A corrective release for administrators. The sealed recovery envelope added in 1.7.0 could not actually be copied to the standby node or into backups, even though the recovery check said all was well. 1.7.1 fixes that, makes the check honest, and adds recovery custody to the operator manual.

The sealed recovery envelope could not be copied anywhere. It was created with permissions that the standby synchronisation and the backup writer could not read, so it reached neither the peer nor any backup, while the recovery check reported the problem as solved. Sealing now gives the envelope to the right owner, and the check reports separately whether it can be reached. An unreachable envelope is reported as critical . The recovery check could never report "ok" on a correctly sealed node. A current, reachable envelope now counts as a valid copy of the secrets it covers. An old, unreachable

If you sealed the recovery envelope on 1.7.0, run the seal command again on the primary after upgrading ( satom execute seal recovery ), then run the recovery check and confirm it reports the envelope as reachable. 1.7.0 remains available, but carries this defect.

The operator manual now explains recovery custody: why the envelope is needed (a backup restored onto a rebuilt node otherwise has unreadable secrets), where the passphrase comes from, why sealing belongs on the primary, the related commands, and the "unreachable envelope" symptom in troubleshooting. The manual no longer states a fixed number of CLI commands, which went out of date; it points to the generated command reference instead.

docs.h: Recovery custody for the secrets no backup carries
docs.x: SATOM has two secrets that are deliberately left out of backups, standby synchronisation and version control: the key that opens every encrypted value in the database, and the internal certificate authority key. Without them, a backup restored onto a rebuilt node holds secrets nobody can read. Sealed envelope. The two secrets can now be sealed into an envelope protected by a passphrase. The envelope is copied to the standby within five minutes and is included in every backup from then on. Someone who steals a backup only gets encrypted data; you, holding the passphrase, can rebuild the install

Site-specific redaction rules are now copied to the standby and included in backups. Before, this file was carried by nothing, so a standby could run for days with outdated rules. The old location is still read so existing nodes keep working. A missing or broken redaction rules file is now reported as an error on a deployed installation, instead of quietly redacting less. Backups now include node-local configuration. On restore it is only placed where the node has none, because the live copy is more likely to be current. Documentation corrected. A retired mechanism was still described as live

Nine health checks answered "I could not tell" with "fine". Among them: scoping fell back to the Global console and showed every product; a damaged access-control entry read as "no restriction"; an unreadable repository reported itself clean; high availability was taken as standalone and the standby check skipped; a safety check before a reset reported "nothing to keep"; hypervisor certificate checks reported "verified" without using your certificate authority; an unreadable SSH host-key store was treated as a first connection; an unreadable colour skipped the contrast check. Each now reports

After upgrading, plan to export the recovery key and keep the seal passphrase outside the fleet . Note that sealing in this version has a defect fixed in 1.7.1 ; if you sealed on 1.7.0, seal again after upgrading to 1.7.1.

One shared implementation of SSH host-key pinning is now used for every SSH connection SATOM opens. A new check stops private-key text from being written into the source code, so it is caught when the change is made rather than by aborting a release.

Check the new licence terms if you offer SATOM to others as a hosted or managed service. That use now needs a commercial licence.

docs.k: release 1.3.5 what's new changelog
docs.s: Signing in now works behind a NAT or proxy on a non-standard port, and the node certificate covers the DNS names you actually use.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-04 · All releases

An installer fix release. The installer guessed the names a node is reached by from the machine's short name, and two problems came from that guess. The node could not be signed in to behind a NAT or proxy on a non-standard port, and its certificate did not cover its full DNS name. An existing node needs one command to pick up the fix.

The installer asks for the DNS names the node answers to , in its first step. The default is the machine's full name, and you can set the names in advance for unattended installs. New repair command. satom execute repair nginx brings an installed node's web server settings up to date. It takes backups, tests the new settings, and rolls back automatically if they fail. Two new web server checks. The operator console's web server check now reports a configuration that loses the port number, and a certificate that does not cover every full DNS name the node answers to.

Signing in failed behind a NAT or proxy on a non-standard port. Every form, including the login, was rejected with an "expired session" message. On the standard HTTPS port, where browsers leave the port out, the problem did not show. The certificate did not match the full DNS name. A node reached by its full DNS name only answered because it was also the default site, and its certificate did not include that name. The redirect from HTTP to HTTPS no longer adds an explicit :443 to the address.

The web server settings are not part of the code, so updating alone cannot fix an installed node. After upgrading, run satom execute repair nginx --yes as root, or reinstall from this release. Every release from 1.3 to 1.3.4 produces the faulty settings.

docs.k: release 1.3.4 what's new changelog
docs.s: The offline install bundles now include git, without which one of the backup copies was never made on air-gapped nodes.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-04 · All releases

A fix for nodes installed from an offline bundle. The bundles never included git. On those nodes, the copy of the device configurations that is kept in git was never made, while every other indicator stayed green.

Air-gapped nodes were missing a backup copy. Every hour, the job that publishes the configuration source of truth to git failed because git was not installed. Backup copy 3 (the device configurations versioned in git) did not exist on the node. The console, the health check, sign-in and the other diagnostics all looked normal. Online installs were not affected, because git is installed along the way. git is now required on every supported Linux family and is included in all three offline bundles. The operator console's git check now names the missing program. Before, it only said "repository u
This release only changes the install bundles. To fix a node already installed offline, install git from your distribution media or from the bundle. Nothing else needs to be redeployed.

docs.k: release 1.3.2 what's new changelog
docs.s: The installer now completes on openSUSE and RHEL, fails loudly when something goes wrong, and reminds you to switch on the scheduled protections.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-04 · All releases

The installer had never finished on openSUSE or RHEL. This was found by running the published 1.3.1 installer on a blank openSUSE machine, the way an operator would. This release fixes those installs, makes the installer report its errors, and tells you what to do once it finishes.

The installer's last message now tells you to switch on the protections. No scheduled action is created for you, by design. The closing banner says so and tells you to run satom execute seed actions . Without them, a new node takes no database backups and does not refresh the device configurations.

Database sign-in failed on openSUSE and RHEL. On a standalone install, the installer wrote the database access rules but never made the database reload them. On openSUSE and RHEL the database then rejected SATOM's account with Ident authentication failed , and creating the database failed. The rules are now applied in every install mode, and the login is checked straight away. The installer could stop without saying why. Three steps (creating the database, setting the administrator password and starting SATOM) could fail silently. The last thing on screen was an unrelated line. Each now stops

docs.k: release 1.3.1 what's new changelog
docs.s: Rebuilt offline bundles, factory settings that no longer point at someone else's network, a new manual for the device APIs, and the documentation published in one place only.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-03 · All releases

The offline bundles shipped with 1.3 were built before several fixes went in. On an unattended install they tried to download SATOM from a private server and hung. This release rebuilds all three bundles (Debian 12, RHEL 9 and openSUSE 15). It also: removes factory settings that named one company's own network tightens what the public code mirror publishes adds a manual for the device APIs publishes the documentation in one place only: the public site, with an offline copy in the operator console

docs.h: Device APIs and the endpoint registry: a new manual
docs.x: A new manual, Device APIs & the endpoint registry , describes how SATOM talks to your appliances. It covers: The consoles. The three API consoles SATOM uses to drive an appliance. The catalog behind them. 826 entries: 507 for FortiWeb, 255 for FortiADC and 64 for FortiAnalyzer. Your corrections survive updates. A fix you make to an entry stays in place through every update. Access. The four permissions involved, and how ADOMs limit what you see. Firmware changes. If a firmware upgrade moves an API address, you edit one entry in the browser; you do not need a new SATOM release.

docs.h: The manual from the operator console
docs.x: satom show docs shows the manual straight from the node, with no network. A management network usually has no route to the public site, so this keeps the manual readable offline. New documents appear in the list automatically.
The documentation index, which lists every document and suggests a reading path for each role, was the one document available in the application but not on the public site. It is now published too.

The application no longer serves its own copy of the documentation. The in-app documentation pages are removed and now answer "not found". The sign-in page and the sidebar link to the public documentation site instead. On a node with no route to that site, use satom show docs . The staging copy of the documentation site was retired too, so there is now only one published copy. Trusted proxies now default to the local machine only. The old default named another network's proxy address. Elsewhere, that made every user share one rate-limiting bucket. On a network whose addresses overlapped it, an

The public code mirror exposed internal details. It carried an internal network map and the names and email addresses of the people who made changes. The old filter checked file names and commit messages but not what was inside the files it kept. Publishing now removes internal identifiers from every file in the whole history, replaces every author identity, and checks its own output again . If anything is found, it stops and publishes nothing. 71 links in the published manual were broken. Links between documents now point at the published pages, and links to documents that are not published b
Test data no longer uses real-looking network addresses. It now uses addresses reserved for documentation. Two lab helper scripts are no longer published. They only worked against one specific lab.

docs.k: release 1.3 what's new changelog
docs.s: An operator console for when the web interface is down, a Service Monitor with per-policy traffic, two years of monitoring history, honest health badges and alerts, and an installer that works on openSUSE.
docs.x: Released: 2026-08-02 · All releases

This is a large release with five themes: Operator console. A command-line console, satom , lets you inspect, diagnose and repair a node when its web interface is down. It includes twelve built-in recovery runbooks. Service Monitor. A new monitoring page shows traffic for each appliance and each server policy, and keeps two years of history. Health and alerts that tell the truth. The health badge can now turn red, device alerts send mail when the badge does, and failing automations raise their own alerts. Monitoring in every ADOM. Monitoring is available in each ADOM and stays within it. openS

A console for when the web interface is down The new satom command works like the command line on the appliances SATOM manages. It has four kinds of command: get , show , diagnose and execute . Help and modes. Type ? at any point to list the options. You can run a single command (handy for scripts) or open an interactive prompt. It still works when SATOM is broken. The console depends only on the basic system, so it can report on a node even when the application itself is broken. Who can run what. Any user can run get , show and diagnose . execute needs root, and if you are not root it refuses

Service Monitor Runtime traffic monitoring has its own page: Monitoring → Service Monitor , available in all four ADOMs. Which page has which probes. Service Monitor has the four traffic probe types: sessions, per-policy sessions, throughput and transactions. Deep monitors keeps the five that look inside the appliance: HTTPS, interface, CPU, memory and the proxy daemon. One page per probe. A probe belongs to exactly one page, and each page only shows, edits and runs its own probes. The same tools on both pages. Both pages share the same charts, history and controls, so they always match. Traff

The manual is linked from the sign-in page , so someone who cannot get in can still reach the installation guide, the console reference and the recovery runbooks without signing in. The API manual is a top-level entry in the public site's navigation and footer. The changelog is readable in three places: the repository, the application's Documentation section and the public site. The manual is published from the same source as the repository. Its command table is generated from the console itself. Internal addresses, names and email addresses are replaced before publishing. If anything is left,

New offline bundle for openSUSE and SLES 15. Installing on openSUSE used to need internet access, which an isolated management network does not have. It is kept apart from the RHEL bundle, because the two are not interchangeable. Using the wrong bundle is refused before anything is changed. The bundle is used without touching the system's own software sources, and nothing is left registered afterwards.

Monitoring is in every ADOM. Fleet health, Metrics and Deep monitors now appear in the FortiWeb, FortiADC and FortiAnalyzer ADOMs as well as Global. Each ADOM sees only its own devices and probes. Anything created from Global for a device of that product appears there too. Probes run every 3 minutes instead of 5. CPU, memory and proxy daemon probes moved from 5 to 3 minutes. Interface and transactions probes stay at 15. All intervals are now multiples of the sweep, so a probe does not silently drift to a slower rhythm. Measured from start to finish, a probe actually runs about every 3.4 to 3.7

The Fleet health badge could never turn red. Each device was graded only on capacity headroom, so even a powered-off appliance with no data showed green. The badge now combines four signals: recent harvests, the age of the cached data, enabled deep monitors and capacity. It has a separate unknown state, and the reasons are printed under it. A red badge never sent mail. The device alert only checked whether the device answered on its port, so devices whose data collection had been failing for a week never triggered an email. The alert now uses the same signals as the badge, sends one alert per

The transactions probe could report zero for a busy policy. A real load test with about 2,700 requests per second showed zero transactions until a web protection profile was attached. The probe now double-checks whenever it reads zero, and warns if the policy is carrying traffic. A "Working…" window with a dead Stop button kept reappearing. Test runs had been writing unfinished jobs into the live application. Leftover jobs are now cleaned up while SATOM runs, not only at start-up. A job that never started is considered dead after 10 minutes instead of an hour. Device cards on the probe pages a

An HA pair on openSUSE never copied files between nodes , along with five other problems found by installing a real pair: Pasting the join key on the second node failed, because the key was read with a program that is not installed yet at that point. The key is now read without it, and both certificates in it are checked. The remote login service was installed but not started on openSUSE, so the standby could never fetch data. It is now switched on on both nodes, since either may need to serve after a promotion. A failed check of the peer's identity was ignored, which would have broken file co

docs.h: The console and the public site
docs.x: The application showed version 1.0 for four releases. The footer and Settings → System Information now show the real version, and so does the public site. The public API manual was readable without signing in and showed internal details , including a management host name and an internal address. Every public document is now cleaned before it is shown. If anything internal remains, the page is not served at all. The sign-in pages and public documentation needed internet access to display properly. They now use files that ship with SATOM. The site name in the navigation bar was almost invisible

The console could crash while printing on a terminal that only supports plain ASCII, such as a serial console. Special characters are now replaced instead. Two checks changed the files they were checking. They left files owned by the administrator in SATOM's folders, which another check then reported as a problem. The database backup command wrote a file nothing could restore. It now writes the same backup bundle as System Backup & Restore . The backup status command also reported "no bundles" while twenty were on disk; this is fixed. Rebuilding the Python environment could leave the node wors

Internal names change from the old product name to SATOM. The database, the database account, the Linux service account and the database certificate folder are renamed. New installations use the new names from the start. Existing installations migrate with the migration script that ships with this release. It takes a database dump first and checks health before reporting success. Three names are kept on purpose: the Fortinet product names, which SATOM has to use the database replication slot, which cannot be renamed safely under a live standby the external backup server, which the appliances p

Monitoring history uses very little disk: under 400 KB per probe for two years, against roughly 35 MB if raw samples were kept. The public site and the in-app documentation now use one shared list of what may be published and how it is cleaned.

docs.s: Certificate renewal, Node TLS and the Certificate Manager work again after a fault shipped in the 1.2 and 1.2.1 bundles.
docs.x: Released: 2026-07-27 · All releases

A fix release for certificate handling. A coding fault in the 1.2 and 1.2.1 offline bundles stopped SATOM's certificate component from loading. Everything that depends on it failed, even though the rest of SATOM ran normally.

While the fault was present: Nightly certificate renewal failed on both nodes. Node TLS settings and the Certificate Manager showed errors. The certificate alert reported the loading error instead of the certificate's real state. All three work again in this release.

A new automated check makes sure every part of SATOM can actually load, including parts that load only when they are needed. The full test suite had stayed green for a day with this fault, because nothing loaded the component during testing.

docs.k: release 1.2.1 what's new changelog
docs.s: A documentation release that adds the safeguards catalog and spells out the protections you must switch on after a fresh install.
docs.x: Released: 2026-07-27 · All releases

A documentation release. No application code changed. The offline bundles were rebuilt so that they include the new documents. The 1.2 bundles were built a few minutes before the safeguards catalog was added, so they shipped the protections without the document that describes them.

Safeguards catalog. One document lists every protection in SATOM: what it prevents, where it lives, and how to check it is switched on . It covers: the code history, self-updates and dependencies the privilege boundary and correctness between nodes changes written to appliances certificates, external files, sessions and alerts It ends with the limits that are deliberately not covered. - "Protections you must arm" in the installation guide. Scheduled actions, alert recipients and the timers on each node are settings stored in the database, not part of the code, so a fresh install starts with no
The in-app Documentation index now gives all 18 manuals a proper title, order and description. Half of them had only an automatic title and no description, so they were hard to find.

Checking an offline bundle's checksum failed in the folder you downloaded it to. Checksums now work wherever the file is. The RHEL offline bundle had no certificate (ACME) support when built the documented way. It now includes the certificate client.

docs.k: release 1.2 what's new changelog
docs.s: SATOM stops running as root, issues Let's Encrypt certificates through your DNS provider, keeps its code repository safe through git outages, and takes the name SATOM.
docs.x: Released: 2026-07-27 · All releases

This release changes SATOM's security model: the application no longer runs with administrator (root) rights. It also adds: automatic Let's Encrypt certificates through your DNS provider, with a renewal history backups of the code repository that survive a git server outage a preflight check in the installer the real interfaces of each device on the fleet map The product takes its name: SATOM — System Automation & Task Orchestration Manager . Existing installations must run a migration. See Before you upgrade .

Let's Encrypt (ACME) certificates through your DNS provider. A catalog of 30 DNS providers comes ready to use, and you can edit it. The credentials for each provider are stored encrypted. The process that requests certificates gets only what it needs and never sees SATOM's other secrets. Renewal history and a Renewals page. Every renewal attempt is recorded with its result and any error text, for each node. A failed renewal now raises its own alert, instead of showing up only later as an expiry warning.

Repository bundles in four places. Full copies of the code repository are kept on the node, on the standby, on the external backup server, and as a download. Updates never discard unsaved work. Before an update overwrites the local code, any changes not yet sent to the main repository are set aside. If that is not possible, the update stops. A new alert warns when changes have been waiting to be sent for too long, based on the age of the oldest one.

The installer has a preflight mode that checks everything before it changes anything, and reports all problems at once: write access the service manager and the package manager Python 3.10 or later disk and memory an existing installation ports already in use the clock outbound access

docs.h: Real interfaces on the fleet map
docs.x: A device card on the fleet map now shows the interfaces harvested from the device. MAC addresses are fetched when you ask, over a read-only connection. Each port gets a role badge based on the cached configuration.

The product is now SATOM — System Automation & Task Orchestration Manager . The Fortinet product names (FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer) are unchanged, because SATOM manages those appliances and has to name them.

SATOM no longer runs as root. The web application, scheduler, reconciler, alerts, certificate renewal, git publishing and HA sync all run under an unprivileged service account. Only the update process keeps administrator rights, by design: it installs services and libraries and restarts SATOM. The account setting is kept separately from each service definition, so updates do not quietly put services back under root. Administrator rights are limited to two commands: testing and reloading the web server configuration. Wider rights were refused on purpose: permission to install any package is the

The scheduler and git publishing stopped working after SATOM dropped its administrator rights. No scheduled action ran. Git publishing failed while still reporting success, so the git copy of the device configurations stopped being updated. Both work again, and git publishing now reports its failures. Installing from an offline bundle on a minimal system passed the preflight but then failed partway, after the service account had already been created. The bundles now include the missing system tools for administrator rights and remote login. Seven known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries

Run the de-privilege migration on every existing installation, one node at a time, standby first . It needs root and ships with this release. It keeps rollback material so you can return to the previous setup.

The device API proxy now also refuses to connect to the local machine, which closes a way to reach internal services through it. An internal AI-assisted security review produced 14 findings. One was real and is fixed. The other 13 were checked and found to be false alarms or out of date.

docs.k: release 1.0 what's new changelog
docs.s: The first production release, with DNS record management, an alert engine, certificate auto-renewal, configuration drift detection, safer restores and a Linux installer.
docs.x: Released: 2026-07-14 · All releases

The first production release. It adds: DNS record management an alert engine with email delivery automatic certificate renewal detection of configuration drift health snapshots around upgrades and restores a safer, gated way to restore a device's configuration It is also the first release with a Linux installer and offline bundles.
The DNS & LB lookup tool has a new +DNS Records section. You can create, view, edit and delete DNS records there. The records live in your IPAM system: EfficientIP SOLIDserver, phpIPAM or NetBox.

SATOM sends alerts in the console and by email for four situations: certificates about to expire the git copy of the configurations drifting from the main repository devices that cannot be reached backups that are out of date Administrators set the thresholds.
A nightly renewal job can either only alert (the default) or automatically fetch the renewed certificate from the edge.

SATOM compares each device's configuration with the copy in the configuration source of truth (kept in git) and reports differences. Values that change on their own all the time are ignored, so you see real changes only.

Health snapshots are taken before and after an upgrade or restore, so you can compare them. Gated restores. Restoring a device's configuration is first tried as a small test and goes ahead only if it passes.
The list of firmware images is rebuilt automatically whenever you upload, pull or delete an image.
A Linux installer, with offline bundles for Debian and RHEL. Support for the common package managers. A public website. Published release packages.
Upgrade event times are now shown in your local time instead of UTC.
